sparks.why: Passing on useful information is a low-cost way to invest in a relationship, which is why practical content circulates in professional networks even when it is obviously branded.
sparks.apply: Write one piece of content so specifically useful that a customer could send it to a colleague with no explanation attached at all.

sparks.hook: Wrap the message in a story, or people keep the story and drop you.
sparks.insight: Stories are how information travels between people, so a fact that lives inside a good story gets carried further than one that does not. But there is a catch most campaigns ignore: the story must not work without the product. If the amusing part can be retold with your brand removed, it will be, and you will have paid for entertainment that carries no message at all. The brand has to be load-bearing in the plot, not decoration around the edge of it.
sparks.why: Retelling strips out anything not needed for the story to make sense. That is the mechanism behind memorable adverts nobody can attribute, a well-documented and very expensive failure mode.
sparks.apply: Tell your story to someone and have them retell it a day later. If your product falls out of their version, the story is built wrong.

carousel.title: Find the real detail
carousel.body: Start from something true and specific about how the product came to be, or what it did for someone. Invented drama is easy to spot and expensive when caught.

carousel.title: Make the brand structural
carousel.body: Build the plot so the product causes the interesting turn. If the anecdote still works without you, the retelling will quietly delete you from it.

carousel.title: Cut to retellable length
carousel.body: A story that survives passing between people is short enough to tell in under a minute and contains one surprise, not four competing ones.

carousel.title: Test the retelling
carousel.body: Have someone repeat it a day later without prompting. Whatever they drop is the part you should not have paid to produce.

sparks.hook: Telling people that most others do the wrong thing makes it worse.
sparks.insight: Campaigns often warn that a large share of people behave badly — littering, wasting energy, missing appointments — in the hope of shaming them. It backfires, because the message actually received is that this behaviour is normal, and people follow what appears normal. The effective version says the opposite: name the majority who already do the right thing, and make that majority visible. Social proof works in whichever direction you point it, including the one you did not intend.
sparks.why: Cialdini and colleagues showed this reversal in field studies of littering and hotel towel reuse, and the effect has been repeated in energy-use interventions. It is one of the more reliable findings in this area.
sparks.apply: Check your messaging for any statistic about how many people do the wrong thing, and replace it with the number who already do the right one.

sparks.hook: Most viral hits were not planned, and the planned ones are the exception.
sparks.insight: The honest version of this field is that variance dominates. Content features shift the odds, sometimes substantially, but the distribution of outcomes is extremely skewed and much of what determines a hit is timing, seeding and luck you cannot buy. The productive use of a framework like this is not to manufacture a phenomenon. It is to stop shipping things that had no chance — the messages with no trigger, no feeling, no social payoff and no story.
sparks.why: Studies of information cascades find that repeated runs of the same content produce wildly different outcomes, which limits predictability. Design raises the floor far more reliably than it raises the ceiling.
sparks.apply: Judge your campaigns on the share of content that gets any organic passing on, not on whether one thing went unusually large.

sparks.hook: Word of mouth is mostly offline, and most of it is not about brands.
sparks.insight: The mental image of sharing is a screen, but the large majority of recommendations still happen in person — a comment at work, an answer to a question, a remark in a car. Offline conversation is slower, less measurable and considerably more persuasive, because it comes with a face attached. Building for spread therefore means giving people something easy to say out loud, not only something easy to click, and accepting that the most valuable channel is the one you cannot instrument.
sparks.why: Survey work consistently finds most brand conversation happens face to face rather than online. Measurable channels attract the budget precisely because they are measurable, not because they carry more influence.
sparks.apply: Write the one sentence you want a customer to say out loud about you, and check it is short enough to survive being spoken in a busy room.

actions: Score your next three pieces of marketing against the six sharing properties and refuse to ship anything that scores below two of them.
Identify one thing your customers encounter every day and deliberately attach your message to it so that the environment does the reminding.
Replace every statistic in your communications about how many people do the wrong thing with one about the majority already doing the right thing.
Tell your brand story to a colleague, ask them to retell it a day later, and rewrite it if your product disappears from their version.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a repeatable formula for guaranteed virality, or you distrust popular-psychology framings built on correlational studies and selected case examples.

verification.notes: Published 2013 by Simon & Schuster. The six-factor framework synthesises existing social psychology with Berger's own studies; findings are largely correlational and virality remains heavily luck-driven. All prose here is original.

books.title: Crossing the Chasm
books.subtitle: Marketing and Selling High-Tech Products to Mainstream Customers
books.author: Geoffrey A. Moore
books.why_it_matters: It explained why promising technology companies stall right after their first burst of success, and gave them a specific remedy rather than a diagnosis. Three decades on it remains the standard reference for taking a new product from enthusiasts to a real market.

crux.headline: Early enthusiasm does not become mainstream demand
crux.body: The people who buy something new first do it because it is new, and they will tolerate rough edges to get an advantage. The mainstream buys for the opposite reason: to avoid risk and to keep working. Nothing carries you from one group to the other automatically. The way across is to abandon breadth, pick one narrow group with an urgent problem, and become the obvious complete answer for exactly them.

sparks.hook: Your first customers bought because it was new. Nobody else will.
sparks.insight: Early adopters are drawn to a product precisely because it is unproven, since being early is how they get an advantage over their peers. That makes their enthusiasm a poor signal for everyone who comes after. The pragmatic majority want the opposite: proof that other people like them already use it without incident. So the qualities that won your first wave, novelty and ambition, are the exact qualities that make the next wave hesitate. Growth stalls not because the product got worse but because the buyer changed.
sparks.why: The two groups have opposite risk preferences, which is why testimonials from enthusiasts do not persuade pragmatists. A pragmatist reads an enthusiast's endorsement as evidence the product is still experimental.
sparks.apply: Look at your last ten customers and mark which bought for advantage and which bought to avoid risk. The mix tells you which side of the gap you are on.

sparks.hook: The pragmatist's first question is who else already uses this.
sparks.insight: Mainstream buyers reduce risk by copying other people in their own situation. Not any customer, and not a famous logo from a different industry: someone recognisably like them, with the same constraints, who has already done this successfully. That makes references the currency of the whole transition. It also explains the trap of scattered early wins across many industries, which produces a list of customers where no single buyer can find anybody similar to themselves.
sparks.why: Reference-seeking is rational behaviour when a purchase carries career risk. The practical implication is that ten customers inside one industry are worth far more than fifty spread across ten.
sparks.apply: Count how many of your customers sit in one industry with one job title. If the largest cluster is under five, stop selling broadly and concentrate.

sparks.hook: Attack one narrow segment as if you had no other option.
sparks.insight: The way across is not gradual expansion but concentration. Pick one specific group with a problem urgent enough that they are already spending money or losing money on it, and aim everything at them: the product roadmap, the sales effort, the partners, the case studies. The segment should be small enough that you can plausibly become the standard choice within it, because a dominant position in a small pond generates the references and word of mouth that carry you into the next one.
sparks.why: The logic is that word of mouth travels inside communities, not between them. Dominating a small connected group creates compounding referrals, while spreading thin creates none at all.
sparks.apply: Name one segment, defined by industry and role, that you could plausibly dominate this year, and decline the next deal that falls outside it.

carousel.title: Find urgent pain
carousel.body: Look for a problem the segment is already losing money on. Convenience will not persuade a risk-averse buyer to adopt something unproven; only an expensive, visible problem will.

carousel.title: Make it small enough
carousel.body: Choose a group you could realistically become the default choice for within twelve months. If it is too large to dominate, it is too large to start with.

carousel.title: Check it is connected
carousel.body: The members must talk to each other through conferences, associations or shared suppliers. Referrals cannot travel through a group whose members never meet.

carousel.title: Say no to everything else
carousel.body: Turning away good deals outside the segment is the hardest part and the whole mechanism. Every exception dilutes the focus that makes dominance possible.

sparks.hook: Nobody buys your product. They buy the whole solution to their problem.
sparks.insight: What you sell is only part of what a customer needs to get the outcome they want. There is also the integration, the training, the data migration, the compatible hardware, the consultants who know how to run it. Enthusiasts will assemble that themselves and enjoy doing so. Mainstream buyers will not, and a gap anywhere in the chain stops the purchase entirely. So the job is to define everything required for a customer in your chosen segment to succeed, then supply or arrange all of it, whether or not you build it.
sparks.why: This reframes the roadmap from features to completeness. It also explains why narrowing the segment is essential, since assembling everything needed is only affordable for one group at a time.
sparks.apply: Write every step a customer must complete to get value from you. Circle the ones you do not currently supply and find a partner for the biggest.

sparks.hook: Buyers do not want to be first. They want to be seventh.
sparks.insight: The mainstream buyer's calculation is dominated by what happens if this goes wrong, because the personal cost of a failed project exceeds the personal reward of a successful one. Being early offers upside they do not particularly want and risk they very much do not. Understanding this changes how you sell: emphasising innovation makes things worse, while emphasising that this is now the normal choice among their peers makes things better. You are not selling excitement to this group. You are selling the absence of career risk.
sparks.why: The asymmetry between the punishment for a visible failure and the reward for a quiet success is real in most organisations, and it makes conservative buying behaviour perfectly rational.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your main sales page so the first thing a cautious buyer sees is who already uses it, not what is new about it.

sparks.hook: Position yourself against an alternative, not against a description.
sparks.insight: Buyers cannot evaluate something with no reference point, so a product described only in its own terms gets filed under interesting and then forgotten. Positioning works by naming the thing you replace and the specific way you differ from it. That means choosing a competitive alternative deliberately, which is uncomfortable because it appears to shrink your ambition. It does the opposite: it gives the buyer a budget line to take the money from and a comparison their colleagues will already understand.
sparks.why: Comparison is how people assign value, and if you do not choose the comparison the buyer will pick one for you, usually the least flattering available.
sparks.apply: Write one sentence naming what you replace and the single dimension on which you are clearly better, then test it on someone outside your company.

sparks.hook: You cannot cross this in stages. It is a jump or nothing.
sparks.insight: The temptation is to hedge: keep serving the early enthusiasts while gradually courting the mainstream, keep the broad market message while adding some segment-specific material. That produces a product that is not focused enough for anyone and a sales effort spread across incompatible buyers. The transition requires committing the company to one segment with enough resource that dominance is achievable, and accepting the revenue you lose in the meantime. Half a crossing lands you at the bottom of the gap with less money than you started with.
sparks.why: The all-or-nothing framing is the most criticised part of the argument, and in practice many companies do transition gradually. It holds best where the whole product requirement is heavy and resources are scarce.
sparks.apply: Decide what share of engineering and sales capacity goes to your chosen segment. If it is under seventy percent, you have not actually committed.

sparks.hook: The people who won your first customers may not be able to win the next ones.
sparks.insight: Selling to enthusiasts rewards technical depth, improvisation and comfort with an unfinished product. Selling to the mainstream rewards process, references and reassurance. These are different skills and often different people, and the shift is one of the more painful parts of the transition because it can mean changing a team that has just succeeded. The same applies to the product organisation, where the emphasis moves from adding capability to removing rough edges nobody had complained about because early users worked around them.
sparks.why: The change is structural rather than a question of effort. A team optimised for one kind of buyer will keep producing what that buyer wanted, because that is what their instincts and their incentives reward.
sparks.apply: Audit whether your sales conversations lead with capability or with reassurance. If the wrong one dominates, change the script before changing the team.

carousel.title: Change the pitch
carousel.body: Lead with the problem and the proof rather than with the technology. A pragmatist stops listening once a conversation becomes a description of how clever the system is.

carousel.title: Build the reference set
carousel.body: Treat every early win in your segment as an asset to be documented properly. A named customer with a number attached is worth more than a new feature.

carousel.title: Industrialise delivery
carousel.body: Replace bespoke implementations with a repeatable process. Mainstream buyers are paying for predictability, and heroic custom work cannot be sold twice.

carousel.title: Fix the boring gaps
carousel.body: Documentation, onboarding, support hours, billing. Early users tolerated all of it. The next group will abandon the purchase over any one of them.

sparks.hook: The adoption curve was borrowed, and the gap in it was the new part.
sparks.insight: The underlying model of how new things spread through a population came from earlier research on the diffusion of innovations, which described adopters ranging from the venturesome few to the reluctant last. The contribution here was to argue that the transition between two of those groups is not smooth but a genuine discontinuity, because the two groups buy for incompatible reasons. Knowing which part is borrowed and which is the argument helps you judge how much weight each deserves.
sparks.why: The diffusion research is decades of empirical work across many fields. The claim of a specific discontinuity is an interpretation built on top of it, supported by cases rather than by systematic testing.
sparks.apply: Before applying the model, check whether your buyers genuinely fall into groups with different motives, or whether they are one population buying for one reason.

sparks.hook: The model was built for expensive sales, and much software no longer sells that way.
sparks.insight: The book assumes a purchase decided by a committee, carrying career risk and requiring a salesperson. A great deal of software now enters organisations from the bottom: an individual signs up, uses it, and the company formalises it later. That route inverts several conclusions, since the individual user faces little risk and needs no references. The framework still applies where the purchase is large, regulated or disruptive to operations. Check which world you are in before adopting the remedy.
sparks.why: Adoption mechanics changed with cheap distribution and self-service pricing. The underlying insight about differing buyer motives survives; the specific prescription about beachheads and heavy whole products does not always.
sparks.apply: Ask whether one person can adopt your product without permission. If they can, invest in the individual user experience before building a segment strategy.

actions: Cluster your existing customers by industry and job title, and identify the largest group that could plausibly be dominated within a year.
Map every step a customer must complete before they get value from you, then find a partner to close the largest gap you do not fill yourself.
Rewrite your main sales message to lead with proof from similar buyers rather than with what is new about your technology.
Decide what share of engineering and sales capacity is committed to your chosen segment, and write down the deals you will now turn away.
books.not_for_you_if: You sell a low-cost self-service product that individuals adopt without approval, or you want quantitative evidence rather than a well-argued model.

verification.notes: First published 1991 by HarperBusiness, revised several times since. The adoption curve derives from earlier diffusion of innovations research; the discontinuity claim is the book's own argument. All prose here is original.

books.title: Good Strategy Bad Strategy
books.subtitle: The Difference and Why It Matters
books.author: Richard P. Rumelt
books.why_it_matters: By 2011 the word strategy had drifted into meaning ambition with a deadline attached. Rumelt handed managers a test they can run inside a single meeting: does this document diagnose anything, or is it a wish list wearing a suit?

crux.headline: Strategy is a diagnosis, not a wish list
crux.body: A working strategy has three connected parts. You name the crux of the problem honestly. You choose a general approach for dealing with that specific problem. You commit resources to actions that fit together and reinforce each other. Anything missing one of the three is not a strategy, however impressive the deck. Most corporate plans skip the first part, because naming the real obstacle means admitting something uncomfortable about your own company in front of the people who caused it.

sparks.hook: Bad strategy is not an absence of strategy. It is an expensive presence.
sparks.insight: Plans that fail were rarely unplanned. They tend to be assembled from four recognisable materials, each of which takes real effort to produce. That is why bad strategy survives review after review: it looks like work, it flatters everyone in the room, and nobody has to say out loud what the company is bad at. Learning to spot the four materials is faster and more useful than learning to write a good plan, because you can apply the test to documents that already exist and see immediately which part of the thinking was skipped.
sparks.why: Turning a vague unease into four named failure modes makes the problem addressable. You can hold a plan against the list in ten minutes and say precisely which piece is missing rather than complaining that it feels thin.
sparks.apply: Take your team's current plan and mark every sentence that names a specific obstacle. If you mark fewer than two, you are holding a wish list.

carousel.title: Hunt for empty language
carousel.body: Abstract nouns stacked into sentences that would survive being pasted into any competitor's plan. If swapping your company name for a rival's changes nothing, the words carry no decision.

carousel.title: Check the obstacle is named
carousel.body: A plan that never states what is standing in the way has not chosen anything. Ambiguity here is usually political rather than analytical: someone would be embarrassed by the honest sentence.

carousel.title: Separate goals from choices
carousel.body: Targets say what will be measured. They do not say what anyone does differently on Monday. A number with a date on it is an aspiration that still needs a strategy underneath it.

carousel.title: Test the objectives connect
carousel.body: Objectives should be reachable steps that follow from the approach. A long list of unrelated priorities usually means the leadership team wrote down everything rather than deciding between things.

sparks.hook: Every strategy worth the name has the same three moving parts.
sparks.insight: Strip away the vision statement and the five-year projections and a real strategy has a small hard centre. First, an explanation of what is actually going on and why it is difficult. Then a general approach chosen to deal with that difficulty. Then a set of specific, funded, coordinated actions. The three have to connect. If the actions do not follow from the approach, or the approach does not answer the diagnosis, you are looking at decoration. The centre is deliberately small, because it is the part you can argue about and the part you can be wrong about.
sparks.why: Most planning processes produce volume instead of a centre. Forcing the argument onto one page exposes whether anyone has actually made a choice, since a real choice always rules something out.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your current plan on one page under three headings: what is going on, how we will deal with it, what we will actually do. Notice which heading you cannot fill.

carousel.title: Diagnose the situation
carousel.body: Say what is going on in a way that simplifies a messy reality into something you can act on. A good diagnosis discards most of the facts and keeps the few that decide the outcome.

carousel.title: Choose a guiding approach
carousel.body: One overall method for dealing with the diagnosed obstacle. It rules out whole categories of action, which is what makes it useful and what makes it uncomfortable to sign off.

carousel.title: Commit to coherent action
carousel.body: Specific moves with money and people behind them, arranged so each one makes the others work better. Actions that merely coexist are a budget; actions that reinforce are a strategy.

sparks.hook: Doubling revenue is not a strategy. It is a description of what you want.
sparks.insight: Leaders regularly confuse setting a target with deciding how. The target tells people what will be measured; it says nothing about what anyone should do differently. Strategy is the missing half: given a real obstacle and limited resources, what do we do, and what do we therefore stop doing? The give-away is a plan where every function has a number and nobody has a constraint. If the leadership team could sign the same document while pursuing completely opposite activities, no strategic work has been done.
sparks.why: Targets feel like decisions because they are hard to say out loud and can be missed. But the difficulty is emotional, not analytical, and organisations quietly notice when demands arrive without direction.
sparks.apply: For each number in your annual plan, write the sentence that begins 'to hit this we will stop'. Any number without a matching sentence is unfunded ambition.

sparks.hook: Rename the problem and the answer changes with it.
sparks.insight: A diagnosis is a choice, not a description. Call a sales decline a motivation problem and you get a new incentive scheme. Call the same decline a product that stopped being different and you get a roadmap. Neither label is objectively true at the moment you pick it, and the one you settle on silently decides which options anyone will even consider. That makes diagnosis the highest-stakes step in the whole process, and the one most teams rush through on their way to the action list.
sparks.why: Diagnosis works by analogy: you decide what kind of situation this is, and the reference case supplies your default moves. Choosing a bad analogy fails quietly, because everything downstream still looks rigorous.
sparks.apply: Write three competing one-sentence diagnoses of your biggest business problem, then list what each would commit you to. Argue about the sentences before arguing about the plan.

sparks.hook: Pick the next objective your organisation can actually reach.
sparks.insight: Ambition arrives as a fog: become the leader, transform the business, win the market. None of that can be worked on directly. The skill of a strategist is converting an overwhelming aim into a target close enough that the organisation can see it and hit it, which then makes the next target reachable. This is not lowering ambition. It is recognising that solvable problems are created, not found, and that a leader who hands down an unsolvable objective has passed the hard part of the job downwards.
sparks.why: Difficulty is relative to accumulated capability. Objectives that looked impossible become routine once the groundwork exists, so sequencing decides feasibility as much as ambition or resources do.
sparks.apply: Take your most ambitious goal and name the single nearest objective that would make it obviously easier. Fund that one this quarter and shelve the rest.

sparks.hook: Strength applied at one point beats the same strength spread evenly.
sparks.insight: Resources spread across every opportunity produce no effect anywhere, because most competitive situations have a threshold below which effort does nothing. Leverage comes from finding a point where a small push produces an outsized result, usually because something is already unstable there: a shift buyers have noticed but rivals have not priced, a rival committed to a position they cannot abandon, a capability of yours that suddenly matters more. Then you concentrate. The uncomfortable part is that concentration means deliberately underfunding things that are working.
sparks.why: Anticipation, a pivot point and concentration have to arrive together. Any one alone is common and useless; the combination is rare, which is why it produces returns at all.
sparks.apply: List where your budget goes, then move a visible chunk of it onto the single point where you think one extra push changes the outcome. Tell people why.

sparks.hook: Some systems are exactly as good as their worst part, and no better.
sparks.insight: In certain organisations every link in the chain has to work for anything to work at all, so improving a strong link changes nothing. Marketing gets better and sales stay flat, because the product is the binding constraint. These systems look permanently stuck and resist ordinary incremental improvement, which is exactly why they are hard for competitors to copy: catching up means fixing every link at once, and the interim period looks like money burned with nothing to show. Excellence in such a system is a fortress once you build it.
sparks.why: Where performance is limited by the weakest element, the return on improving anything else is zero until the weak link moves. That maths explains both the stagnation and the durability.
sparks.apply: Ask which single link, if fixed, would let the improvements you already made start showing up. Redirect effort there and pause the other initiatives.

sparks.hook: Your rival's biggest weakness is usually their own inability to change.
sparks.insight: Established competitors are far more predictable than they look, because their behaviour is governed by routines, culture and customer habits that are slow and expensive to alter. Forecasting what a rival will decide is nearly impossible; forecasting what they cannot bring themselves to do is often easy. The same force works on you. Left alone, organisations drift: focus blurs, product lines sprawl, standards slip, and a strategy that was sharp five years ago becomes a general-purpose business with no particular reason to exist.
sparks.why: Routine, culture and customer habit each change on a timescale of years. That inertia is why incumbents lose slowly and predictably rather than suddenly, and why maintaining focus is itself managerial work.
sparks.apply: Name one thing your main competitor structurally cannot do without hurting themselves. Build this year's plan around doing more of exactly that.

sparks.hook: Growth is the result of a strategy, not a replacement for one.
sparks.insight: Buying revenue is the easiest thing a large company can do and the most common substitute for thinking. Acquisitions produce a bigger reported number without answering why the combined business should be worth more than the parts, and the market usually charges you a premium for the privilege. Healthy growth is a by-product: you develop something people want, you get better at supplying it, and scale arrives as evidence that the underlying advantage was real. Growth chased directly tends to consume the advantage that made it possible.
sparks.why: Roll-ups have a long record of destroying value once integration costs and paid premiums are counted. The pattern repeats because size is visible to boards and advantage is not.
sparks.apply: Before any acquisition, write the sentence explaining why the two businesses are worth more together. If it needs more than two lines, walk away.

sparks.hook: A good strategy is a bet that could be proved wrong.
sparks.insight: A strategy is a hypothesis about how a piece of the world works: if we do this, that will happen, because of this mechanism. Treating it that way changes your behaviour. You look for the anomaly that does not fit the industry's shared story, because that gap is where an untaken opportunity usually sits. You state in advance what evidence would show you were mistaken. And you accept that a plan nobody could disagree with is a plan that predicts nothing, and therefore cannot be tested, corrected or defended.
sparks.why: Framing strategy as a testable claim gives you an exit from sunk-cost thinking. If the mechanism is stated up front, failure produces information instead of blame.
sparks.apply: Write your strategy as an if-then sentence with a mechanism, then name the observation in the next six months that would tell you it is wrong.

actions: Take the most recent strategy document in your company and mark each paragraph as diagnosis, guiding approach, coherent action or filler. Share the marked-up version with your team.
Write a one-page kernel for your own area: the obstacle in one sentence, the approach in one sentence, and no more than three funded actions that reinforce each other.
Identify the single point of leverage where concentrating resources would change the outcome, then move real budget onto it and name what you are defunding to pay for it.
List three things your largest competitor cannot do without damaging their existing business, and test whether any of them is a viable position for you.
books.not_for_you_if: You want templates and checklists. This is an argument about thinking clearly, and it deliberately refuses to hand you a fill-in-the-blanks framework.

verification.notes: First published 2011 by Crown Business. All prose original; no wording, headings or examples are reproduced verbatim from the book.

books.title: Good to Great
books.subtitle: Why Some Companies Make the Leap and Others Don't
books.author: Jim Collins
books.why_it_matters: It set the template for evidence-driven business writing: find companies that beat the market for fifteen years, match them against near-identical rivals, and ask what differed. The method has been attacked hard since, but the questions it forced into boardrooms are still the right ones.

crux.headline: Greatness is a discipline, not a burst of brilliance
crux.body: Sustained outperformance did not come from a charismatic saviour, a bold acquisition or a clever slogan. It came from modest, stubborn leaders who put the right people in place before setting direction, faced the ugliest facts about their position without flinching, and then pushed relentlessly on the one narrow thing they could be best in the world at. No single push looked decisive from the outside. The accumulated weight of them was.

sparks.hook: The best chief executives were ones you would struggle to name.
sparks.insight: The leaders who presided over the largest sustained turnarounds were not the magazine-cover kind. They were awkward, self-effacing people who talked about the company rather than themselves, and who saved their ferocity for the work instead of the spotlight. The mix is the whole point: personal modesty sitting on top of an almost fanatical drive. Ambition was there, but it pointed at the institution rather than the individual. When results were good they credited luck and colleagues. When results were bad they looked in the mirror.
sparks.why: This is a correlation drawn from a small hand-picked sample, so treat it as a hypothesis rather than a law. It is still a useful corrective to the belief that rescue arrives in the form of a celebrity hire.
sparks.apply: In your next team review, name one failure and take the blame yourself before anyone else speaks. Then name one success and credit a specific person for it.

sparks.hook: Decide who is on the bus before you decide where it is going.
sparks.insight: Most plans start with a destination and then recruit people to reach it. The companies that made the leap did the reverse. They gathered an unusually capable, self-motivated group first, moved out the people who did not belong, and only then argued about direction. The logic holds up: a strong team can change course when the world changes, while a weak team executing a brilliant plan simply arrives late somewhere that no longer matters. Strategy is perishable. The people are the durable asset.
sparks.why: It reframes hiring from a support function into the strategy itself. The catch is that it only works if you act quickly on people who do not fit, which is the part almost every manager postpones.
sparks.apply: List everyone reporting to you and mark who you would enthusiastically hire again today. For anyone you would not, book the honest conversation inside two weeks.

carousel.title: Hire ahead of the plan
carousel.body: Recruit for judgement and drive rather than for a role on an org chart you have not finalised. If the person is genuinely excellent, the seat can be invented around them later.

carousel.title: Be rigorous, not ruthless
carousel.body: Rigorous means applying the same high standard to everyone, consistently, including yourself. Ruthless means cutting heads whenever the numbers wobble. The first builds trust, the second destroys it.

carousel.title: Put the best on the biggest chance
carousel.body: Most firms staff their strongest people onto their worst problems. Move at least one of them onto your largest opportunity instead, and accept that the problem may need to be sold or closed.

carousel.title: Stop waiting for improvement
carousel.body: If you are managing someone hard just to get ordinary output, you already know the answer. Delaying the conversation costs the rest of the team more than having it costs you.

sparks.hook: The optimists broke first. The survivors held two beliefs at once.
sparks.insight: The pairing is uncomfortable but necessary: unshakeable faith that you prevail in the end, held at the same time as a refusal to lie to yourself about how bad things are right now. Pure optimism collapses when each hoped-for deadline passes without rescue. Pure realism drains the will to keep working at all. Holding both is unpleasant, which is exactly why it is rare. The example that made the idea famous comes from a US officer held for years as a prisoner of war in Vietnam, who watched hope without honesty destroy the men around him.
sparks.why: This is one vivid anecdote, not evidence, and it has been retold so often that it now functions as folklore. The underlying tension between keeping morale up and keeping the books honest is real in any turnaround.
sparks.apply: Write two columns for your current project: the outcome you genuinely believe in, and the three facts you have been avoiding saying aloud. Then share the second column.

sparks.hook: Three questions, one small answer, and everything outside it gets cut.
sparks.insight: Focus is not picking what you are good at. It is locating the narrow overlap between three separate things: what you could genuinely become the best in the world at, what actually drives your economic engine, and what you and your people care about deeply. Any two without the third builds a business that works for a while and then stops. The overlap is usually far smaller and far less glamorous than the ambitions people bring to the exercise, and it tends to take years to see clearly rather than a weekend offsite.
sparks.why: The discipline lives in the subtraction. Naming the overlap is easy. Killing the profitable but off-strategy lines sitting outside it is the part that separates the companies that changed from the ones that talked about changing.
sparks.apply: Draw the three circles for your business or your career this week, then name one activity that falls outside the overlap and put a date on stopping it.

carousel.title: Test best in the world
carousel.body: Not what you are currently competent at, and not what you wish you were. Ask where you could plausibly become better than anyone else, and accept that the honest answer may be nowhere yet.

carousel.title: Find the economic engine
carousel.body: Identify the single ratio that moves profitability more than any other: profit per customer, per employee, per store, per visit. Knowing which one it is changes where every pound goes.

carousel.title: Check for real passion
carousel.body: Not manufactured enthusiasm from an away day. Ask what work your strongest people would still care about after a bad quarter, because that is what sustains years of unglamorous grinding.

carousel.title: Use it as a filter
carousel.body: The idea only pays off when it starts refusing things. Write a stop-doing list alongside your to-do list and treat the stop list as the more important of the two documents.

sparks.hook: There was never a single moment when the turnaround began.
sparks.insight: Insiders at the transformed companies were often baffled when asked to name the turning point. There was no launch event, no rousing speech, no decisive acquisition. What happened instead was a heavy wheel being pushed in a consistent direction, quarter after quarter, until momentum started doing the work that effort used to do. The outside world only noticed once the wheel was already spinning fast, and then wrote a story about a sudden breakthrough that nobody inside the company recognised.
sparks.why: This is a direct attack on how business media narrates change. It also explains why imported turnaround programmes fail: they supply the announcement without the years of consistent pushing in one direction.
sparks.apply: Name the two or three moves in your business that reinforce each other, then commit to repeating them for four straight quarters before judging whether they work.

sparks.hook: Charisma is a liability if it stops people telling you the truth.
sparks.insight: A leader whose opinion is obvious to the room gets a filtered version of reality, and filtered reality kills companies slowly. The fix is structural rather than personal. Lead with questions instead of answers, argue hard without assigning blame afterwards, and build a channel where inconvenient information reaches the top without being softened on the way up. The aim is not a nicer culture. It is an accurate one, because no amount of courage saves a decision that was made on a sanitised picture.
sparks.why: The mechanism is plain information economics. People withhold bad news when the expected cost of delivering it exceeds the expected benefit. Change that calculation and the news starts arriving early enough to act on.
sparks.apply: At your next meeting, state your own view last rather than first, and thank the person who contradicts you most loudly in front of everyone else.

carousel.title: Ask before you assert
carousel.body: Walk in with questions rather than conclusions. The moment the room knows what you think, you stop receiving information and start receiving agreement dressed up as analysis.

carousel.title: Argue, do not decree
carousel.body: Run real debate with the people who hold the facts, and let it get heated. A decision that has survived genuine argument is much harder to quietly sabotage afterwards.

carousel.title: Autopsy without blame
carousel.body: When something fails, dissect it in public and forbid naming a culprit. Blame teaches people to hide the next failure until it has become expensive to fix.

carousel.title: Build a truth channel
carousel.body: Create one route by which frontline reality reaches you unedited: skip-level sessions, raw complaint logs, a standing agenda item nobody is allowed to summarise for you.

sparks.hook: Technology never made a company great. It magnified what was already there.
sparks.insight: The transformed companies were often early and aggressive adopters, but never for the sake of being modern. They asked one question first: does this fit the narrow thing we have decided to be best at? If yes, they invested hard and early. If no, they ignored it however loudly the market insisted otherwise. Technology behaves like an amplifier bolted onto an existing engine. Attach it to a good engine and you travel faster. Attach it to a bad one and you reach the wall sooner.
sparks.why: Written before smartphones and cloud computing, the claim is less safe than it was. For some incumbents a platform shift genuinely rewrote the economics rather than amplifying them. The filter question survives even so.
sparks.apply: Before approving the next tool or platform, write one sentence explaining how it strengthens the specific advantage you already have. If you cannot write it, decline.

sparks.hook: Bureaucracy exists to compensate for having hired the wrong people.
sparks.insight: Rules multiply in proportion to how much managing your people need. The alternative is to hire people who arrive with their own discipline and then give them a great deal of freedom inside a very tight frame. What makes it work is that the frame really is narrow: everyone knows exactly what the company is and is not doing, so autonomy never turns into drift. Most organisations get the ratio backwards, offering a vague strategy with tight process control, then wondering why their strongest people leave.
sparks.why: The trade-off is real and rarely admitted. This only works at hiring standards most firms will not hold, and it fails badly in settings where process exists for safety rather than for control.
sparks.apply: Find one approval step your team resents. Remove it for a quarter and replace it with a written principle people can apply for themselves.

sparks.hook: Companies on the great list later went bankrupt or needed a bailout.
sparks.insight: The list has not aged kindly. An electronics retailer on it liquidated within a decade. A mortgage giant on it had to be taken into government conservatorship during the financial crisis. A bank on it later became a byword for sales-target scandals. The deeper problem is not luck but method: the companies were selected because they had already outperformed, then examined for shared traits. Do that and you will always find traits, including ones that also show up in the firms that collapsed.
sparks.why: Choosing cases on the outcome and then reasoning backwards cannot establish cause. Critics have also shown that judgements about a company's culture tend to follow its share price rather than predict it.
sparks.apply: Whenever you read a business success study, ask what the failed companies did. If nobody looked, downgrade the conclusion from a finding to a hypothesis worth testing.

sparks.hook: The main obstacle to a great business is a perfectly acceptable one.
sparks.insight: Nothing forces change on an organisation that is doing fine. Adequate results fund adequate habits, and the absence of crisis removes the only pressure most companies reliably respond to. That is why the majority of decent businesses stay decent forever. Escaping means manufacturing the discomfort that reality is not supplying: setting a standard your current setup cannot meet, and being willing to stop activities that are profitable but merely fine. The real choice is rarely between good and bad. It is between good and something harder.
sparks.why: Comfortable performance is a genuine trap because it removes urgency while consuming the resources a change would need. The honest counterpoint is that plenty of businesses should simply stay good and stop reaching.
sparks.apply: Write a stop-doing list of three activities that make money but sit off strategy, and take the smallest one to your board this month.

actions: Run a two-hour session that answers the three focus questions honestly, and close it by naming one profitable activity you will stop doing this year.
Grade every direct report against the test of whether you would hire them again today, and schedule the difficult conversations before you touch the strategy deck.
Write the two or three reinforcing moves that make up your flywheel on a single page, and commit publicly to running them unchanged for four quarters.
Read a serious critique of the study's method next to the book, then re-read your own strategy documents hunting for the same backwards reasoning from outcomes to causes.
books.not_for_you_if: You want statistically defensible causal claims, or you run a small business and get little from a sample of large American corporations.

verification.notes: Published 2001 by HarperBusiness. Several featured companies later failed or were rescued, and the research design has been widely criticised for selecting cases on the outcome. All prose here is original.

books.title: High Output Management
books.author: Andrew S. Grove
books.why_it_matters: It treats management as a production process with measurable output rather than a personality trait, and it has aged better than almost any book of its era. Much of what technology companies call modern management is a direct descendant.

crux.headline: Your output is what your team produces, not what you do
crux.body: A manager produces nothing personally. What counts is everything their organisation delivers, plus everything they cause neighbouring organisations to deliver. That single definition reorganises the whole job. Time spent answering email is worth what it changes downstream; time spent training ten people pays back for years; a decision delayed by a week costs the whole team a week. Rank every activity by how many people's output it moves, and spend your hours accordingly.

sparks.hook: A manager's output is measured in other people's work.
sparks.insight: Individual contributors are judged by what they make. Managers are judged by what their group makes, plus what other groups make because of their influence, and by nothing else. That definition is uncomfortable because it means a productive-feeling day of personal work can be worthless, while an hour that unblocks six people is enormously valuable even though you produced no artefact. It also means influence outside your reporting line counts fully: advice, standards and information that improve another team's output belong in your total.
sparks.why: Defining output at the level of the organisation makes managerial time comparable to other investments. It is the only definition under which prioritising your calendar becomes a solvable problem.
sparks.apply: Review last week's calendar and write beside each block how many people's work it changed. Cut the ones where the answer was zero.

sparks.hook: Rank your hours by how many people's work each one moves.
sparks.insight: If output is what the organisation produces, then a manager's central skill is choosing activities with high leverage: things that affect many people, that affect them over a long period, or that shift a critical decision at the moment it is still cheap to shift. Approving a plan early has enormous leverage. Reviewing the same plan after three months of work has almost none, and worse, negative leverage arrives too: a leader's visible indecision or bad mood multiplies across everyone who has to work around it.
sparks.why: Leverage explains why some managers with the same hours produce far more than others. It also explains why interruption and delay are so costly at senior levels, where the multiplier is largest.
sparks.apply: Identify one recurring decision you make late in a process and move it two weeks earlier. Measure the rework it prevents.

sparks.hook: Catch the mistake at the cheapest possible stage. It never gets cheaper.
sparks.insight: Any production process, whether it makes chips or software or contracts, has a rule: the cost of fixing a problem rises sharply at each stage the problem survives. Rejecting a faulty component before it enters the line costs almost nothing; discovering the same fault in a finished product costs a rebuild plus a customer. So the discipline is to place your inspection early, and to be willing to stop and fix rather than push a known problem forward because a deadline is close. Pushing it forward is always more expensive than it looks.
sparks.why: The cost multiplier is structural: each stage adds value that gets destroyed when the underlying fault surfaces. This is the same logic behind reviewing designs before building and testing before shipping.
sparks.apply: Add one checkpoint at the earliest stage of your team's process where a serious error could still be caught for free, and give someone authority to stop.

sparks.hook: Measure anything alone and you will get exactly that, and nothing else.
sparks.insight: Every indicator invites people to optimise it at the expense of something you did not measure. Count tickets closed and quality falls. Count lines shipped and complexity grows. The correction is to pair each measure with its natural opposite: volume with quality, speed with error rate, cost with customer satisfaction. Watching the pair together tells you something a single number cannot, and it removes the incentive to win on one dimension by quietly sacrificing another that nobody is looking at.
sparks.why: Any single measure is a partial description of the work, and the gap between the measure and the actual goal is where gaming happens. Pairing closes the most obvious gaps cheaply.
sparks.apply: For every metric on your team dashboard, add its counterweight this week. Delete any metric whose counterweight you cannot name.

sparks.hook: Meetings are not what stops managerial work. They are the work.
sparks.insight: Complaining about meetings treats them as an interruption to the real job, when for a manager they are the medium through which the job happens: information moves, decisions get made, standards get set. The useful distinction is between meetings that run continuously to keep information flowing and meetings called to reach one specific decision. The first kind should be scheduled, predictable and disciplined. The second should have a named decision, a named decider, and no attendees who are not required to make it.
sparks.why: Framing meetings as the medium rather than the obstacle changes the question from how to have fewer to how to run each type correctly, which is where the actual waste is.
sparks.apply: Label every recurring meeting in your calendar as information-flow or decision, then give the decision ones a named owner and a stated question.

carousel.title: The private conversation
carousel.body: A recurring one-to-one where the report sets the agenda. Its purpose is teaching and surfacing problems early, which is the highest-leverage use of a manager's hour.

carousel.title: The team meeting
carousel.body: Peers together with the manager, handling matters that affect several people at once. It exists so information reaches everyone in the same version at the same time.

carousel.title: The wider review
carousel.body: Groups that do not normally meet present work and get questioned. Its real function is exposure: people learn how other parts of the business think about problems.

carousel.title: The decision meeting
carousel.body: Called for one specific question, with the smallest group that can answer it. It ends with a decision recorded and an owner, or it has failed regardless of how good the discussion was.

sparks.hook: Ninety minutes with one person can shape two weeks of their work.
sparks.insight: The recurring private conversation is the highest-leverage meeting available to a manager, and it should be long enough that the other person is willing to raise something difficult. It is not a status update; the useful material is the problem they have been sitting on, the customer they are worried about, the technical decision they are unsure of. The manager's job is mostly to ask one more question than feels necessary, because the first answer is usually the prepared one and the second is the real one.
sparks.why: This is a mutual teaching session and an early warning system. Problems raised here cost an hour; the same problems discovered in a project review cost weeks.
sparks.apply: Schedule weekly one-on-ones of at least forty-five minutes, ask your report to bring the agenda, and keep asking after their first answer.

sparks.hook: Disagree fully, decide clearly, then support it as if you had won.
sparks.insight: Good organisational decisions have a shape. Everyone with real knowledge argues openly, and rank does not settle technical questions. Then a clear decision is made and stated, by a named person, with a date. Then everyone supports it in public regardless of which side they took, because an organisation cannot execute a decision that half its members are still relitigating in corridors. Skipping the first stage produces resentment and hidden resistance. Skipping the second produces drift. Skipping the third produces politics.
sparks.why: Each stage fails differently and visibly. Most organisations are chronically weak at exactly one of the three, and naming which one is usually enough to start fixing it.
sparks.apply: At the end of your next contested meeting, state the decision, the owner and the date out loud, and ask everyone to commit to it publicly.

carousel.title: Open the argument properly
carousel.body: Get the people with direct knowledge into the room and make it safe for them to contradict senior people. Silence here is not agreement, it is information you failed to collect.

carousel.title: Name the decider in advance
carousel.body: Say before the debate who will decide and by when. Ambiguity about who owns the call is what turns a technical disagreement into a political one.

carousel.title: State the decision explicitly
carousel.body: Write down what was decided, who owns it and when it takes effect. A decision everyone thinks they understood differently is not a decision, it is a delay.

carousel.title: Require visible support
carousel.body: Ask people who disagreed to back the outcome in front of their teams. Private dissent after a decision costs more than the wrong choice usually does.

sparks.hook: There is no best management style. There is only the right one for this task.
sparks.insight: How closely you should supervise someone depends not on their general seniority but on how experienced they are at the specific task in front of them. A brilliant engineer running their first negotiation needs detailed direction; the same person writing code needs none. Managers get this wrong in both directions, either micromanaging veterans or leaving a capable newcomer to fail alone at something they have never done. When someone stumbles, the first question is not whether they are good, but whether the style you applied matched the task.
sparks.why: Task-relevant experience varies within a person, not just between people. Treating style as a fixed personal trait produces both over-management and abandonment, often on the same team in the same week.
sparks.apply: For each direct report, list their current tasks and rate their experience at each one. Adjust how closely you supervise task by task, not person by person.

sparks.hook: Someone is underperforming for one of two reasons. There is no third one.
sparks.insight: When someone is not doing their job, exactly two explanations exist: they cannot do it, or they do not want to. Everything else is a symptom of one of these. That is a blunt frame and a useful one, because the two have completely different remedies and managers routinely apply the wrong one. Motivational pressure applied to a capability gap produces anxiety and no improvement. Training applied to someone who has quietly stopped caring produces an expensive course and no change either.
sparks.why: The diagnosis is easy to test: could they do it if their life depended on it? A yes points to motivation, a no points to training, and the answer determines the entire response.
sparks.apply: For your weakest performer, answer the life-depends-on-it question honestly, then choose either a training plan or a motivation conversation, not both.

sparks.hook: Training your own people is your job, not a department's.
sparks.insight: Teaching people how to do their work is among the highest-leverage things a manager can do, because a few hours of preparation improves the output of everyone in the room for years. It is also the first thing dropped when the quarter gets busy, precisely because the return arrives late and never appears on this month's numbers. Outsourcing it entirely to a training function fails for a specific reason: the person who knows what good work looks like here, and whose standards actually apply, is the manager.
sparks.why: Leverage is the ratio of hours invested to output changed, and training has one of the best ratios available. The delay in payback is what makes it feel optional and what makes it get skipped.
sparks.apply: Pick one thing your team does inconsistently and prepare a one-hour session teaching it yourself. Run it within a fortnight.

sparks.hook: Rules, contracts or culture. Which one applies depends on the situation.
sparks.insight: Organisations coordinate behaviour in three ways. Where interests are aligned and the situation is simple, prices and self-interest handle it. Where the situation is more complex but interests still roughly align, written agreements and procedures work. Where things are highly uncertain and nobody can specify in advance what should happen, only shared values keep people acting sensibly. Trying to run a fast-changing, ambiguous situation on detailed procedure is the most common and most expensive mismatch, and it usually produces more procedure.
sparks.why: The right mode depends on how uncertain the environment is and how far individual and group interests diverge. Writing more rules for an ambiguous situation adds cost without adding coordination.
sparks.apply: Identify one area where your team keeps adding process without improving outcomes, and replace the next rule with a stated principle instead.

actions: Redefine your own job description in one line as the output of your organisation plus your influence on neighbouring ones, and share it with your team.
Audit two weeks of your calendar for leverage, then delete or delegate every recurring commitment that changes nobody's work but your own.
Set up weekly one-on-ones with an agenda owned by the other person, and treat them as the first thing protected when the schedule gets tight.
Pair every metric your team reports with a counterweight measure, and remove any number that has no honest counterweight.
books.not_for_you_if: You want warmth and stories. This is a precise, slightly cold operating manual written by an engineer, with examples drawn from 1980s manufacturing.

verification.notes: First published 1983 by Random House, with a revised edition in 1995. Grove was chief operating officer of Intel at the time of writing. All prose original.

books.title: Made to Stick
books.subtitle: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die
books.author: Chip Heath and Dan Heath
books.why_it_matters: It took the question of why some ideas stick and turned it into six concrete properties a writer or manager can check before speaking. It changed how a generation of executives, teachers and journalists structure a message.

crux.headline: Ideas stick when they are simple, concrete and human
crux.body: A memorable idea is rarely the most complete one. It is stripped to a single core claim, made unexpected enough to hold attention, described in things people can picture, backed by something credible they can check themselves, connected to a feeling about a person rather than a number, and delivered inside a story. None of that is talent. It is a checklist you can run on any message before you send it.

sparks.hook: The more you know, the worse you get at explaining it.
sparks.insight: Once you understand something deeply, you cannot easily reconstruct what it is like not to. Your explanations skip steps, lean on jargon that feels ordinary to you, and start in the middle. This is why experts consistently overestimate how clear they are being, and why the person who understands a subject best is often the worst person to introduce it. The remedy is not simplification for its own sake — it is deliberately rebuilding the path a newcomer has to walk.
sparks.why: In a well-known Stanford study, people tapping out familiar tunes on a table vastly overestimated how often listeners would identify them. Knowing the tune made silence feel like melody, which is exactly the trap.
sparks.apply: Explain your idea to someone outside your field and ask them to repeat it back. Rewrite every part they could not reproduce accurately.

sparks.hook: Six checks separate a message that sticks from one that evaporates.
sparks.insight: Sticky ideas share a pattern, and the pattern is testable before you speak. Is there one core claim rather than five? Does it break an expectation somewhere near the start? Can it be pictured, not merely understood? Would a sceptic have a way of checking it? Does it connect to a specific person or a value rather than a statistic? And is it carried in a story someone could retell? Most business communication fails all six and then calls the result a communication problem.
sparks.why: The framework is a synthesis of existing psychology of memory and persuasion rather than new research. Its value is as a pre-flight checklist, and its weakness is that it is easier to apply after the fact than before.
sparks.apply: Run your next important message through all six checks in writing before you deliver it, and fix the two weakest ones first.

carousel.title: Strip to one core
carousel.body: Decide the single thing that must survive if everything else is forgotten. Two priorities in one message reliably produce zero, because the listener does the choosing.

carousel.title: Break an expectation
carousel.body: Open a gap between what people assume and what is true, then close it. Surprise buys attention; curiosity is what keeps it after the surprise wears off.

carousel.title: Make it picturable
carousel.body: Replace abstractions with things a person can see, hold or count. Concrete language also stops two listeners walking away with two different meanings.

carousel.title: Let them verify
carousel.body: Give a detail a sceptic can test themselves rather than an authority to trust. Credibility a listener checks personally is far stickier than credibility you assert.

carousel.title: Aim at one person
carousel.body: Attach the idea to an individual or a value people already hold. Numbers describe the scale of a problem; a person is what makes anyone act on it.

sparks.hook: If everything in the message is important, nothing in it is.
sparks.insight: The instinct in any serious communication is to include everything relevant, because leaving things out feels like negligence. The listener experiences the opposite: a list of eight priorities is received as no priority at all, and they select whichever one suits them. Finding the core means deciding what you would keep if you could keep only one thing, which is genuinely painful because the discarded items are all true. The difficulty is the point — you are prioritising so the audience does not have to.
sparks.why: Attention and memory are heavily capacity-limited, so unranked information gets ranked by the listener according to their own interests, which is rarely the ranking you intended.
sparks.apply: Cut your next message to a single sentence someone would repeat, then rebuild only the support that particular sentence actually needs.

carousel.title: List everything true
carousel.body: Dump every point you could make. You cannot choose a core by starting from the important things, because everything looks important from the inside.

carousel.title: Force a single winner
carousel.body: Ask which one point, kept alone, would still change what the audience does. Two winners means you have not finished, and the audience will pick for you.

carousel.title: Say it in one line
carousel.body: Compress it to a sentence a listener could repeat accurately at lunch. If it needs a subordinate clause, it is probably still two ideas.

carousel.title: Rebuild around it
carousel.body: Keep only the support that sentence needs. Everything else goes in an appendix nobody reads, which is exactly where it belongs.

sparks.hook: Concrete beats abstract, and almost nothing in business is concrete.
sparks.insight: Words like alignment, value, synergy and quality feel precise to the person saying them and mean something different to everyone listening. Concrete language does not have this problem: a specific object, action or number lands the same way in every head in the room. It is also far easier to remember, because the mind stores images and events better than categories. Most corporate communication is abstract not because the subject is complicated but because abstraction is a safer place to be wrong.
sparks.why: Concrete words are recalled better than abstract ones, one of the more reliable findings in memory research. Concreteness also creates a common reference point, which stops a team quietly disagreeing while nodding.
sparks.apply: Underline every abstract noun in your next document and replace at least half of them with a specific object, action or example.

sparks.hook: Let people verify the claim themselves instead of citing an authority.
sparks.insight: Credibility is usually attempted by borrowing it — a consultant's name, an industry statistic, a familiar logo. The stronger form hands the listener a test they can run in their own head or in the next five minutes. Ask a question they can answer from their own experience, or give a detail specific enough that they can check whether it holds. A person who has verified something themselves believes it in a way that no amount of citation ever reproduces.
sparks.why: Self-generated evidence is more persuasive than received evidence because it comes with no suspicion of motive. It also converts a passive listener into someone actively working on your argument.
sparks.apply: Replace one borrowed statistic in your pitch with a question the listener can answer from their own experience in under a minute.

sparks.hook: One person moves people. A number about thousands does not.
sparks.insight: Human response to suffering does not scale with its size. A single identified individual with a name and a face produces strong feeling and action, while the same story presented as a large aggregate produces noticeably less. Adding statistics to the individual story tends to reduce the response rather than reinforce it. This is uncomfortable, but it is how attention works, and any message aimed at getting someone to act is either fighting it or using it.
sparks.why: The identifiable victim effect is well supported in experimental work, including studies where adding statistical information to an individual case reduced giving. It is a real limit on data-driven persuasion.
sparks.apply: Lead your next appeal with one named, specific person or case, and move the aggregate numbers to the end if you use them at all.

sparks.hook: Curiosity starts when someone notices a gap in what they know.
sparks.insight: People do not become interested because a subject is objectively important. They become interested when they notice a hole in their own understanding — a question they cannot answer, a fact that does not fit. That means the opening move is not stating what you will cover, but making the audience feel the absence of something. Once the gap is open, the information you provide is wanted rather than delivered, which is a completely different kind of reception.
sparks.why: Curiosity behaves like a response to a perceived deficit rather than a stable trait, an account developed by George Loewenstein and broadly supported since. Openings that summarise remove the gap before it can form.
sparks.apply: Rewrite the first thirty seconds of your next talk so it poses a question the audience cannot answer, instead of previewing your agenda.

sparks.hook: A story is the closest thing to a flight simulator for a situation.
sparks.insight: Hearing a well-told account of how someone handled a problem does two things a set of instructions cannot: it rehearses the situation mentally, and it supplies a reason to try. That is why the story of one branch that fixed a process spreads through a company while the policy memo about the same fix does not. Collecting and retelling real examples is usually more effective than writing better guidance, and it is considerably cheaper.
sparks.why: Mentally simulating a specific scenario improves later performance on related tasks. Stories also carry the social proof that someone comparable already did this, which plain instruction entirely lacks.
sparks.apply: Find one real example of the behaviour you want inside your organisation and retell it in every meeting for a month instead of restating the policy.

sparks.hook: Surprise gets attention. Only a mystery holds it.
sparks.insight: An unexpected opening works once. If you have nothing after the shock, attention drops back within seconds and you have spent your only card. What sustains interest is an unresolved question the audience wants closed — a puzzle, a contradiction, a promised answer you delay. The structure of a good briefing is closer to a detective story than to a summary: withhold the resolution long enough that people are still present when you finally give it.
sparks.why: Surprise is a brief orienting response, while sustained attention needs an open loop the listener wants closed. Most presentations do the reverse by putting the conclusion on the first slide.
sparks.apply: Take your most important slide deck and move the conclusion to the end, replacing the opening with the question that it answers.

sparks.hook: People decide by asking what someone like them would do here.
sparks.insight: Persuasion usually assumes a calculation: what do I gain, what does it cost. A large share of real decisions run on a different question — what kind of person am I, and what does someone like me do in a situation like this. Messages that appeal only to self-interest miss this entirely, which is why appeals to professional identity, group membership or role often outperform incentives. It also explains why paying people to do something can weaken their reason for doing it.
sparks.why: This draws on James March's account of decisions made by identity and role rather than pure consequence, and it fits evidence that financial incentives sometimes crowd out intrinsic motivation.
sparks.apply: Rewrite one request as a statement about what people in that role do, rather than what the person will get for doing it.

actions: Take your most important recurring message, cut it to one sentence a listener could repeat, and delete every supporting point that sentence does not need.
Explain your core idea to someone outside your field and rewrite every part they could not accurately repeat back to you afterwards.
Replace one borrowed statistic in your standard pitch with a detail or question the listener can verify from their own experience.
Collect three real stories from inside your organisation that show the behaviour you want, and retell those instead of restating the policy.
books.not_for_you_if: You already write clearly for a living, or you want original research rather than a well-organised synthesis of existing psychology dressed in business examples.

verification.notes: Published 2007 by Random House. It synthesises existing work on memory, curiosity and persuasion; the tapping experiment is Elizabeth Newton's Stanford research. All prose here is original.

books.title: Management
books.subtitle: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices
books.author: Peter F. Drucker
books.why_it_matters: It is the closest thing management has to a foundational text, assembling a scattered set of practices into a discipline with its own questions and responsibilities. Much of what business schools now teach as basic was first set out at length here.

crux.headline: A business exists to create a customer
crux.body: Profit is not the purpose of an enterprise but the test of whether it is working and the cost of staying in existence. The purpose sits outside the organisation, in someone who chooses to buy. That reversal drives everything else: only two functions actually produce results, which are marketing and innovation, and every other activity is a cost. It also makes the central question what the customer considers value, which is rarely what the company thinks it sells.

sparks.hook: Profit is not why a business exists. It is the cost of continuing to exist.
sparks.insight: Treating profit as the purpose gives you no guidance about what to actually do, and it misdescribes what profit is for. It covers the risks of being in business, funds the replacement of what wears out, and pays for whatever comes next. A business that fails to earn enough of it is destroying resources, so the requirement is real and non-negotiable. But the purpose lies outside the company, in creating someone willing to buy. Profit is how you know that purpose is being served, not the reason you were founded.
sparks.why: The distinction changes what you measure and what you optimise. A firm managed as if profit were the goal will reliably harvest its own future, since cutting investment always improves this year's number.
sparks.apply: Write what your business exists to do for someone outside it, then check whether your top three metrics measure that or only measure the money.

sparks.hook: The customer decides what your business is, and they rarely agree with you.
sparks.insight: Companies describe themselves by what they produce. Customers describe them by what problem gets solved, and the two descriptions can be startlingly different. A firm that thinks it sells equipment may in fact be selling uptime, and one that thinks it sells software may be selling the ability to fire a supplier. Since the customer's definition is the one that determines whether they buy, the useful exercise is to ask what they consider valuable and to accept the answer even when it makes your engineering achievements look irrelevant.
sparks.why: Getting the definition wrong misdirects investment for years, because the company keeps improving the thing it believes it sells rather than the thing being bought.
sparks.apply: Ask ten customers what they would lose if you disappeared tomorrow. If their answer differs from your product description, rewrite the description.

sparks.hook: Only two activities produce revenue. Everything else on the payroll is a cost.
sparks.insight: An enterprise gets results from finding out what people need and creating something that meets it, and from producing something genuinely new. Both point outward at the market. Every other function, however necessary, consumes resources rather than generating them. That is not an argument for cutting them, since a business without finance or operations collapses quickly. It is an argument for knowing which is which, because organisations drift towards spending their attention on internal activity, where the meetings are and where the politics are.
sparks.why: The framing is a useful corrective to internally focused management. It undersells the competitive advantage that operations can create, which several modern firms have built entire positions on.
sparks.apply: Count the hours your leadership team spent last month on internal matters versus on customers and new offerings, and rebalance the calendar.

sparks.hook: Answer what our business should be, not just what it is.
sparks.insight: Two questions have to be asked together and rarely are. What is our business, answered honestly from the customer's side, and what should it be given where the market and technology are going. Asking only the first produces a company that describes its present accurately and walks into the future backwards. Asking only the second produces fantasy strategy disconnected from what you currently do well. The pairing is uncomfortable because the honest answer often implies abandoning something profitable that everyone is fond of.
sparks.why: Most planning answers neither question and instead extrapolates last year. The value here is in forcing an explicit statement that can later be checked against what happened.
sparks.apply: Write one paragraph on what your business is and one on what it should be in five years, then name the first thing that has to be given up.

carousel.title: Define it from outside
carousel.body: Describe the business in the customer's terms: what problem they hand to you and what they would do without you. Internal descriptions are almost always too flattering.

carousel.title: Ask what it should be
