sparks.apply: Book five conversations this week with people who fit your target customer, and ask about their current workaround before you describe your product at all.

sparks.hook: Four steps stand between a guess and a company that can scale.
sparks.insight: Customer development runs in a fixed order, and skipping ahead is why startups explode. First you discover whether the problem and the customer are real. Then you validate that you can sell the solution repeatedly, yourself, at a price that works. Only then do you spend on creating demand, and only after that do you convert the search team into a functioning organisation. Each step has an exit test, and failing it sends you backwards rather than forwards. That backwards move is what a pivot actually is.
sparks.why: The order encodes cost. Every step forward multiplies your burn rate, so proving the cheap things first is what keeps a wrong answer survivable rather than terminal.
sparks.apply: Identify which of the four steps you are honestly in right now, then stop any spending that properly belongs to a later step.

carousel.title: Discover the problem
carousel.body: Turn your assumptions into testable statements and take them to real customers. You are looking for a problem people already spend time or money trying to solve badly.

carousel.title: Validate the sale
carousel.body: Sell to strangers with the founders doing the selling. If you cannot close repeatedly without heroics, you have not found a business model yet, only interest.

carousel.title: Create demand
carousel.body: Now spend on marketing to pull buyers into the funnel. How much you spend and how you spend it depends entirely on which kind of market you are entering.

carousel.title: Build the company
carousel.body: Only once the model repeats do you replace the search team with departments, process and the ordinary machinery of execution.

sparks.hook: The kind of market you enter changes every number in your plan.
sparks.insight: Entering an existing market is a race on features against known rivals, and customers already understand what you sell. Creating a new market means nobody is searching for you, adoption takes years, and your early budget goes on education rather than competition. Resegmenting means carving a niche or a cheaper position inside somebody else's market. Cloning means bringing a proven model to a new country. These paths have completely different spending curves, and borrowing the wrong one's plan is a reliable way to die on schedule.
sparks.why: Market type determines when revenue can plausibly arrive. New-market companies that budget like existing-market companies run out of cash during the education phase, which was always the expected phase.
sparks.apply: Name your market type in one word, then rebuild your first three years of forecasts around its adoption curve rather than a competitor's.

sparks.hook: Your first customers should already be trying to fix this themselves.
sparks.insight: The best early buyers are not the ones who enjoy your demo. They are people who have the problem, know they have it, have gone looking for a solution, and have already improvised something ugly — a spreadsheet, a manual process, three tools taped together. That improvisation is the strongest evidence of demand you will ever get, and it also means they will tolerate your unfinished product, because their current alternative is worse. Selling to anyone earlier on that ladder means doing the customer's realising for them.
sparks.why: Awareness of a problem is a prerequisite for buying. A customer who has not yet built a workaround is telling you the pain has not reached the threshold where money moves.
sparks.apply: For each prospect, ask what they do about this problem today. Deprioritise anyone whose honest answer is that they do nothing at all.

sparks.hook: A pivot is a change to the model, not a change of mind.
sparks.insight: The word gets used for any wobble, which makes it useless. Use it precisely: a pivot is a substantive change to one component of the business model — the customer, the problem, the channel, the pricing, the value proposition — made because a test told you the current version is wrong. That definition has teeth. It means a pivot requires a failed test to justify it, it means you change one component and re-test rather than rebuilding everything, and it means constant pivoting is a sign you are not testing at all.
sparks.why: Naming the specific component stops you discarding the parts that were working. Most failed pivots throw away validated learning along with the broken assumption, and start again from zero.
sparks.apply: Before your next big change, write down which single component of the model is changing and what evidence forced it. If you cannot, it is not a pivot.

sparks.hook: Do not hire a salesperson until you have sold it yourself.
sparks.insight: Founders often treat selling as beneath them and hire a sales team to find out whether the product sells. It never works, because the first sales are not a sales job. They are research that happens to produce revenue. Until you know who buys, which objection kills the deal, what creates urgency and what price sticks, there is no roadmap for a salesperson to follow, so you are asking somebody to execute a process nobody has discovered. Sell it yourself until the sale is boringly repeatable.
sparks.why: An early sales hire fails for structural reasons and then looks like a bad hire. The company loses a year and frequently concludes, wrongly, that the market was the problem.
sparks.apply: Set an explicit threshold before your first sales hire, such as ten closed deals you personally ran using the same pitch and the same price.

sparks.hook: Build the smallest thing capable of proving you wrong.
sparks.insight: A minimum viable product is not a cheap version of the finished product. It is an instrument for answering one question you currently cannot answer, built to the lowest fidelity that still gives a trustworthy answer. Sometimes that means working software, and often it means a page, a document, a demo or a service you perform by hand. The test of a good one is not whether customers like it but whether their reaction changes what you do next. If every outcome leaves your plan unchanged, you built the wrong instrument.
sparks.why: Cost per experiment sets how many wrong guesses you can survive. Anything in the build that does not serve the current question is money you will not get back.
sparks.apply: Write the question your next build answers, plus the two possible results and the different action each would trigger, before anyone writes code.

carousel.title: State the question
carousel.body: Name the single uncertainty that matters most right now, phrased so that it can come back false. Vague questions produce builds that cannot fail and therefore cannot teach.

carousel.title: Pick the cheapest instrument
carousel.body: Choose the lowest-fidelity thing that would still convince you: a landing page, a manual service, a clickable mock. Fidelity costs money and rarely changes the answer.

carousel.title: Set the threshold first
carousel.body: Decide before the test what result counts as a pass. Deciding afterwards guarantees you will find some way to read the data as encouraging.

carousel.title: Run it on strangers
carousel.body: Test with people who have no relationship with you. Friends and advisers give you politeness, which is indistinguishable from demand right up until you invoice.

carousel.title: Act on the answer
carousel.body: Write down the decision the result forces and take it within the week. An experiment nobody acts on is an expensive kind of procrastination.

sparks.hook: Failing a checkpoint sends you backwards. That is the system working.
sparks.insight: Every stage of customer development has an exit condition, and if you do not meet it the instruction is to go back, not to press on with a smaller version of the same plan. That is uncomfortable, because backwards looks like failure to everybody watching, investors included. But the alternative is scaling a model you have not proven, which converts a recoverable setback into an unrecoverable one. Startups that die have usually passed a checkpoint they had actually failed.
sparks.why: The cost of continuing rises steeply at each step, so an unproven assumption carried forward gets more expensive the longer it goes unexamined, and harder to admit to.
sparks.apply: Define the pass condition for your current stage in one measurable sentence, and agree with your co-founders in advance what happens if you miss it.

sparks.hook: This is a manual, not a book. Use it like one.
sparks.insight: It runs to several hundred pages of checklists and is close to unreadable cover to cover, which is a format rather than a flaw. Used properly you open it at the stage you are in, follow the specific list for that stage, and close it again. That makes it far more useful as a shared reference for a founding team than as something one person reads alone. The checklist form also imposes a real discipline: it is much harder to pretend you completed a step when the step has a list attached.
sparks.why: Checklists work by removing reliance on memory and optimism, the same reason they hold up in aviation and surgery. Their weakness is that they invite box-ticking in place of judgement.
sparks.apply: Print the checklist for the single stage you are actually in, put it on the wall, and review it with your co-founder every Friday.

actions: Write your business model out as numbered assumptions, rank them by how fatal each would be if wrong, and design a cheap test for the top three this month.
Do ten customer conversations yourself, with no slides, asking only about how they handle the problem today and what that workaround costs them.
Name your market type in writing and rebuild your revenue forecast around the adoption curve that type implies, not the one your pitch deck wants.
Agree a written pass condition for your current stage with your co-founders, including what you will do if the condition is not met.
books.not_for_you_if: You want an evening read or a narrative. This is a dense reference volume of checklists, and reading it straight through will exhaust you well before it helps you.

verification.notes: Published 2012 by K&S Ranch. Expands the customer development method Blank first set out in 2005. Prose here is original.

books.title: Venture Deals
books.subtitle: Be Smarter Than Your Lawyer and Venture Capitalist
books.author: Brad Feld and Jason Mendelson
books.why_it_matters: Term sheets used to be understood mainly by the people writing them. This lays out clause by clause what each one does and who it favours, which changed how well informed founders arrive at the table. It remains the standard explainer.

crux.headline: Only two things in a term sheet really matter
crux.body: Every clause resolves into one of two questions: how the money gets divided, and who gets to decide. Valuation is the number founders argue about and it is frequently the least important of the economic terms, because a preference structure can quietly take back more than a higher price ever gave you. Control sits in the board seats and the veto rights, and those determine whether you can still run the company after the money arrives.

sparks.hook: Valuation is the number you argue about. It is rarely the one that matters.
sparks.insight: Founders negotiate hard on price and then sign terms that undo the win. A liquidation preference decides who gets paid first and how much before ordinary shares see anything. An option pool carved out before the investment quietly lowers the real price you received. Anti-dilution terms reprice the earlier round if a later one is lower. Each is worth real money, and unlike valuation none of them announce themselves. Read the whole structure and calculate what you own under several different outcomes.
sparks.why: Economic terms interact with one another. A high headline valuation combined with an aggressive preference stack can leave founders worse off than a lower price with clean terms, particularly in modest exits.
sparks.apply: Model your term sheet at three exit prices, including a disappointing one, and see what the ordinary shares receive in each. Do this before negotiating anything else.

sparks.hook: Preference decides who gets paid first when the company is sold.
sparks.insight: Investors typically buy a class of share that ranks ahead of yours in a sale. At its simplest they get their money back before anything is distributed, which is reasonable. The variations are less so: a multiple that returns several times the investment first, or a participating structure that returns the money and then also takes a share of the remainder. Stack a few rounds of the aggressive versions and a sale price that sounds impressive can distribute nothing at all to founders and staff.
sparks.why: Preferences are contract terms rather than market forces, so they are negotiable at signing and effectively permanent afterwards. Their real cost only becomes visible in a mediocre outcome.
sparks.apply: Ask for a preference that is a single return of capital without participation, and treat any multiple or participation as a real price you are paying for the headline valuation.

sparks.hook: The option pool usually comes out of your side of the table.
sparks.insight: Investors will require a pool of shares reserved for future employees. Where that pool is created determines who pays for it. Carved out before the investment, it dilutes existing shareholders only, which means the effective price per share you received is lower than the headline number suggests. Created afterwards, everybody shares the dilution. This single point is worth negotiating carefully, and the honest defence is a hiring plan showing what the company actually needs rather than a round number.
sparks.why: Placing the pool inside the pre-money valuation transfers its whole cost to founders and earlier holders. It is one of the most common quiet adjustments inside an otherwise attractive offer.
sparks.apply: Build a hiring plan for the next eighteen months with real roles and grants, then use it to argue for the smallest defensible pool rather than accepting the proposed figure.

sparks.hook: Who sits on the board matters more than what you own.
sparks.insight: Ownership and control are separate things. A founder can hold a majority of the shares and still be unable to hire, sell the company or approve a budget, because those decisions sit with the board and with a list of matters the investors can veto. Board composition is therefore the most consequential paragraph in the document: how many seats each side appoints, who holds any independent seat, and how that person is chosen. Negotiate it before valuation, because you will live inside it for years.
sparks.why: Protective provisions and board seats govern decision rights regardless of shareholding. Founders removed from their own companies usually still held substantial equity at the time it happened.
sparks.apply: Write down every decision you would hate to lose control of, then check the term sheet for which of them require investor consent or a board majority.

carousel.title: Count the seats
carousel.body: Work out who appoints each board member and what happens as later rounds add seats. A structure that looks balanced today may not be after the next round.

carousel.title: Name the independent
carousel.body: The independent seat often decides contested votes. Agree in advance how that person gets chosen and that both sides have to approve them.

carousel.title: Read the vetoes
carousel.body: The protective provisions list decisions investors can block. Push to keep that list short and confined to genuinely major events rather than routine operations.

carousel.title: Check the drag
carousel.body: Drag-along rights can force you to accept a sale approved by others. Understand who can trigger it and what threshold is required before you sign.

sparks.hook: Understand how the fund makes money before you take its money.
sparks.insight: A venture fund raises capital from institutions, charges an annual management fee of a few percent, and keeps a share of the profits, conventionally about a fifth. It has a fixed life, usually around a decade, and needs a small number of enormous outcomes to return the whole fund. That structure explains almost every behaviour you will encounter: the pressure to grow faster, the reluctance to approve a modest sale, the keen interest in follow-on rounds. None of it is personal. It is arithmetic.
sparks.why: Fund economics determine which outcomes an investor can accept. A result that would make you wealthy for life can be close to irrelevant to a fund that needs many times its total capital back.
sparks.apply: Ask any prospective investor the size and vintage of their fund, then work out what exit value would be meaningful to them relative to what would satisfy you.

sparks.hook: Leverage in a fundraise comes from having somewhere else to go.
sparks.insight: Every negotiating technique matters less than the existence of an alternative. One term sheet means you are negotiating with yourself. Several means the terms improve without you having to be clever about it. This is why a raise is run as a compressed process rather than a series of conversations spread over months: you want interested parties reaching a decision at roughly the same time. Without that, you will be told what the market rate is and have no way to check it.
sparks.why: Competitive tension is the main determinant of terms in private financing, since there is no public price. Sequential conversations remove that tension and hand all the timing leverage to the other side.
sparks.apply: Run your raise as a defined process: build the list, start every first meeting inside the same fortnight, and aim for any offers to arrive within the same window.

carousel.title: Build the target list
carousel.body: Research which investors back companies at your stage and in your sector. A broad untargeted list produces meetings that were never going to end in an offer.

carousel.title: Get warm introductions
carousel.body: Ask founders they have already backed to introduce you. An introduction from somebody with money at stake reads very differently from a cold approach.

carousel.title: Run them in parallel
carousel.body: Start first meetings within the same fortnight so decisions arrive together. Sequential processes give away every scrap of timing leverage you had.

carousel.title: Negotiate two things
carousel.body: When offers arrive, concentrate on economics and control. Arguing every minor clause spends goodwill you will need on the terms that actually matter.

sparks.hook: Convertible notes postpone the argument. They do not remove it.
sparks.insight: Raising on a note or a simple agreement defers the valuation question, which is genuinely useful when a company is too early to price. The cost is that the terms still exist, hidden inside caps and discounts, and they all convert at once during the next round. Founders who raise several small amounts this way can discover at conversion that they own far less than they assumed. Track the effect on your own ownership every time you sign one, rather than at the end.
sparks.why: Deferred pricing does not remove dilution, it just makes it invisible until conversion. A cap functions as a valuation ceiling, so stacked notes can convert into a much larger share than expected.
sparks.apply: Keep a running capitalisation model showing what you own after every outstanding note converts at its cap, and update it before you sign each new one.

sparks.hook: Vesting protects you from your co-founder more than from investors.
sparks.insight: Founder shares that vest over several years look like an imposition from the investor, and they are also the only sensible arrangement between founders. Without them, a co-founder who leaves after six months keeps a large permanent stake in a company built by everybody else, and the remaining team has to fund the gap out of their own equity. Agreeing vesting early, while nobody expects to leave, is far easier than proposing it once somebody already wants to.
sparks.why: Vesting aligns ownership with contribution over time. Its absence is one of the most common structural problems investors find in early companies, and it becomes unfixable once relationships sour.
sparks.apply: Put founder vesting in place now, with a standard cliff and a multi-year schedule, and agree in writing what happens to unvested shares if somebody leaves.

sparks.hook: You are choosing a colleague for a decade, not just a cheque.
sparks.insight: The person who joins your board will be involved in the hardest decisions you make, including whether you keep your job. Terms are negotiable and replaceable; that relationship is not. So diligence runs both ways. Speak to founders of companies this investor backed which did not work out, because how somebody behaves during a failure is the information you actually need, and it is the one thing no reference list will offer you voluntarily.
sparks.why: Investor behaviour under stress is hard to observe in advance and is not reflected anywhere in the terms. Failed portfolio companies are the most informative reference class available to you.
sparks.apply: Before signing, speak to two founders whose companies this investor backed and which did not succeed. Ask specifically what happened when things went wrong.

sparks.hook: Most companies should not raise venture capital at all.
sparks.insight: Taking this money commits you to pursuing an outcome large enough to matter to a fund, which rules out a profitable business that would have made its founders comfortable. That is a legitimate trade for a small number of companies attacking large markets with a real need for capital ahead of revenue. For everyone else it converts a good business into a failed attempt at a great one. Understanding the terms is useful. Deciding whether to be at the table at all comes first.
sparks.why: Venture funding suits a narrow set of businesses. This explains the mechanics well and is not a neutral guide to whether the mechanism fits you, since it is written by people inside the industry.
sparks.apply: Before raising, write down the smallest outcome that would satisfy you and check whether a fund's return model can accept it. If not, look at other funding routes.

actions: Model your term sheet at three exit prices including a poor one, and record what the ordinary shares receive under each of them.
Build an eighteen-month hiring plan with real roles, and use it to negotiate the size and the placement of the option pool.
Speak to two founders backed by your prospective investor whose companies did not succeed, and ask what happened when things went wrong.
Put founder vesting in writing now, with a cliff and a multi-year schedule, before anybody has a reason to object to it.
books.not_for_you_if: You are bootstrapping with no intention of raising, or you need guidance outside the United States, whose conventions and law the book assumes throughout.

verification.notes: First published 2011 by Wiley, with several updated editions since. Prose is original; terms are explained in our own words and conventions described as typical rather than exact.

books.title: An Elegant Puzzle
books.subtitle: Systems of Engineering Management
books.author: Will Larson
books.why_it_matters: It treats management as a systems problem with measurable stocks, flows and delays rather than a people-skills problem, which is why it survives contact with a real organisation. It remains the reference text for anyone running engineering teams at scale.

crux.headline: Manage the system, not the individual incidents
crux.body: Most management problems recur because they are produced by a structure rather than by the people caught inside it. Teams are the unit that matters, not individuals. Their size, their state of health, how work arrives and how debt accumulates all obey rules you can reason about. Once you see the org as a system with inputs, delays and feedback loops, the daily crises stop looking like separate emergencies and start looking like symptoms with a small number of underlying causes.

sparks.hook: Adding people to a struggling team usually makes it slower for months.
sparks.insight: The reflex when a team is drowning is to hire. But new people consume the capacity of the existing ones for a quarter or more before they contribute, so if the team is merely overloaded rather than genuinely under-resourced, hiring makes the next three months worse. What a stretched team usually needs is fewer things in flight, so it can finish something. What a permanently under-resourced team needs is people. Diagnosing which situation you are in is the whole decision.
sparks.why: Onboarding has a real, front-loaded cost paid by the people already there. That cost is invisible in a headcount plan, which is why hiring gets applied to problems it cannot solve.
sparks.apply: Before requesting headcount, cut your team's concurrent projects in half for six weeks and see whether throughput recovers on its own.

sparks.hook: Every team is in one of four states, and each needs a different fix.
sparks.insight: Teams are not simply good or bad. A team can be falling behind, where the backlog grows faster than it shrinks. It can be treading water, keeping the critical work alive but never getting ahead. It can be actively repaying accumulated debt. Or it can be innovating, with slack to spend on new things. Each state has one appropriate intervention and applying the wrong one wastes a quarter. You also cannot skip states: an overwhelmed team has to pass through the middle two before it can innovate.
sparks.why: The states form a sequence rather than a menu, which is why interventions that worked for one team fail for another that looks superficially similar but sits at a different point.
sparks.apply: Place each team you own into one of the four states this week, then apply only the matching intervention for the next quarter.

carousel.title: Falling behind: add people
carousel.body: The queue grows faster than the team can clear it and morale is dropping. This is the one situation where hiring genuinely is the answer, and it takes a quarter to land.

carousel.title: Treading water: cut the work
carousel.body: Critical things get done and nothing improves. Reduce concurrent projects hard so the team can finish something, because finishing is what creates the room to get ahead.

carousel.title: Repaying debt: add time
carousel.body: The team is fixing the foundations. Protect the schedule and resist the urge to inject new work; this stage looks unproductive from outside and is the one that pays for everything after it.

carousel.title: Innovating: leave them alone
carousel.body: There is slack, the backlog is short, and new work is being invented. Your job here is to defend the slack against the constant pressure to consume it.

sparks.hook: The team is the unit of work. Individuals are just where it happens.
sparks.insight: Organisations that assign projects to individuals get brittleness: knowledge concentrates in one head, the work stops when that person leaves, and nobody can take a holiday. Assigning ownership to teams instead is slower to feel productive and vastly more durable. It also changes how you plan. You stop trying to match a specific person to a specific task and start asking whether a team has a coherent area, enough people to sustain it, and a clear boundary with the teams next to it.
sparks.why: Team-level ownership survives turnover, illness and promotion; individual ownership does not. The cost is a short-term loss of the efficiency that comes from always using the best-matched person.
sparks.apply: List every critical system you own and name the team that owns it. Anything owned by a single person is a risk to be fixed this quarter.

sparks.hook: Teams below six are fragile. Above ten they need another manager.
sparks.insight: Team size is not a matter of taste. Below roughly six people, a team cannot sustain an on-call rotation, absorb a departure, or take a holiday without stalling, so it stays permanently anxious. Above roughly ten, a manager can no longer hold real context on each person's work and coordination overhead starts eating the gains from having more people. The band in between is where most teams work well, and drifting outside it produces problems that get misdiagnosed as culture or motivation.
sparks.why: Both limits come from concrete constraints: rotation coverage and resilience at the bottom, the manager's attention and communication paths at the top. Neither depends on how good the people are.
sparks.apply: Count the members of every team you own. Merge anything under five and split anything over ten, planning both moves this quarter.

sparks.hook: Migrations are the only way large systems ever pay down debt.
sparks.insight: Beyond a certain size, technical debt cannot be cleaned up incrementally, because the rate of new debt matches the rate you fix it. The only mechanism that changes the picture is a full migration: everything moves to the new approach and the old one is genuinely removed. Half-finished migrations are worse than none at all, because you now maintain two systems and every engineer must learn both. That means the deciding question is not whether the new approach is better but whether you will actually finish.
sparks.why: Partial migration leaves permanent duplicate cost, so the ability to complete matters more than the quality of the destination. Most organisations underestimate the tail of the work by a wide margin.
sparks.apply: List your unfinished migrations, pick the one closest to completion, and staff it until it is finished before starting anything new.

sparks.hook: Write policy for the common case and treat exceptions as exceptions.
sparks.insight: Managers make two opposite mistakes with rules. One is deciding everything case by case, which is exhausting, inconsistent and rewards whoever argues hardest. The other is writing a policy so comprehensive it covers every edge case and nobody can read it. The workable middle is a short policy that handles the ordinary situation well, plus an explicit route for exceptions that a named person approves. Exceptions handled openly are fine. Exceptions granted quietly are how a policy dies.
sparks.why: A policy exists to remove repeated decisions, so complexity defeats its own purpose. Making the exception path visible is what keeps the rule credible for everyone who did not get one.
sparks.apply: Take your most contested recurring decision, write a policy for the common case in under a page, and name who approves exceptions.

sparks.hook: You cannot mandate a change sideways. You can make it obvious.
sparks.insight: Most of the changes an engineering leader wants involve people they do not manage. Instructions do not work there, and neither does arguing in meetings. What does work is a sequence: build the thing yourself so it demonstrably exists, write down clearly how and why it works, and only then invite others to adopt it. Each step lowers the cost of the next person saying yes. Attempting the last step first is why so many good technical proposals die in a review committee.
sparks.why: Adoption without authority depends on lowering risk for the adopter. A working example plus documentation removes most of that risk; a proposal document alone removes none of it.
sparks.apply: Pick one change you have been arguing for, stop arguing, build a working version in one team, and write up what happened.

carousel.title: Build it somewhere real
carousel.body: Implement the change in one team, ideally your own, and run it long enough to hit the problems. A working example ends most of the theoretical objections by itself.

carousel.title: Write down what happened
carousel.body: Document the approach, the results and the parts that went badly. Including the failures is what makes the write-up credible to people who did not choose this.

carousel.title: Make adoption cheap
carousel.body: Provide the templates, tooling or migration script so the next team spends hours rather than weeks. Adoption cost is usually the real objection behind a stated one.

carousel.title: Let it spread, then standardise
carousel.body: Once several teams have chosen it, make it the default. Standardising before there is evidence turns a good idea into an imposed one people work around.

sparks.hook: A career ladder is mostly a device for reducing arguments about promotion.
sparks.insight: Without written levels, promotion decisions get made on visibility, advocacy and who is closest to a decision-maker, and everyone can feel it even when nobody can prove it. A ladder that describes observable behaviour at each level does not remove judgement, but it moves the argument to a shared document instead of a private one. It also makes the manager's job easier: instead of defending a decision, you point at the gap between what somebody does and what the next level describes.
sparks.why: Legible criteria reduce the influence of proximity and self-promotion on advancement. The ladder is imperfect and gameable; the undocumented alternative is worse and less fair.
sparks.apply: Write one paragraph of observable behaviour for each level on your team, share it, and use it in your next promotion discussion.

sparks.hook: Interviewing is expensive engineering time nobody puts on the plan.
sparks.insight: Every interview loop consumes several hours from people who were otherwise building things, plus the recovery time around it. Organisations rarely count this, so they run wasteful processes and then wonder why delivery slipped during a hiring push. Counting it changes decisions: you shorten loops, you stop interviewing for roles you are not going to fill, and you concentrate interviewing among people who are good at it rather than spreading it evenly as a tax on everyone.
sparks.why: Unmeasured costs are always overspent. Making interview hours visible turns hiring into a resourcing decision rather than an invisible drain on the same teams under delivery pressure.
sparks.apply: Total your team's interview hours for last month, put the number in your capacity plan, and cut one stage from the loop.

sparks.hook: Do the work that only you can do. Give away the rest, even the fun parts.
sparks.insight: Every manager has a set of tasks that they alone can perform: the organisational decisions, the conversations that require your authority, the strategy nobody else has the context to write. Around that sits a much larger set of work you happen to be good at and enjoy. Holding onto the second set is understandable, since it is where you feel competent, and it is also what stops your team growing. The test is not whether you do it well. It is whether anyone else could.
sparks.why: Doing work others could do has a hidden cost: it removes their development opportunity and occupies the time your unique work needed. Both costs land later, which is why the trade feels free now.
sparks.apply: List everything you did last week, mark each as only-you or someone-else, and hand over the largest someone-else item this month.

actions: Place every team you own into one of the four states and apply only the matching intervention for a full quarter.
Count your unfinished migrations, staff the one closest to completion until it is genuinely done, and start nothing new until then.
Write a one-page policy for your most contested recurring decision and name the person who approves exceptions to it.
Add your team's monthly interview hours to the capacity plan, then remove one stage from the hiring loop.
books.not_for_you_if: You do not lead engineers or you want narrative and encouragement rather than dense operational advice organised as a reference.

verification.notes: First published 2019 by Stripe Press. Practitioner writing drawn from the author's experience leading infrastructure and engineering organisations; the numeric team-size bands are heuristics rather than measured thresholds.

books.title: Confidence
books.subtitle: How Winning Streaks and Losing Streaks Begin and End
books.author: Rosabeth Moss Kanter
books.why_it_matters: It explains why organisations that are already winning keep winning and losers keep losing, using the same mechanism across sports teams, companies and schools. It is the clearest account of momentum as something leaders can engineer.

crux.headline: Confidence is an investment decision, not a feeling
crux.body: Confidence is the expectation that effort will pay off, and that expectation determines whether people put in the effort at all. When a group believes it can win, individuals invest more, help each other and tell the truth about problems. When it does not, they hoard, blame, hide and stop trying, which makes the next result worse. Streaks in either direction are self-reinforcing, and turning one around means changing the behaviour before the belief.

sparks.hook: Winning streaks are not luck running long. They are behaviour changing.
sparks.insight: When a group starts winning, something concrete changes in how people act. They put in discretionary effort because it looks likely to pay off, they share information because the group's success is now their success, and they take the small risks that produce the next win. The results cause the behaviour and the behaviour causes the results. That loop, not talent, is what makes streaks last longer than any statistical model of the underlying ability would predict.
sparks.why: Honest caveat: the evidence is a set of case studies chosen because they had striking streaks, which is selection on the outcome. The mechanism is convincing, but the case list cannot prove it.
sparks.apply: Find the smallest genuine win your team could produce in two weeks, ship it, and make sure everyone hears about it specifically.

sparks.hook: Losing does not make people try harder. It makes them go quiet.
sparks.insight: Failure sets off a recognisable sequence. Information stops moving because bad news is punished. People stop taking responsibility and start assigning it. Meetings become defensive and the strongest performers, who have options, leave first. Nobody decides to sabotage anything. Each person is making a rational choice given what they now expect, and the sum of those choices produces the next failure. Recognising the pattern early matters more than diagnosing which department is to blame.
sparks.why: Each symptom is individually reasonable under low expectations, which is why the spiral is so hard to argue people out of. The behaviour changes only when the expected payoff changes.
sparks.apply: Look for the three warning signs this week: secrecy, blame and passivity. If two are present, treat it as an emergency rather than a mood.

carousel.title: Watch information stop moving
carousel.body: Bad news arrives later and in softer language. Problems get raised only when they are undeniable. Secrecy is the first symptom and the one that makes every other one worse.

carousel.title: Notice blame replacing analysis
carousel.body: Post-mortems become about who, not what. Departments start describing each other as the problem. At this stage people are protecting position rather than solving anything.

carousel.title: See the isolation set in
carousel.body: Teams stop helping across boundaries because collaboration now feels like exposure. Meetings shrink to the people who already agree with each other.

carousel.title: Catch the passivity
carousel.body: Nobody proposes anything. Decisions wait for someone senior. Effort drops to what is checkable, because discretionary work no longer looks like it will pay off.

sparks.hook: Restore the facts before you try to restore the mood.
sparks.insight: The reflex in a turnaround is a rousing speech, and it is almost always the wrong first move. People who have been losing do not trust optimism, and a leader who supplies it without evidence looks either dishonest or uninformed. The first job is to make the real numbers visible to everyone, including the ugly ones. Shared facts end the private theories, kill the rumour economy, and give people something they can act on rather than something they are asked to believe.
sparks.why: Confidence rebuilt on encouragement collapses at the next bad result. Confidence rebuilt on visible information survives it, because people can see for themselves that the trend has changed.
sparks.apply: Publish the three numbers that actually show whether your team is winning, including the one you would rather not share, and update them weekly.

sparks.hook: Accountability, collaboration and initiative are the three legs. Any two will not hold.
sparks.insight: Groups that recover tend to rebuild three things together. People take responsibility for outcomes rather than for effort. They work across boundaries instead of defending them. And they start proposing things without being asked. Each supports the others: accountability without collaboration produces defensive silos, collaboration without accountability produces pleasant meetings and no results, and initiative without either burns out the few people who still try.
sparks.why: The three map onto the three symptoms of decline: blame, isolation and passivity. Fixing one alone leaves the other two to regenerate the spiral, which is why partial turnarounds relapse.
sparks.apply: Score your team one to five on each of the three this week, then pick the lowest and design one visible change against it.

sparks.hook: Small wins are not consolation prizes. They are the mechanism.
sparks.insight: A group that has lost repeatedly cannot be talked into believing in a large goal. It can be shown a small one and then shown that it was achieved. The win must be real, visible and clearly attributable to the group's own effort, or it reads as a manufactured morale exercise and makes cynicism worse. Sequence enough of them and the expectation shifts, which is what changes how much effort people are willing to risk on the next thing.
sparks.why: Expectation is updated by evidence, not by assertion, and it updates fastest from outcomes people were personally involved in producing. Manufactured wins do not work because everyone can tell.
sparks.apply: Break your biggest goal into a two-week piece that is genuinely useful on its own, and let the team present the result themselves.

sparks.hook: The advantage of winning is that people tell you the truth.
sparks.insight: In a confident group, raising a problem is a contribution because everyone expects it to be fixed. In a frightened one, raising a problem marks you as the source of it. The difference in how much a leader actually knows about their own organisation is enormous, and it compounds: the confident group catches errors early and cheaply, while the losing group discovers them at the point where they are expensive and someone must be blamed.
sparks.why: The information advantage is arguably the real mechanism behind streaks. It also means a leader's own view of the organisation is least reliable exactly when things are going worst.
sparks.apply: Ask three people this week what problem they have decided not to raise, and respond to the first one by fixing something rather than investigating.

sparks.hook: Too much confidence produces the same blindness as too little.
sparks.insight: The streak that runs long enough starts to erode the behaviour that created it. Success is attributed to inherent superiority rather than to effort and circumstance, warnings get filed as pessimism, and the group stops examining its own results because examining them seems disloyal. Arrogance looks like confidence from the inside and produces the opposite behaviour: less listening, less preparation, less willingness to hear the person who says the model is wrong.
sparks.why: Confidence works because it drives investment of effort. Once success feels guaranteed, the effort is no longer seen as necessary, so the loop that produced the wins quietly disconnects.
sparks.apply: After your next clear success, run a session on what nearly went wrong and what you got lucky on, before anyone celebrates.

sparks.hook: Leaders in a losing streak spend too much time on strategy and not enough on contact.
sparks.insight: The instinct under pressure is to withdraw and work on the plan, because the plan is where the leader feels competent. Meanwhile the organisation reads absence as either abandonment or panic and fills the gap with rumour. Turnarounds are unusually contact-heavy: standing in front of people repeatedly, taking hard questions in public, being visibly present when the news is bad. The plan matters, but nobody executes a plan handed down by someone they have stopped seeing.
sparks.why: In an information vacuum people assume the worst, and the assumption itself changes behaviour. Presence is not symbolism, it is the channel through which any new expectation has to travel.
sparks.apply: Book a recurring open session where anyone can ask you anything, start it during the bad period rather than after, and answer the hardest question first.

sparks.hook: Fixing the culture without fixing the process just moves the blame around.
sparks.insight: You can run every workshop about trust you like, and it will not survive a system where two teams are measured on conflicting numbers or where nobody can find out what was decided last week. Confidence rests on structures that make responsibility legible and cooperation possible: clear ownership, information people can actually reach, and forums where cross-boundary problems get resolved rather than escalated. Behaviour follows the structure far more reliably than it follows the values statement.
sparks.why: People behave well when the system makes it rational to. Attempting to change attitudes while leaving the incentives untouched produces temporary compliance and lasting cynicism.
sparks.apply: Find one place where two teams are measured on conflicting numbers and change one of the measures this quarter.

sparks.hook: The same mechanism runs in a school, a football team and a bank.
sparks.insight: Streaks look like different phenomena in different settings, so people explain a struggling school by policy, a struggling team by coaching and a struggling company by strategy. Underneath, the sequence is recognisably the same: expectations fall, information stops moving, responsibility disperses, effort withdraws. That generality is useful because it means the interventions travel. A head teacher can borrow from a turnaround chief executive, and both are working on the same underlying loop.
sparks.why: Be careful with the strength of the claim. Pattern-matching across very different institutions is suggestive rather than proof, and each setting has causes the model does not capture.
sparks.apply: Describe your current situation using only the loop, with no industry vocabulary. If the description still fits, borrow a fix from an unrelated field.

actions: Publish a small set of honest performance numbers on a weekly rhythm, including at least one you would prefer not to share.
Design and ship a genuine two-week win that the team can attribute to its own work, and let them present the result.
Score your group on accountability, collaboration and initiative, then make one structural change against whichever is weakest.
Start a recurring open question session during the difficult period rather than after it, and answer the hardest question first each time.
books.not_for_you_if: You want controlled evidence rather than case studies selected because they had dramatic streaks, or you are after tactics for a stable, well-performing team.

verification.notes: First published 2004. Built on comparative case studies of sports, business and education, which is selection on the outcome; flagged in sparks one and ten. All prose original.

books.title: Crucial Conversations
books.subtitle: Tools for Talking When Stakes Are High
books.author: Kerry Patterson, Joseph Grenny, Ron McMillan and Al Switzler
books.why_it_matters: It gave ordinary managers a usable procedure for the handful of conversations that decide whether a team functions, and made silence visible as a failure mode rather than as politeness. Most modern feedback training borrows its structure.

crux.headline: Safety first, content second
crux.body: In any conversation that matters, people stop processing what you are saying the moment they feel unsafe. They go quiet or they go hard, and either way the useful information stops flowing. So when a discussion turns bad, the move is not a better argument. It is to step out of the content, rebuild the sense that you respect the person and share a purpose with them, and only then go back to the thing you disagree about. Content without safety is noise.

sparks.hook: The conversations that shape your life are the ones you keep postponing.
sparks.insight: A conversation turns crucial when three things line up: the stakes are real, opinions differ, and feelings are running. Those are exactly the conditions under which people perform worst, so the usual response is to defer it, hint at it, or send an email that pretends not to be about it. The cost is invisible and enormous. Projects fail slowly, resentment accrues, and the thing everyone knew is finally said at the exit interview.
sparks.why: Avoidance feels like restraint but functions as a decision: you have chosen the worse outcome quietly. Difficulty is not evidence that a conversation should wait, it is usually evidence of the opposite.
sparks.apply: List the three conversations you are currently avoiding. Pick the one whose cost is growing fastest and book fifteen minutes for it this week.

sparks.hook: There are only two ways to leave a hard conversation: go quiet or go hard.
sparks.insight: Under pressure people either withdraw or attack. Withdrawal looks like joking it off, changing the subject, agreeing in the room and complaining afterwards. Attack looks like interrupting, exaggerating, labelling the other person, or moving from the issue to their character. Both are ways of removing yourself from an honest exchange, and both feel justified from the inside. Learning to spot which one you personally reach for is most of the skill, because you cannot stop a reflex you never notice.
sparks.why: Both patterns are threat responses, so they arrive before your reasoning does. Naming your own default converts an automatic reaction into something you can catch a second earlier.
sparks.apply: After your next tense meeting, write one line: did I withdraw or did I push? Do this for two weeks and your pattern will be obvious.

sparks.hook: A decision can only be as good as what people were willing to say out loud.
sparks.insight: Every group has a pool of information that has actually been shared, and a much larger pool of what individuals privately know, suspect or fear. Decisions are made from the first pool only. When someone holds back a concern because the room feels hostile or the boss has already signalled a preference, the group does not merely lose politeness, it loses data. Meetings that end quickly and unanimously are often the ones that will cost the most later.
sparks.why: The mechanism is simple and unforgiving: information that is not said cannot be used. Groups routinely converge on what everyone already agreed with rather than pooling what only one person knows.
sparks.apply: End your next decision meeting by asking each quiet person directly what they would want on record if this goes badly. Wait through the silence.

sparks.hook: Notice when you swap what you want for the urge to win.
sparks.insight: You walk in wanting a working relationship and a fixed problem. Two minutes later you want to be proved right, or to make them uncomfortable, or simply to end the discomfort. The goal quietly changed and nobody announced it. The correction is a question you ask yourself mid-conversation: what do I actually want here, for me, for them, for the relationship? Asking it forces your behaviour back toward the goal you came in with rather than the one your ego picked up on the way.
sparks.why: You cannot control the other person, and trying to is what produces most escalation. The only reliable lever is your own aim, and it drifts fastest exactly when the conversation matters most.
sparks.apply: Before a hard conversation, write one sentence naming what you want the relationship to look like afterwards. Reread it if you feel yourself scoring points.

sparks.hook: You do not react to what happened. You react to the story you told about it.
sparks.insight: Between an event and your feeling about it sits an explanation you invented in under a second and then forgot inventing. Someone does not reply for two days, and you have already decided they are dismissive. The feeling is real, but it was generated by the story, not the silence. Learning to walk that chain backwards, from action to feeling to story to what actually happened, gives you a place to intervene. Usually the facts support several stories and you picked the least generous one.
sparks.why: The favourite stories are the ones that make you blameless, the other person malicious, or the situation hopeless. Each conveniently removes your obligation to do anything difficult.
sparks.apply: Write the bare facts of a recent annoyance in one column and your explanation in another. Then write two other explanations that also fit the facts.

carousel.title: Write only what a camera saw
carousel.body: Strip out adjectives and motives. Not that they ignored you, but that a message sent Tuesday had no reply by Thursday. Facts are boring, which is the point.

carousel.title: Name the story you added
carousel.body: Say the interpretation out loud in your own head. Once it is a sentence rather than a feeling, you can see it is a claim about someone else's mind.

carousel.title: Test the flattering ones
carousel.body: Ask whether you are casting yourself as blameless, them as hostile, or the situation as impossible. Those three stories are common because they excuse inaction.

carousel.title: Look for a decent motive
carousel.body: Ask what a reasonable and busy person might have been doing that produces exactly these facts. You are not required to believe it, only to hold it open.

carousel.title: Open with the facts
carousel.body: Start the conversation from the camera version and ask for their side before you offer your reading. The story is a hypothesis, so present it as one.

sparks.hook: When someone gets defensive, stop arguing and fix the safety.
sparks.insight: Defensiveness is information. It usually means one of two things has gone missing: the other person no longer believes you want something they also want, or they no longer believe you respect them. Neither is repaired by more evidence. Step out of the topic, say plainly what you are not suggesting and then what you are, restate the goal you share, and watch the temperature drop. Then return to the content that was going nowhere thirty seconds ago.
sparks.why: The threat response narrows attention and hardens position, so persuasion attempted during it mostly adds fuel. Restating shared purpose and respect removes the reason for the response rather than overpowering it.
sparks.apply: Keep one repair sentence ready: name the thing you are not saying, then the thing you are. Use it the moment tone shifts, not at the end.

sparks.hook: Lead with what you saw. Hold your conclusion loosely and last.
sparks.insight: Most feedback opens with the verdict, which is the most disputable part, and buries the observation, which is the least. Reverse it. Start with what happened in terms the other person would also recognise, then offer your reading as a reading rather than a finding, then genuinely ask for theirs. The order matters because the first sentence sets what the conversation is about: either a shared look at some facts, or a defence against a charge.
sparks.why: Facts are hard to argue with and conclusions are easy to argue with. Putting the arguable part last, and marking it as tentative, keeps the exchange on the evidence for longer.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your next piece of feedback so the first sentence contains no adjectives about the person and the last sentence is a real question.

carousel.title: Open with the observable
carousel.body: Describe what you saw or read in terms they would agree with. Two missed deadlines and a rewritten spec, not a pattern of unreliability.

carousel.title: Say your reading is a reading
carousel.body: Offer your interpretation as one possible explanation you are holding, not as a verdict already reached. The wording costs nothing and changes what they hear.

carousel.title: Ask, and mean it
carousel.body: Invite the other account and be visibly willing to change your mind. If you have already decided, they will know, and the question will make things worse.

carousel.title: Stay soft on delivery, firm on substance
carousel.body: Tentative wording is not the same as backing down. You can be gentle about how you say it and completely unmoving about the standard you need met.

sparks.hook: When they go silent, ask before you guess.
sparks.insight: Getting your own view out is the easy half. The hard half is drawing out someone who has decided it is safer to say nothing. Ask directly and then wait through the pause that feels far too long. Reflect back what you notice about their manner, not just their words. Restate their position in your own sentences until they agree you have it. Only when all of that stalls should you offer a guess at what they might be thinking, and offer it as a guess.
sparks.why: Silence is usually a judgement about risk, not about content. Each of these moves lowers the cost of speaking, and the pause matters most because most managers fill it themselves.
sparks.apply: In your next one to one, ask one open question and then say nothing for a full ten seconds. Count them. Let them fill the gap.

sparks.hook: A conversation with no owner and no decision rule will happen again.
sparks.insight: Teams have the same discussion four times because they never agreed how the decision would be made or who would carry it. Settle the method before the debate: is this one person's call after listening, a genuine vote, or something that needs everyone on board? Then close with who does what, by when, and how anyone will know it happened. Without that last minute, agreement in the room decays into four different memories of what was agreed.
sparks.why: Ambiguity about the decision rule is what makes people relitigate. If you never said whose call it was, everyone who disagreed can reasonably believe the matter is still open.
sparks.apply: At the start of your next contentious meeting, state who decides and how. At the end, read the owner and the date back to the room.

sparks.hook: One person with these skills helps. A team with them changes the place.
sparks.insight: Learning to handle a hard conversation makes you more effective on your own, but the compounding happens when a group shares the same expectations about how disagreement works. When everyone knows that raising a concern is normal and that going quiet will be noticed, the cost of speaking drops for the most junior person in the room. That is the difference between a manager with a technique and an organisation where problems surface early enough to be cheap.
sparks.why: Be honest about the evidence: most of the outcome claims come from the authors' own training firm rather than independent trials. The practices are sensible and widely echoed elsewhere, but treat the numbers with caution.
sparks.apply: Teach your team one shared move, such as separating facts from stories, and use its name in meetings until people use it on you.

actions: Pick the conversation you have been avoiding longest, write the facts with no adjectives, and hold it inside seven days.
For two weeks, log after each tense exchange whether you withdrew or pushed, then share your pattern with someone who will call it out.
Add two lines to your meeting template: who decides this, and who owns the outcome by when. Refuse to close without both filled in.
Run one team session on separating what happened from the story you told about it, using a real recent disagreement rather than a made-up case.
books.not_for_you_if: You want the underlying psychology rather than a procedure, or you are dealing with genuine bad faith and abuse, where conversational technique is not the right tool.

verification.notes: First published 2002; later editions in 2011 and 2021. Four co-authors, of whom the batch listed two. Outcome evidence comes largely from the authors' own consultancy, flagged in spark ten.

books.title: Dare to Lead
books.subtitle: Brave Work. Tough Conversations. Whole Hearts.
books.author: Brené Brown
books.why_it_matters: It moved vulnerability out of the therapy room and into the management meeting, giving a generation of managers usable language for the part of the job that is uncomfortable rather than technical. The evidence is interview-based and soft; the vocabulary has genuinely changed how teams talk.

crux.headline: Courage at work is the willingness to stay uncomfortable
crux.body: The hard parts of leading are not analytical. They are the conversation you keep postponing, the feedback you soften until it means nothing, the decision you announce without admitting you are unsure. All of it is avoidance of discomfort, dressed up as professionalism. The skill on offer is not confidence. It is the ability to stay inside a difficult conversation without retreating into certainty, sarcasm, silence or a rewritten story about the other person.

sparks.hook: Armour looks like professionalism until nothing risky ever gets said.
sparks.insight: Self-protection at work rarely looks defensive. It looks like always having the answer, needing everything perfect before it is shown, deflecting with a joke, staying coolly detached, or treating cynicism as realism. Each of these reads as competence, which is exactly why they survive. Each also tells the room that this is not a place to bring something half-formed or worrying. You end up with a team that is technically compliant, personally guarded, and no longer supplying you with the information you need.
sparks.why: Protective behaviours are the hardest to see in yourself because they feel like standards, rigour or realism. The cost is not paid by you. It is paid by everyone else, in the form of silence.
sparks.apply: Name your default armour — certainty, sarcasm, perfectionism or permanent busyness — and go through one whole meeting without using it.

sparks.hook: Your version of what just happened is a first draft, not a finding.
sparks.insight: When information is missing, a mind fills the gap fast, and the story it invents is almost never generous. Your colleague did not reply because they are undermining you. The silence in the meeting meant they disagree. You then act on that invented story as though it were established fact, and the other person experiences the consequences of a conversation they were never in. The repair is unglamorous: say your interpretation out loud, label it as an interpretation, and let it be corrected.
sparks.why: Under uncertainty people generate an explanation quickly and then treat it as evidence. Speaking it aloud converts a private conclusion back into a question, which is the only state in which it can be updated.
sparks.apply: The next time a colleague's behaviour stings, open by describing the story you have privately constructed, then ask them what you are missing.

sparks.hook: Being vague to spare their feelings is the unkindest option available.
sparks.insight: Hedged feedback protects the person giving it. You get to feel considerate, avoid the flinch, and leave the room quickly. The other person leaves without knowing where they stand and discovers it later at a review, a reorganisation or an exit conversation, at which point the kindness you thought you were showing looks like something much worse. Being direct costs you ten uncomfortable minutes. Being unclear costs them months of working hard on the wrong thing.
sparks.why: Ambiguity does not remove the bad news, it only delays it and removes the chance to act on it. The discomfort you avoided is transferred to the other person, with interest, at a later date.
sparks.apply: Take the feedback you have been softening for weeks and write the single sentence you actually mean. Say that sentence first in the meeting.

sparks.hook: The conversation you keep rescheduling is the whole job this week.
sparks.insight: Most managers know precisely which conversation they are avoiding. It has been on the list for a month, it gets bumped for anything at all, and the avoidance is expensive: the problem grows, the team notices you are not handling it, and your own respect for yourself erodes a little each week. The conversation is almost never as bad as the version you have rehearsed. What makes it survivable is having a shape to follow, so that you are not improvising while your heart is going.
sparks.why: Avoidance is maintained by uncertainty about how the conversation will go. A rehearsed structure removes most of that uncertainty, which is why preparation reduces avoidance more reliably than resolve does.
sparks.apply: Book the conversation you have been avoiding for a time in the next three days, and write your opening two sentences before you book it.

carousel.title: Name the discomfort
carousel.body: Open by saying this is hard to raise and that you are raising it anyway. Naming the awkwardness lowers it for both of you and signals that you are not attacking.

carousel.title: State only what happened
carousel.body: Describe observable facts with no adjectives: what was said, what was late, what the effect was. Anything the other person could reasonably dispute belongs in a later step.

carousel.title: Offer your interpretation
carousel.body: Say what you have concluded and flag it as your read rather than the truth. This is the step that gives them room to correct you without a fight.

carousel.title: Ask for theirs, then wait
carousel.body: Ask how they see it and then tolerate the silence. The first answer is usually defensive; the useful one arrives after a pause you did not fill.

carousel.title: Agree what changes
carousel.body: End with a specific behaviour, a date, and who checks. Without this the conversation was catharsis rather than management, and you will be having it again.

sparks.hook: Nobody decides to trust you. They accumulate reasons in tiny amounts.
sparks.insight: Trust is not granted in one moment by one impressive act. It is deposited in fragments so small that neither side consciously registers them: remembering the name of somebody's daughter, not repeating what was said to you privately, admitting a mistake before anyone else found it, arriving when you said you would. Each is trivial on its own. The total is the only thing that will hold weight when you eventually need it, and there is no way to make a large deposit quickly.
sparks.why: Trust is built by accumulation rather than by declaration, so the timeline cannot be compressed. This also explains why one breach costs so much: it puts every earlier deposit back under review.
sparks.apply: Write down three small commitments to three different people this week, keep every one of them, and make sure none of the three is impressive.

sparks.hook: Telling your team how stressed you are is not the same as being brave.
sparks.insight: Vulnerability at work gets confused with disclosure, and the two are close to opposite. Unloading your anxiety onto your team hands them a job they did not ask for: managing you. Real exposure is narrower and much harder. It is asking for help in front of people you manage, saying you were wrong when nobody had caught you, taking an unpopular position first, or shipping something you know is unfinished. What makes it vulnerable is the risk you are carrying, not the emotion you are showing.
sparks.why: The distinction is between exposure with no guaranteed outcome and emotional offloading. Only the first builds credibility; the second transfers the burden downward while looking like openness.
sparks.apply: Ask for help with something concrete in front of your team this week, from someone who reports to you, and let it be genuinely useful help.

sparks.hook: Guilt says the work was bad. Shame says you are. Only one helps.
sparks.insight: Feedback aimed at a person's character does not produce better work, it produces defence or collapse. Telling somebody they were careless attacks who they are, and there is no available response except denial or shrinking. Telling them the report went out with three wrong figures attacks a thing that happened, which leaves an obvious path forward. The difference is not politeness — both versions can be blunt. The difference is whether the target is a behaviour they can change or an identity they must defend.
sparks.why: Research on self-conscious emotions consistently finds that focusing on the act supports repair while focusing on the self drives concealment and withdrawal. In a team, concealment is the more expensive outcome.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your next piece of critical feedback so every sentence names an action or an effect, and no sentence contains an adjective about the person.

sparks.hook: Half of poor performance is somebody guessing what finished looks like.
sparks.insight: You hold a detailed picture of the finished thing. The person doing the work holds a much vaguer one, assembled from a short brief and some guessing. They then work hard in a direction you did not intend, and both of you experience the result as a performance problem. It is a specification problem. Describing the finished state in tedious detail before anyone starts feels condescending and takes twenty minutes. Reworking a week of misdirected effort costs considerably more than that.
sparks.why: Expectation gaps are invisible to the person who holds the fuller picture, so they surface only at delivery. The cost is always paid at the end, when it is most expensive to correct.
sparks.apply: Before handing over the next piece of work, describe out loud what the finished version looks like and ask them to describe it back to you.

carousel.title: Describe the finished thing
carousel.body: Say what it looks like when it is done, in concrete terms: the format, the audience, the length, the decision it should enable. Vagueness here gets paid for later.

carousel.title: Name the hard constraints
carousel.body: Budget, deadline, the two things that must not change, the person who has to approve it. Constraints discovered late feel like moving goalposts to whoever is doing the work.

carousel.title: Say what good enough is
carousel.body: Not every task deserves the best version you can imagine. Say explicitly whether this is a rough draft, a solid working version, or something that has to be perfect.

carousel.title: Have it repeated back
carousel.body: Ask them to describe the finished thing in their own words. The gap between their version and yours is the rework you have just avoided paying for.

sparks.hook: A value you have never said no because of is just a pleasant word.
sparks.insight: Most organisations hold a list of values long enough that nobody can recite it, which is the same as having none. A value only functions if it can lose you something: a deal you turned down, a strong candidate you did not hire, a launch you delayed. Cut the list to two, define what each one looks like as an observable behaviour, define what violating it looks like, and then use them out loud in an actual decision. Anything else is decoration on a wall.
sparks.why: A value that never constrains a choice cannot be distinguished from a preference. Naming the behaviour that breaches it is what makes the value testable rather than aspirational.
sparks.apply: Cut your team's values to two, write one behaviour that demonstrates each and one that breaches it, then use them in your next real decision.

carousel.title: Cut the list to two
carousel.body: More than two and nobody remembers them, including you. Choose the two you would defend when defending them costs money, not the two that sound best in a deck.

carousel.title: Turn each into a behaviour
carousel.body: Write the specific thing a person does that shows this value in a normal week. If you cannot picture somebody doing it on a Tuesday, it is still an abstraction.

carousel.title: Write the violation
carousel.body: Describe what breaching each value looks like, precisely enough that people recognise it in themselves. A value with no visible breach cannot guide any decision.

carousel.title: Invite the audit
carousel.body: Ask your team where you personally fall short of the two, and thank whoever answers honestly. Values you exempt yourself from stop being values within a fortnight.

sparks.hook: Empathy is not agreeing with them. It is recognising the feeling.
sparks.insight: When somebody brings you something painful, the standard reflexes make it worse. Silver linings, comparisons to a worse situation, and immediate problem-solving all quietly say the feeling is the wrong reaction and should stop. What actually connects is much plainer: recognise the emotion, say you can see why it lands that way, and resist filling the silence. You do not have to agree with their read of the situation to acknowledge that the experience is real, and the acknowledgement is what lets them move.
sparks.why: Attempts to fix the feeling read as dismissal, which is why they reliably produce more distress. Naming the emotion without judging it is the move that lowers it.
sparks.apply: Next time someone brings you a problem, say what emotion you think they are feeling and check whether you got it right before offering anything else.

actions: Book the conversation you have been avoiding for a slot within three days, and write your opening two sentences before you book it.
Cut your team's stated values to two, write the behaviour that demonstrates each and the behaviour that breaches each, then publish both.
Rewrite the last piece of critical feedback you gave so that every sentence names an action or effect rather than a trait.
Ask three people what they need from you that they have not asked for, then act visibly on at least one answer within a week.
books.not_for_you_if: You want measured research rather than themes drawn from interviews, or the emotional vocabulary will feel like an obstacle rather than a tool.

verification.notes: First published October 2018 by Random House. Built on the author's grounded-theory interview work, which is qualitative rather than experimental; the sparks describe the ideas in original wording only.

books.title: Extreme Ownership
books.subtitle: How U.S. Navy SEALs Lead and Win
books.author: Jocko Willink and Leif Babin
books.why_it_matters: It made total accountability a usable operating stance rather than a slogan, and it is unusually clear about the practical mechanics of planning, prioritising under pressure and getting a team to act without waiting for instructions.

crux.headline: If it happened in your area, it is yours to own
crux.body: The most useful thing a leader can do with a failure is refuse every available excuse. Not because the excuses are false — the brief really was unclear, the other team really did miss the deadline — but because as long as the cause sits outside you, there is nothing you can change. Taking ownership of everything in your area, including the parts you did not cause, is what converts a complaint into a problem you can actually work on. It is a stance chosen for its usefulness.

sparks.hook: The moment you find someone else to blame, you stop being able to fix it.
sparks.insight: Blame is usually accurate and always useless. When a project fails, there genuinely are contributing causes outside your control, and cataloguing them changes nothing about your next attempt. Taking ownership of the whole outcome is a deliberate move that hands you the only lever you have. It also propagates: a team whose leader visibly absorbs the failure stops constructing defences, and starts spending that energy on the actual problem. Nobody below you will own anything you refuse to own first.
sparks.why: The stance is chosen for its effects rather than its accuracy. Attributing failure externally is psychologically comfortable and removes every route to improvement, which is why capable teams treat it as a warning sign.
sparks.apply: Take the last thing that went wrong and write down your contribution to it, without a single sentence about anybody else.

sparks.hook: Swap the leaders between a failing team and a winning one, and watch.
sparks.insight: The claim is that performance follows leadership more than it follows the composition of a team, illustrated by boat crews in selection training where moving the leaders moved the results. It is a memorable demonstration and it is one anecdote from a highly unusual environment, so hold it loosely. What is more defensible is the practical version: before concluding you have a weak team, check what the person leading it is doing, because that is the variable you can change fastest and it is the one nobody examines.
sparks.why: This rests on a single training anecdote rather than a controlled comparison, and selection environments are unlike workplaces. The weaker version — check leadership before blaming the team — survives the scrutiny.
sparks.apply: Take your lowest-performing team and spend a week observing how it is led before you make any change to who is on it.

sparks.hook: If you cannot explain why, do not pass the instruction down.
sparks.insight: Managers routinely relay decisions they do not understand, and the team hears the uncertainty regardless of the words. The alternative is to go back up and ask until you can explain the reasoning in your own words. Sometimes you will discover the decision is worse than you thought and you have a case to make. Usually you will find a rationale nobody bothered to communicate. Either way, relaying an order you cannot justify teaches your team that reasons are optional here.
sparks.why: A leader's visible conviction is a large part of what makes a decision executable. Passing along an instruction while privately disagreeing produces compliance without effort, which looks like agreement and performs like resistance.
sparks.apply: Before relaying the next decision from above, write the reason in your own words. If you cannot, go back and ask before you announce it.

sparks.hook: If the newest person cannot repeat the plan, the plan is too complicated.
sparks.insight: Complex plans fail under pressure because pressure removes the capacity to hold them. The test is simple and slightly humiliating: ask the most junior person to explain what happens and what they do if the first step goes wrong. If the answer is vague, the problem is not their attention. It is that you have built something that only works while everyone is calm, well-briefed and reading from the document. Simplicity is not a lack of ambition; it is what allows an ambitious plan to survive contact with a bad day.
