sparks.hook: The postwar boom was the exception. We keep mistaking it for the rule.
sparks.insight: People who came of age between the nineteen fifties and the nineteen eighties grew up inside an unusual window: capital had been destroyed by two wars and a depression, taxes on high incomes and estates were punishing, and growth was fast because of reconstruction and a rising population. Inequality fell and mobility rose. Then the special conditions expired. The long historical pattern has been reasserting itself since, which feels like decline only because we benchmarked against an anomaly.
sparks.why: The compression of wealth in the mid twentieth century is visible in the records of several countries at once, and lines up with the destruction of capital and the tax regimes of the period rather than with any smooth market process.
sparks.apply: Check whether your assumptions about housing, pensions or careers come from your parents' era. Ask what conditions made that era work before you plan around it.

sparks.hook: Wealth is far more concentrated than income, and it is not close.
sparks.insight: Debates about inequality usually quote income, because income is what tax systems measure well. Wealth tells a much sharper story. In most rich countries the bottom half of the population holds almost no net assets at all, while the top tenth holds the majority of everything. That gap matters because wealth buys security, opportunity and political attention in a way that a monthly salary does not. Two households on identical incomes can live in different countries.
sparks.why: Wealth accumulates and inherits while income resets each year, so the same forces produce a much longer tail. Measuring wealth is harder, and figures vary with how pensions and housing are counted.
sparks.apply: Calculate your household net worth once, not your salary. Then work out how many months it would cover with no income at all.

sparks.hook: Bigger fortunes tend to earn better returns than small ones.
sparks.insight: The return on capital is not the same for everyone. Large fortunes can afford professional management, take illiquid positions, wait out bad decades, pay for tax structuring and access investments that small savers cannot reach. Records from large university endowments show the biggest funds consistently outperforming the smallest ones. If returns rise with size, then concentration feeds itself, and the gap widens even when everybody behaves identically well.
sparks.why: Scale buys diversification, patience and expertise, all of which raise risk-adjusted returns. The endowment comparison is one of the cleaner pieces of evidence because the institutions publish comparable long-run figures.
sparks.apply: Cut the two costs that scale away from small investors: fees and forced selling. Use low-cost index funds and hold enough cash to avoid selling at the wrong time.

sparks.hook: Top pay is set by committees and norms, not by a market for talent.
sparks.insight: The rise in top incomes in English-speaking countries is driven less by owners of capital than by senior corporate managers whose pay climbed away from everyone else's. The justification is that they produce proportionate value, but nobody can measure an individual executive's contribution to a large firm with any precision. What actually determines the number is bargaining power, a compensation committee, comparison with peer companies, and the prevailing social tolerance for large gaps.
sparks.why: Marginal productivity is unobservable at the top of a big organisation, so pay gets set by norms and process. Countries with similar firms and different norms produce very different executive pay, which is hard to explain by talent alone.
sparks.apply: When judging any pay claim, ask what would have happened to output if the person had not been there. If nobody can answer, you are looking at bargaining, not measurement.

sparks.hook: The real contribution is the data, not the prediction.
sparks.insight: Long before the argument, there was a decade of unglamorous work assembling income and estate records from national archives across several countries and centuries. That series is what made the debate possible, and it remains in use by researchers who disagree strongly with the conclusions drawn from it. Theories in economics are cheap and plentiful. Consistent long-run measurement is rare, expensive and slow, and it is what actually moves a field.
sparks.why: Once a shared dataset exists, arguments become testable instead of rhetorical. That is why the database has outlived the specific forecasts and is cited by critics as often as by supporters.
sparks.apply: In any argument you care about, spend your next hour improving the measurement rather than sharpening the position. Better data settles more than better rhetoric.

sparks.hook: Serious economists attacked the numbers, and some of the hits landed.
sparks.insight: A financial newspaper published an analysis alleging errors and questionable adjustments in the wealth series, particularly for Britain. The author replied in detail and most economists concluded the central pattern survived, though not every adjustment was well documented. Separately, other researchers argued that much of the rise in the capital share comes from housing rather than from productive capital, which changes what policy would follow. None of that makes the book worthless. It makes it a live argument.
sparks.why: Long historical series require judgement calls where records are patchy, and those calls deserve scrutiny. Knowing which parts are contested is the difference between using a book and quoting it.
sparks.apply: Before citing any headline finding, spend ten minutes reading its strongest published critic. Note which parts of the claim survive that reading and which do not.

sparks.hook: Slow growth is what makes old money powerful again.
sparks.insight: When an economy grows quickly, each generation builds so much that inherited wealth is small in comparison, and a person can plausibly out-earn their family history. When growth slows to the low rates that ageing rich countries now show, existing stocks of wealth loom much larger relative to annual output, and inheritance regains the importance it had in the nineteenth century. Demographic slowdown is therefore not just a fiscal problem, it is a distributional one.
sparks.why: The ratio of accumulated wealth to yearly income rises mechanically as growth falls, even with no change in saving behaviour. That ratio is what determines how much inheritance matters relative to work.
sparks.apply: When you read a growth forecast, translate it into a question about inheritance: in that world, does what your family owns matter more or less than what you earn?

sparks.hook: The proposed remedy is a tax the author admits is nearly impossible.
sparks.insight: The suggested response is a coordinated tax on wealth levied across borders, so that capital cannot simply move to whichever country charges least. The proposal is honest about its own unlikelihood, which is unusual in a policy book. Its more practical descendant is the push for automatic exchange of financial information between tax authorities, which has actually happened. National wealth taxes tried alone have mostly been repealed, because capital left or the administrative cost exceeded the revenue.
sparks.why: Mobile capital defeats an uncoordinated tax, so the enforcement problem is real rather than ideological. The information-sharing agreements that did arrive show the transparency half of the idea was more achievable than the tax half.
sparks.apply: When you meet any policy proposal, ask who has to cooperate for it to work. If the answer is every country at once, treat it as a direction rather than a plan.

sparks.hook: Education alone cannot outrun compounding capital.
sparks.insight: The standard answer to inequality is more schooling and better skills, on the argument that technology rewards the educated and the fix is to educate more people. Skills matter enormously for individuals, and the evidence for that is strong. But the top of the wealth distribution is not made of people with slightly better qualifications. It is made of accumulated assets and the returns on them, and no amount of training changes the arithmetic that separates a salary from a portfolio.
sparks.why: Skill-based explanations account for much of the spread within wages, but very little of the concentration at the very top, which is dominated by capital income and inheritance rather than pay.
sparks.apply: Treat education as your defence against the middle of the distribution and ownership as your only exposure to the top. Build both rather than assuming one covers the other.

carousel.title: Separate the two questions
carousel.body: Inequality among wage earners and concentration at the very top have different causes. A policy or a plan that addresses one will usually do nothing about the other.

carousel.title: See what skills do
carousel.body: Better skills reliably move an individual up the wage ladder. That is a strong, well-supported result and worth acting on for your own life.

carousel.title: See what they do not do
carousel.body: No qualification converts a salary into a compounding asset base. Above a point, the distribution is decided by ownership, not by credentials or effort.

carousel.title: Act on both fronts
carousel.body: Keep raising your earning power, and convert a fixed share of what it produces into assets. One without the other leaves you exposed to whichever engine runs faster.

actions: Calculate your household net worth and the share of it that came from saving versus from asset prices rising. Repeat the exercise once a year.
Read one serious published critique of the book alongside it, and write down which of its claims you still hold and which you have downgraded.
Find the wealth distribution figures for your own country and locate roughly where your household sits, in wealth rather than income terms.
Set an automatic monthly transfer that converts a fixed percentage of your earnings into owned assets, so the conversion does not depend on your attention.
books.not_for_you_if: You want practical investing advice, or you have no appetite for several hundred pages of historical statistics before you reach a conclusion.

verification.notes: First published in French in 2013, English translation 2014. The 2014 Financial Times challenge to the wealth series and the housing-driven critique of the capital share are both flagged in the sparks.

books.title: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits
books.author: Philip A. Fisher
books.why_it_matters: It made the case that a small number of genuinely excellent companies, held for decades, beat constant trading in cheap ones. It is the qualitative half of modern value investing, and Buffett has credited it with reshaping how he judges businesses.

crux.headline: Judge the organisation, not just the accounts
crux.body: Financial statements tell you what a company has already done. What decides the next twenty years is harder to measure: whether research produces products customers want, whether the sales operation can carry them, whether managers are honest when nobody is watching, and whether talented people below the top job are being developed. Find a few companies that pass on those grounds, buy them, and then do very little.

sparks.hook: The most useful facts about a company are not in its report.
sparks.insight: Before buying, talk to the people who deal with the business: customers who chose it over rivals, suppliers who see how it pays and plans, former employees who know how decisions get made, and competitors who will tell you frankly what they fear about it. A pattern emerges quickly, and it is usually a truer picture of competitive position than any set of ratios. Published numbers describe the past. These conversations describe the machine that will produce the future.
sparks.why: Information that requires effort to assemble is less likely to be in the price than information anyone can download. The edge comes from the legwork, not from cleverness.
sparks.apply: For one company you are considering, speak to three people outside it who deal with it professionally before you buy a single share.

sparks.hook: Growth that lasts comes from a machine, not a product.
sparks.insight: A single successful product gives you a decade at best. What compounds is an organisation that reliably converts research spending into new products the market wants, and has a sales operation capable of carrying them. Look for evidence that this has happened repeatedly, across different product cycles and different managers. One hit is luck. Three, in different areas, under different conditions, is a system you can underwrite for years ahead.
sparks.why: Repeatability is the test that separates a durable compounder from a company enjoying one favourable cycle. Single-product firms hit a ceiling that no valuation discount fixes.
sparks.apply: List the products a company depends on today. If most existed a decade ago, treat its growth forecasts sceptically.

sparks.hook: One question about management outranks every other: are they honest?
sparks.insight: Ability without integrity is a liability, because a capable management team acting in its own interest will extract value more efficiently than an incompetent one. Watch how they discuss failure. Honest managers describe problems specifically, before they are forced to, and tell you what they got wrong. Evasive ones describe headwinds. Since you are handing over your money for years, the character question is not soft, it is the hardest constraint in the analysis.
sparks.why: Governance failures rarely show in ratios until after the damage. The available early signal is behavioural: how candidly a management team reports bad news when it has the option not to.
sparks.apply: Read three years of shareholder letters back to back and note every prediction made. Check which ones they later acknowledged missing.

sparks.hook: Ask whether the company is worth owning before asking what it costs.
sparks.insight: Most analysis starts with the price and works backwards to a justification. Reverse the order. First establish whether this is a business you would be content to own for a decade if the market closed tomorrow. Only then examine the price. Doing it this way stops you from talking yourself into a mediocre company because it looks statistically cheap, which is the most common way careful investors lose money slowly.
sparks.why: A cheap price on a deteriorating business is a value trap: the discount widens as earnings fall, so the apparent margin of safety evaporates exactly when you need it.
sparks.apply: Write your case for owning a company without mentioning its share price. If the case is thin, the price is irrelevant.

carousel.title: Test the runway
carousel.body: Does the market this company serves still have years of growth left, or is it saturated and defending share on price alone?

carousel.title: Check the margins
carousel.body: Look at profit margins over a full cycle and ask what protects them. Margins with no explanation behind them are usually temporary.

carousel.title: Look below the chief executive
carousel.body: Depth of management decides whether the company survives a succession. Ask whether capable people are being developed or quietly leaving.

carousel.title: Then, and only then, price it
carousel.body: Value the business you have just described. If it fails any earlier step, no price makes it a good long-term holding.

sparks.hook: There are only three good reasons to sell, and none is that the price rose.
sparks.insight: Sell when you realise your original analysis was mistaken. Sell when the company itself has deteriorated so it no longer meets the standard you bought it for. Sell to move into something clearly better, and only when the difference is large enough to survive the tax bill. Everything else is noise: a run of bad quarters, a scary headline, a price that feels high. Selling a genuinely excellent business because it went up is the most expensive habit in investing.
sparks.why: Compounding is destroyed by interruption. Each sale realises tax and forces two correct decisions, while great businesses do most of their work in the years after they already look expensive.
sparks.apply: Write your three sell conditions for each holding at the moment you buy it, and refuse to sell for any reason not on that list.

sparks.hook: Owning forty stocks you barely know is not diversification, it is dilution.
sparks.insight: If you have genuinely done the deep work, you will find only a handful of companies that qualify. Spreading money thinly across dozens means most of your capital sits in your fifteenth-best idea, and you cannot possibly follow them all closely enough to notice when one deteriorates. A concentrated portfolio of businesses you understand, in different industries, is safer in practice than a wide one you are only nominally tracking.
sparks.why: The caveat is real: concentration raises the cost of being wrong, so it is only defensible if the research is genuinely deep and the businesses are not exposed to the same shock.
sparks.apply: Rank your holdings by how well you could defend them under questioning. Sell from the bottom until only defensible ones remain.

sparks.hook: Haggling over a few cents has cost people entire positions.
sparks.insight: When you have decided a company is outstanding and you intend to hold it for a decade, placing a limit order slightly below the market to feel clever is a bad trade. Often the price never returns, the shares run away, and you own nothing at all. The decision that matters is whether to own the business. The entry price matters at the margin, and the margin is tiny next to a decade of compounding.
sparks.why: The asymmetry is stark: saving a fraction of a percent on entry against the risk of missing the whole position. That trade only makes sense if your conviction was weak to begin with.
sparks.apply: Once your research is finished and the price is reasonable, buy the position in full rather than waiting for a slightly better print.

sparks.hook: Dividends are the least interesting thing a great company can do with cash.
sparks.insight: If a business can reinvest its earnings at high rates of return, every pound paid out is a pound not compounding inside a machine that works. Prefer companies that can genuinely redeploy capital, and be suspicious of a rising payout ratio at a firm that claims to be growing. The exception matters too: when a company has run out of good projects, paying cash out is the honest choice and hoarding it is the destructive one.
sparks.why: The mechanism is return on incremental capital. Reinvestment beats distribution only while the company earns more on that money than you could elsewhere, which is a testable question.
sparks.apply: Check what a company earned on the capital it reinvested over five years before you treat its dividend as good news.

sparks.hook: Forecasting the economy is a different job from owning good businesses.
sparks.insight: People delay buying an excellent company because a recession seems likely. Recessions are hard to time, usually recognised only after they have begun, and an outstanding business generally emerges from one with stronger competitive position. Waiting for macro clarity means waiting permanently, since clarity arrives only in hindsight. The useful question is not what the economy will do next year but whether this company will be larger and stronger in ten.
sparks.why: Macro forecasts have a poor documented record even among professionals, while company-level durability is at least partly assessable from evidence you can gather yourself.
sparks.apply: Ban macro forecasts from your buy decision. Replace the question with: will this business be stronger in ten years, and why?

sparks.hook: This method is expensive if you do half of it.
sparks.insight: The approach demands deep research on few companies and then decades of patience. Done properly it has produced remarkable results. Done partially, it becomes buying a story you like at any price and refusing to sell when the thesis breaks, which is how people justify holding a collapsing company for years. The discipline that makes concentration safe is the research and the written sell conditions, not the optimism.
sparks.why: Selection bias flatters the record here: the famous long holds are remembered, the great companies that stagnated for a decade less so. The method only works with genuine analytical depth.
sparks.apply: Before concentrating, run your process on one company end to end and time it honestly. Then decide if you can repeat that.

actions: Pick one company and spend a month gathering opinions from its customers, suppliers and former employees before forming any view on its shares.
Write a checklist of qualitative tests you require of any company: growth runway, margin protection, management depth and candour.
For every current holding, write down the three specific conditions under which you would sell, and file them with the purchase date.
Cut your portfolio to the companies you can defend in detail, and put the freed money into a broad index fund instead.
books.not_for_you_if: You will not do company research, or you want current examples. The cases come from mid-century American manufacturing and the writing is dated.

verification.notes: First published 1958. Fisher ran a small investment counselling firm in California; his son Ken Fisher is also an investor and writer. Later editions bundle his subsequent essays. All prose original.

books.title: Doughnut Economics
books.subtitle: Seven Ways to Think Like a 21st-Century Economist
books.author: Kate Raworth
books.why_it_matters: It gave the case against growth at all costs a picture simple enough to redraw policy conversations, and cities from Amsterdam onward have used it as a planning frame. Whether or not you accept the conclusion, it forces you to name what an economy is actually for.

crux.headline: An economy should have a floor and a ceiling
crux.body: Draw two rings. The inner one is the minimum every person needs: food, water, housing, health, energy, a political voice. The outer one is what the planet can absorb before its systems break. The safe and just space is the ring between them, and the job of an economy is to get everyone into it. Growth is not the target. It is one tool, useful when it moves people into the ring and harmful when it pushes through the outer edge.

sparks.hook: Ask what an economy is for and most models go quiet.
sparks.insight: Twentieth-century economics inherited a goal by accident: more output, measured as GDP, forever. Nobody argued for it as an aim. It became the default because it was the number being collected. Once you say the aim out loud, its strangeness shows. A country can raise measured output by rebuilding after a flood, by treating preventable illness, or by emptying a fishery in a decade. The measure counts all three as success.
sparks.why: GDP was designed in the 1930s and 1940s to track wartime production, and its own architects warned against reading it as a measure of national welfare. The warning was ignored for eighty years.
sparks.apply: For your organisation or household, write down the one number you optimise for, then list two ways it could rise while things actually get worse.

sparks.hook: The economy is not a closed loop with money going round.
sparks.insight: The diagram most people carry in their heads shows firms and households exchanging money and labour, sealed off from everything else. Energy does not appear. Neither does unpaid care work, the household, the commons, or the atmosphere absorbing the waste. A model that leaves out its own foundations makes those foundations invisible to policy, which is how an economy can look healthy while running down the two things it entirely depends on: a society and a biosphere.
sparks.why: What a diagram omits shapes what its users treat as a cost. Ecological limits and unpaid work were not argued away, they were simply left off the picture and therefore stopped being counted.
sparks.apply: Redraw your team or company's value chain including every input you do not pay for. Mark the ones you would be unable to replace at any price.

sparks.hook: Two rings, and the safe place to live is between them.
sparks.insight: The picture is one reason the argument travelled so far. An inner boundary marks the social floor nobody should fall below. An outer one marks the ecological limits the planet cannot absorb overshooting. Humanity is currently failing on both edges at once: hundreds of millions below the floor while several Earth systems are already past their ceiling. Framed that way, the task stops being growth against environment and becomes a design problem with two constraints.
sparks.why: The outer ring draws on the planetary boundaries framework published by Earth-system scientists in 2009. The inner ring draws on the social priorities governments themselves agreed in the Sustainable Development Goals.
sparks.apply: Pick one boundary, inner or outer, that your work touches. Find the current published figure for it and put that number where you plan.

carousel.title: Set the social floor
carousel.body: Food, water, health, education, housing, energy, income, political voice, gender equality. Below this line a life is stripped of essentials, and no economy leaving people there is succeeding.

carousel.title: Set the ecological ceiling
carousel.body: Climate, freshwater, land use, biodiversity, nutrient cycles, ocean acidity. Past these limits, Earth systems shift into states nobody has ever run an economy inside.

carousel.title: Aim for the ring between
carousel.body: The doughnut is the space where human needs are met within planetary means. It is a target you can miss in two opposite directions, and that is exactly the point.

carousel.title: Design toward it
carousel.body: Judge every policy, product or budget by whether it moves people into the ring. Growth counts when it does that and does not count automatically otherwise.

sparks.hook: Rational economic man is a portrait nobody has ever met.
sparks.insight: The standard actor in economic models is solitary, calculating, endlessly self-interested and fixed in his tastes. Real people are social, reciprocal, dependent on others, roughly rather than precisely calculating, and changed by their circumstances. This matters beyond realism, because teaching the caricature appears to nudge people a little closer to it. Design institutions for the portrait and you will slowly get the portrait.
sparks.why: Studies showing economics students behaving more self-interestedly exist but are contested, since selection into the subject may explain much of the gap. The weaker claim, that models shape institutions and institutions shape behaviour, is solid.
sparks.apply: Look at one incentive scheme you run and ask what kind of person it assumes. Then ask what kind of person a year of it will produce.

sparks.hook: Economies do not sit at equilibrium waiting to be nudged.
sparks.insight: Much of the discipline models an economy as a machine that returns to balance after a shock. Complex systems do not behave that way. They have feedback loops that amplify, thresholds they cross irreversibly, and outcomes that depend on the path taken. Inequality and pollution both compound: money buys influence that protects money, warming melts ice that would have reflected heat. Under those dynamics, waiting for self-correction is a decision to let the loop run.
sparks.why: Complex-systems models reproduce crashes and lock-in better than equilibrium ones, though they forecast poorly and are harder to test, which is part of why the discipline adopted them slowly.
sparks.apply: Draw the reinforcing loop behind a problem you keep re-solving, then look for the one link you could cut instead of the symptom you keep treating.

sparks.hook: Inequality is not a phase that economies grow out of.
sparks.insight: A famous curve suggested that inequality rises as a country industrialises and then falls once it is rich enough, which made concentration look like weather you could wait out. The evidence for the second half is weak, and inequality rose sharply in rich countries after 1980 while they kept growing. That changes the job. If distribution does not fix itself, it has to be designed in through who owns things, not only through taxing results afterwards.
sparks.why: Kuznets himself hedged the claim, and later data undercut it. The mid-century fall in inequality owed much to war, depression and deliberate policy, and growth alone has no reliable equalising mechanism.
sparks.apply: Look at where value ends up in something you run, across wages, ownership, land and patents, and change one structural share rather than one payment.

sparks.hook: Cleaning up later is a promise nobody has kept at scale.
sparks.insight: The parallel hope for the environment is that countries pollute while poor and clean up once rich. Rich countries did clean their local air and rivers, but largely by importing manufactured goods and exporting the emissions, while global emissions kept climbing. A system that produces waste and then pays to reduce it is degenerative by construction. The alternative is to design so that the output of one process is the input to another.
sparks.why: The environmental Kuznets curve holds for some visible local pollutants and fails for carbon once consumption-based accounting assigns offshored emissions back to the countries consuming the goods.
sparks.apply: Take one product or process you own and follow its waste to the end of the line. Redesign the single largest flow so it becomes an input somewhere.

sparks.hook: The country that has stopped growing safely does not exist yet.
sparks.insight: Modern economies are structurally dependent on expansion. Pensions, debt, tax revenue and employment all assume it, so a stall produces a crisis rather than a plateau. The proposal is not to force a halt but to become agnostic: build systems that stay stable whether or not output rises, so that the question of growth stops being an emergency. That is a genuinely unsolved engineering problem, and it is the weakest, most speculative part of the argument.
sparks.why: Raworth is candid that nobody has built a post-growth economy. Critics argue the diagnosis is much stronger than the prescription, and on this point they have a case worth taking seriously.
sparks.apply: Stress-test one plan you own against zero growth for three years. The commitments that break first are your real dependencies.

sparks.hook: Whoever draws the picture sets the terms of the argument.
sparks.insight: Ideas spread as images long before they spread as arguments. Two lines crossing on a chart shaped a century of intuition about prices, mostly without anyone examining what the picture assumed. The doughnut works the same way and is honest about it: two rings, a safe space, a visible failure on each edge. If you want to change how a group thinks, giving them a better diagram often beats giving them a better paper.
sparks.why: The frame has been adopted by cities including Amsterdam for planning, which is evidence that the picture travels. Adoption is not the same as measured results, and it is still early.
sparks.apply: Turn the argument you keep losing into a single diagram with two boundaries or two axes, then test whether people repeat it back to you.

sparks.hook: A theory is a description that starts changing what it describes.
sparks.insight: Physics does not alter the particle. Economics alters the economy, because governments, firms and citizens act on its models. Rules built on the assumption of selfish, endlessly acquisitive actors reward exactly those behaviours, and the results then appear to confirm the assumption. So the choice of model is not purely a scientific question about accuracy. It is partly a decision about the world you are building, which makes it everyone's business.
sparks.why: The effect is well documented in finance, where options markets came to fit the Black-Scholes model more closely after traders adopted it. The broader claim is harder to test, though the mechanism is real.
sparks.apply: Ask what behaviour your own metrics reward, then interview one person they apply to about what they actually do because of them.

actions: Draw your organisation's own doughnut: the social floor it must not breach and the resource ceiling it must stay within, with a real number on each.
Replace one growth target with a target defined by a floor and a ceiling, and run both in parallel for a quarter to compare the decisions they produce.
Find whether your city or country has an existing doughnut-style assessment and read what it says the local failures actually are.
Audit one incentive you control for the model of human nature it assumes, then rewrite it for people who are social and reciprocal.
books.not_for_you_if: You want detailed policy mechanisms or formal modelling. This reframes the goal rather than specifying how to hit it, and critics find the prescriptions thin.

verification.notes: First published 2017 by Random House Business. The planetary boundaries framework is the work of Rockstrom, Steffen and colleagues, published in 2009.

books.title: Fooled by Randomness
books.subtitle: The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets
books.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
books.why_it_matters: It made a generation of investors ask whether a track record is evidence of skill at all. The arguments about survivorship, rare events and mistaking noise for signal have since become standard vocabulary well outside finance.

crux.headline: Success is a poor witness for its own causes
crux.body: When many people try something risky, some will succeed spectacularly by chance alone, and those are the ones who write books, give interviews and get imitated. Their explanations feel convincing because humans construct causes for everything. To judge any strategy you must ask about the outcomes that were possible but did not happen, and about all the people who followed the same approach and vanished.

sparks.hook: Give enough people a coin and someone flips ten heads. Then they write a book.
sparks.insight: Start with thousands of traders following essentially random strategies. Purely by chance, a handful will string together five profitable years. Those few end up on magazine covers, and their methods get studied and copied, while the far larger number who failed leave no trace. The record you are looking at was selected precisely because it was extreme, which is why extreme records are such weak evidence of anything.
sparks.why: This is survivorship bias, and it is a mathematical certainty rather than a criticism of anyone. The larger the starting population, the more impressive the luckiest survivor will look.
sparks.apply: Before copying anyone's method, ask how many people started with the same approach and where those people are now.

sparks.hook: How likely something is matters less than what happens when it does.
sparks.insight: A bet that wins nine times out of ten can still be a terrible bet if the tenth outcome wipes you out, and a bet that loses most of the time can be excellent if the rare win is enormous. People reason about probability and ignore magnitude, which is why strategies that produce a steady drip of small gains feel so safe. The right question is not how often you are right. It is what the full distribution pays.
sparks.why: Expectation combines probability with size of outcome. Ignoring the size term is the single most common error in evaluating risky positions, in markets and in life.
sparks.apply: For your next decision, write the payoff for each outcome as well as its likelihood, then multiply before you judge it.

sparks.hook: Checking your portfolio hourly means drowning in noise you cannot use.
sparks.insight: Any signal in returns is buried under enormous short-term randomness. At a yearly horizon a good strategy shows up clearly. At a daily one it is almost invisible, and at a minute-by-minute one it is entirely obscured. Since losses feel worse than equivalent gains, frequent checking delivers a stream of small emotional injuries in exchange for no information. The optimal amount of attention is far lower than any app is designed to give you.
sparks.why: The proportion of signal to noise rises with the observation period. Combined with loss aversion, frequent monitoring reliably degrades both mood and decisions.
sparks.apply: Set a fixed schedule for reviewing your portfolio, monthly or quarterly, and remove price alerts from your phone entirely.

sparks.hook: Steady profits can be the accounting of a risk that has not arrived yet.
sparks.insight: Some strategies collect small reliable amounts by taking on a rare large loss: selling insurance against events that seldom occur, or holding positions that behave beautifully until the day they do not. For years the results look like skill, with smooth returns and impressive ratios. Then one event returns everything at once. The smoothness was never evidence of safety. It was the shape of the payoff, and it hid the exposure rather than removing it.
sparks.why: Rare events are underrepresented in short samples, so risk measures calibrated on recent history systematically understate them. The exposure is invisible until it is realised.
sparks.apply: For any smooth-returning investment, ask what would have to happen for it to lose a decade of gains, and how likely that truly is.

sparks.hook: The past is one path through a forest of paths that could have happened.
sparks.insight: History records what occurred, not what nearly occurred, so the world always looks more determined than it was. A decision that came within an inch of catastrophe is filed as a success. To assess anything properly you have to reconstruct the alternatives: the outcomes that were plausible at the time, in what proportion, and how the choice would have fared in each. That mental exercise is harder than remembering, which is why almost nobody does it.
sparks.why: Only one history is observed, so realised outcomes are a sample of size one. Judging decisions from them means grading a probability estimate on a single draw.
sparks.apply: After any significant outcome, write down three ways it could plausibly have gone instead, and how your decision would have fared.

carousel.title: Freeze what you knew
carousel.body: Write down the information available at the moment of the decision, without anything you learned afterwards. This is the only fair basis for judging it.

carousel.title: List the other endings
carousel.body: Name three or four outcomes that were genuinely possible from that starting point, including the ones that would have been unpleasant.

carousel.title: Score the decision in each
carousel.body: Ask how your choice would have fared across all of those worlds, not just the one that happened to occur.

carousel.title: Grade the process
carousel.body: A decision that only survives in the world that actually happened was a gamble that paid off. File it as luck, not as method.

sparks.hook: Nobody knows what will happen, but plenty of people know they are exposed.
sparks.insight: Prediction is nearly hopeless for complex systems. Exposure is knowable right now. You cannot say whether markets will fall next year, but you can say whether a fall would force you to sell, cancel your plans or borrow. Shifting attention from forecasting to exposure is the practical move, because it depends on facts about your own position rather than facts about the future that nobody possesses.
sparks.why: Exposure is a property of your balance sheet, which you can inspect. Probability of a rare event is estimated from thin data, which is exactly where estimation fails worst.
sparks.apply: Write down what a fifty percent market fall would force you to do. Change your position until the answer is nothing.

sparks.hook: Your brain builds a story for random data before you notice it happening.
sparks.insight: Pattern-finding is automatic and largely involuntary, which is useful when there are patterns and dangerous when there are none. Show anyone a random sequence and they will find trends, momentum and turning points in it, then explain the causes convincingly. Financial news exists to supply those explanations daily. Knowing this does not stop the mechanism, but it does let you discount your own confident narratives about why a price moved.
sparks.why: Explanation-generation is a fast automatic process, while probabilistic reasoning is slow and effortful. The fast one wins by default unless you deliberately install a check.
sparks.apply: When you catch yourself explaining a market move, write the explanation down and check a month later whether it held up.

sparks.hook: A thousand safe days is not proof that day one thousand and one is safe.
sparks.insight: Evidence accumulated from repeated observation can never establish that something will not happen. A creature fed daily by a farmer gathers steadily stronger evidence of the farmer's goodwill, right up until the day that theory is decisively refuted. Long records of stability are exactly what you would expect to see just before a rare event, which is why they should raise your caution rather than settle it.
sparks.why: This is the problem of induction. Absence of evidence for a rare event is nearly worthless as evidence of its absence, because the event is rare by definition.
sparks.apply: For any system you rely on, ask what a long clean record would look like just before a first failure. Then plan for that failure.

sparks.hook: You cannot reason your way out of feeling losses. Design around it instead.
sparks.insight: Understanding randomness intellectually does not stop the physical reaction to a falling portfolio. The emotional system that produces that reaction is not accessible to argument, and it will not improve with more knowledge. So the practical answer is structural: fewer decision points, automated contributions, positions small enough that no single one can dominate your mood, and rules written when you were calm and consulted when you are not.
sparks.why: Emotional responses to loss are fast, physiological and largely unmodifiable by reasoning. Structure works because it changes the situations you face rather than the reactions you have.
sparks.apply: Write your rules for buying and selling while markets are calm, and commit to consulting them before any decision made under stress.

sparks.hook: The argument is powerful but hard to falsify, which is worth saying out loud.
sparks.insight: Attributing success to luck and failure to bad luck can be made to fit any evidence, and the framework offers few rules for telling a genuinely skilled operator from a fortunate one in real time. Skill does exist in markets, and some records are long and varied enough to be meaningful. Treat the book as a corrective against confident narratives, not as proof that all performance is noise, which is a claim it does not actually establish.
sparks.why: An argument that cannot be contradicted by any observation is rhetorically strong and scientifically weak. That caution applies to this one as much as to the stories it attacks.
sparks.apply: When judging a track record, ask how long it is, how many regimes it covers, and what result would have changed your mind.

actions: Take one investor or fund you admire and find out how many peers began with a similar approach and how they fared, before drawing any conclusion about skill.
Rewrite your three biggest financial decisions as payoffs rather than predictions: what you gain, what you lose, and how likely each is.
Cut your portfolio checking to a fixed monthly slot and remove every price notification from your devices.
Stress-test your finances against a severe market fall and adjust until the answer to what you would be forced to do is nothing.
books.not_for_you_if: You want practical portfolio instructions, or you dislike digressive, opinionated writing that argues with people the author finds foolish.

verification.notes: First published 2001; a substantially revised second edition appeared in 2004 and is the version most people read. Taleb was an options trader before writing. All prose original.

books.title: Freakonomics
books.subtitle: A Rogue Economist Explores the Hidden Side of Everything
books.author: Steven D. Levitt and Stephen J. Dubner
books.why_it_matters: It moved economics off the subject of money and onto the subject of incentives, and taught a very large audience to ask what the numbers show rather than what the story implies. It also became a lesson in how confidently a popular finding can be stated and later disputed.

crux.headline: Follow the incentives, then go and check the data
crux.body: People respond to incentives, including the ones nobody meant to create. When an outcome looks strange, stop asking what people say they want and start asking what the system actually pays them for. Then go to the numbers, because the conventional explanation is usually the one that flatters whoever is telling it. The method is simple and portable. The conclusions, as later argument showed, are not always as durable as the method.

sparks.hook: A fine turned lateness into a service people were happy to buy.
sparks.insight: Nurseries in Israel tried to stop parents collecting children late by charging a small penalty. Lateness went up. The fine had quietly converted a social obligation into a price, and once there was a price, parents could pay it without guilt. Worse, when the fine was withdrawn the new behaviour stuck. Incentives are not knobs you turn up and down. They change what kind of situation people think they are in, and that change can outlast the incentive itself.
sparks.why: Money crowds out moral and social motives rather than adding to them. Once a relationship is priced it is hard to unprice, which is why removing the penalty did not restore the old behaviour.
sparks.apply: Before you attach a penalty or a bonus to anything, ask what the current behaviour is being held in place by. If the answer is shame or goodwill, leave it alone.

sparks.hook: Your agent sells your house faster than they sell their own.
sparks.insight: An estate agent earns a small slice of the sale price, so an extra week of effort to lift your price a little barely moves their pay. Their real incentive is volume: close quickly, move to the next client. Sales records suggest agents keep their own homes on the market longer and accept higher prices for them. The agent is not corrupt. The contract simply pays them for something slightly different from what you want, and nobody in the room says so.
sparks.why: Whenever one side knows more and is paid on a different metric, small misalignments in the contract produce predictable behaviour. The published effect is modest in size and has been debated, but the mechanism is real.
sparks.apply: For any adviser you pay, write out in one line how they earn money. Then ask what advice that formula rewards, and get a second opinion from someone paid differently.

sparks.hook: Cheating is hard to see and surprisingly easy to count.
sparks.insight: People who cheat leave a shape in the data even when no individual case looks suspicious. Teachers under pressure from test scores produced answer sheets with runs of identical corrections that random error does not generate. Sumo wrestlers with a tournament record on a knife edge won crucial bouts at rates that are difficult to explain by effort alone. You are not looking for a smoking gun. You are looking for a pattern that honest behaviour would not produce.
sparks.why: Individual cases are ambiguous, but aggregate patterns have expected distributions. Deviation from the expected shape is evidence, though it is statistical evidence rather than proof about any single person.
sparks.apply: Pick one number your team is judged on and ask what a person could do to move it without doing the underlying work. Then check whether the data shows that shape.

carousel.title: Find the pressure point
carousel.body: Cheating clusters where a threshold sits: a pass mark, a bonus target, a quota. Look for the place where a tiny difference in the number produces a large difference in someone's life.

carousel.title: Ask what honest data looks like
carousel.body: Work out the pattern you would expect if everyone behaved. Random error is messy in specific ways, and knowing that shape is what makes the deviation visible.

carousel.title: Look just above the line
carousel.body: Manipulation shows up as a pile-up of results barely clearing the threshold and a suspicious hole just below it. Nature rarely produces cliffs at round numbers.

carousel.title: Treat it as a lead
carousel.body: A statistical pattern tells you where to investigate, not who is guilty. Use it to open the file, and never as a verdict on an individual.

sparks.hook: The book's most famous claim is also its most contested one.
sparks.insight: The best known argument links the legalisation of abortion in the United States to the fall in crime roughly two decades later, on the reasoning that fewer unwanted children meant fewer young adults in high-risk circumstances. It is a striking piece of thinking. It is also disputed. Economists at the Boston Federal Reserve found a coding error and a specification problem in the underlying analysis, the authors responded, and the argument has run for years without a settled verdict.
sparks.why: Big social outcomes have many causes moving at once, and separating them from tax records and crime statistics is genuinely hard. Treat this as an open question that sharpened a method, not as an established fact.
sparks.apply: When a single elegant cause is offered for a large social change, write down three other things that changed in the same period before you accept it.

sparks.hook: Experts are paid to make you feel that you need an expert.
sparks.insight: Anyone who advises you on a problem also benefits from that problem seeming large and urgent. This does not require dishonesty. It works through emphasis: which risks get mentioned first, which numbers get quoted, which reassuring detail gets left out. Campaigners inflate the scale of a harm because attention follows size. Salespeople describe the worst case because fear closes deals. Once you notice the pattern you start reading advice as a document with an author and a motive.
sparks.why: The incentive to overstate is structural, not personal. It appears wherever the person describing a problem also profits from the response to it, which is most of the advice industry.
sparks.apply: Next time you are given a scary number, ask who produced it, how it was measured, and what they gain if you believe it. Then look for a source with no stake.

sparks.hook: Secrecy was the Klan's main asset, so someone gave it away.
sparks.insight: A hate group runs partly on mystique: private words, private rituals, the idea that it knows things you do not. An activist infiltrated the Ku Klux Klan and fed its inner language to the writers of a popular radio serial, where it was turned into material for children. Ridicule did what confrontation could not, because it attacked the thing the organisation was actually selling. Later reporting showed the activist overstated his own role, which the authors themselves acknowledged.
sparks.why: Groups that trade on secrecy are vulnerable to exposure rather than argument. The correction to the story matters too: it shows how a good anecdote can outrun the evidence behind it.
sparks.apply: When facing an organisation that relies on mystique, publish its ordinary details rather than debating its claims. Then check your best anecdote against a primary source.

sparks.hook: What parents are predicts more than what parenting books tell them to do.
sparks.insight: Comparing large samples of schoolchildren, the things that correlate with test scores are mostly characteristics the parents already had before the child arrived: education, income, the age at which they started a family, the books already in the house. The busy interventions that fill parenting advice, from museum trips to daily reading rituals, show far weaker links. The uncomfortable reading is that a lot of parenting effort is signalling rather than causation.
sparks.why: These are correlations from survey data, not experiments, so they cannot separate genes, environment and money cleanly. What they do show is that the confident causal claims in parenting advice rest on very little.
sparks.apply: Drop one parenting activity you do out of anxiety rather than enjoyment, and spend the time on something that improves the household everyone lives in.

sparks.hook: A name signals where you came from more than where you will end up.
sparks.insight: Naming patterns move down the income distribution over time: distinctive names appear first among wealthier, better educated parents and spread outward, so a name carries information about the household a child was born into. Comparing children with similar backgrounds, the name itself does not appear to determine their later outcomes. That is a genuinely useful correction to a common anxiety, but it sits awkwardly beside audit studies where identical applications with different names get different callback rates.
sparks.why: The two findings are about different things: long-run life outcomes within similar households, versus immediate discrimination by strangers reading a page. Both can be true, and the second is well replicated.
sparks.apply: When a study says something does not matter, check what it was compared against and over what timescale before you extend it to a different question.

sparks.hook: Most street dealers earned less than the minimum wage.
sparks.insight: A sociologist spent years with a crack-selling gang and came away with its actual accounts. The structure looked like a fast food franchise: a small number at the top took most of the money, while the people on the corner taking all the physical risk earned very little and often lived with their mothers. They stayed because the job was a tournament, and the visible winner at the top made the terrible odds feel survivable. Most tournament industries work the same way.
sparks.why: Tournament markets pay a huge premium to a few winners and near nothing to everyone else. People join by looking at the prize rather than the distribution, which is exactly what the prize is there to make them do.
sparks.apply: Before entering any winner-takes-most field, find out what the median participant earns, not the top one. Then decide with that number in front of you.

sparks.hook: The method survives even where the conclusions did not.
sparks.insight: Twenty years on, several headline results have been challenged and at least one core argument remains unresolved. That is not a reason to discard the book, it is a reason to read it for procedure rather than for answers. The procedure is a short sequence you can run on almost any confident claim, and it protects you from the book's own weaknesses as well as everyone else's. Curiosity about mechanisms plus scepticism about stories is the durable part.
sparks.why: Popular social science ages badly when the field moves on. A method transfers, a finding does not, so the reader who copies the questions gets more value than the reader who memorises the results.
sparks.apply: Take one claim you repeat at dinner parties and run it through the four questions below. Be willing to retire it if the answers are thin.

carousel.title: Who is being paid what
carousel.body: Identify every party in the situation and what each one actually gains. Stated motives are for public consumption. The payment structure is usually the better predictor of behaviour.

carousel.title: Ask what it is compared to
carousel.body: A number alone means nothing. Find the comparison group and ask whether it is genuinely similar, because most weak findings hide inside a badly chosen baseline.

carousel.title: Look for the other cause
carousel.body: List three things that changed at the same time as the thing being blamed. If none of them can be ruled out, you have a story rather than a result.

carousel.title: Check who replicated it
carousel.body: A single striking study is a hypothesis. Ask whether anyone independent found the same thing, and whether the original authors published a response to the critics.

actions: Take one metric your workplace optimises and write down the three easiest ways to move it without improving the underlying thing. Then check whether anyone is doing them.
Pick a statistic you have repeated confidently and spend twenty minutes finding its original source, its sample and any published criticism of it.
For every professional who advises you on money, health or property, write one sentence describing exactly how their pay is calculated.
Choose a belief about your own field that everyone treats as obvious, and go looking for the data that would falsify it rather than confirm it.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a coherent theory of the economy rather than a set of clever case studies, or you dislike social science delivered with a showman's confidence.

verification.notes: First published 2005. The abortion-crime analysis was challenged by Boston Fed economists who identified a coding error, and the Klan anecdote was later corrected by the authors. Both flagged in the sparks.

books.title: Good Economics for Hard Times
books.subtitle: Better Answers to Our Biggest Problems
books.author: Abhijit V. Banerjee and Esther Duflo
books.why_it_matters: Two Nobel laureates take the arguments people actually fight about, on migrants, trade, tax, welfare and climate, and check them against evidence rather than intuition. Several results reverse what both political sides assume, which is why it is uncomfortable in every direction.

crux.headline: People are sticky, and the models assume they are not
crux.body: Standard economics assumes people move to where the wages are, retrain when an industry dies, and shift when prices change. In reality people stay, rooted by family, housing, identity and the risk of failing far from home. Almost every failed policy here comes from that gap. Trade and technology deliver aggregate gains and concentrated local ruin, and the people carrying the cost do not, and often cannot, simply move on.

sparks.hook: Poor people move less than the theory says, not more.
sparks.insight: Wage gaps between countries are enormous, so models predict huge migration flows. The actual flows are small, and most people never leave their region, let alone their country. Moving is expensive, risky and lonely, and you give up the network that finds you work and carries you through bad luck. Even inside one country, people stay in towns where the factory shut a decade ago. The puzzle is not why so many move but why so few do.
sparks.why: This is measured, not assumed. Migration rates stay low even where legal barriers are removed and wage differences are large, which points to the cost of leaving a network rather than to policy.
sparks.apply: Before offering someone money to relocate or retrain, ask what network they would lose. Fix that first, or the incentive will not work.

sparks.hook: New arrivals compete for jobs and create them at the same time.
sparks.insight: The intuition is that more workers must mean lower wages. What repeated natural experiments show is that even large sudden inflows have small effects on the wages of existing low-skilled workers, because migrants also spend money, need housing and services, and take jobs that expand demand elsewhere. The effect is not zero and is disputed for particular groups, but the size is nothing like the political claim, and local low-skilled workers are not generally the losers.
sparks.why: The Mariel boatlift of 1980 is the famous case and remains contested, with Card finding little wage effect and Borjas reanalysing a subgroup and finding one. The wider body of studies still points to small effects.
sparks.apply: When a claim about jobs sounds obvious, look for the natural experiment. Ask what happened where the change arrived suddenly and for outside reasons.

sparks.hook: Trade makes a country richer and some towns permanently poorer.
sparks.insight: Both halves are true and only one tends to get said at a time. Cheaper imports lift most people's real income a little, spread thinly across everyone. The losses land on a few places where one industry was the town, and the standard reassurance that workers move to growing sectors mostly did not happen. Wages, employment and even health outcomes in those places stayed depressed for many years. An aggregate gain says nothing about who bears the adjustment.
sparks.why: Autor, Dorn and Hanson documented long-lasting local damage in exposed American regions after Chinese import competition. Trade theory always allowed for this. It assumed the losers would be compensated, and they were not.
sparks.apply: Whenever a policy is defended by a net gain, ask who the losers are, how concentrated they are, and what the compensation actually consists of.

sparks.hook: Nobody knows how to make a country grow faster.
sparks.insight: This is the most deflating finding in modern development economics, and it comes from people who study it for a living. Growth episodes start and stop for reasons visible only afterwards, cross-country regressions are notoriously fragile, and the recipes exported in the 1980s and 1990s produced patchy results at best. The honest position is that we cannot reliably raise a growth rate, so it is better to focus on what demonstrably improves lives at any growth rate.
sparks.why: The question has been open since Robert Lucas framed it decades ago. A candid admission by two Nobel winners is itself the evidence, and it should make you sceptical of confident growth prescriptions from anyone.
sparks.apply: Discount any plan whose case rests on a promised growth rate. Ask instead what it delivers if growth comes in a full point lower than forecast.

sparks.hook: Giving people money does not make them stop working.
sparks.insight: The fear that unconditional transfers create idleness is one of the most tested propositions in development economics, and it keeps failing. Across many programmes in many countries, recipients did not work meaningfully less, did not spend more of the money on alcohol and tobacco, and often invested part of it. What changes is the ability to take a risk. With a floor under you, you can search for a better job or plant a different crop.
sparks.why: This comes from reviews across multiple randomised programmes rather than a single study. The result is strongest for the specific claim about labour supply, and the long-run effects of a full basic income remain untested.
sparks.apply: Where you can, replace a conditional, monitored benefit with a simpler unconditional one, and measure what people actually do with it.

sparks.hook: The incentive was right and nothing happened. That is normal.
sparks.insight: Programmes fail where they meet real lives, not where they are designed. The offer requires moving away from everyone you know. Taking it up marks you publicly as a failure. The form is in the wrong language, or the office opens only when you are at work. The person explaining it belongs to a group you have reason to distrust. Each of these is fixable, and none of them appears in the model that justified the programme.
sparks.why: Randomised evaluations repeatedly find that take-up rather than the size of the incentive is the binding constraint. Small changes to delivery often move outcomes more than large changes to the amount offered.
sparks.apply: Sit with one person going through your process end to end without helping them. Fix every point where they hesitate before you change the offer.

carousel.title: Check the exit cost
carousel.body: Ask what someone gives up by taking the offer: a network, childcare, somewhere to sleep after a bad month. If that cost is high, no realistic payment covers it.

carousel.title: Protect dignity
carousel.body: Take-up collapses when accepting help means being seen as a failure. Design the offer so that using it feels ordinary rather than like an admission.

carousel.title: Fix the last hundred metres
carousel.body: Opening hours, forms, queues, languages, documents people do not have. Most programmes lose more people here than to any economic factor at all.

carousel.title: Choose the messenger
carousel.body: Information moves through trusted people. The same message lands differently from a neighbour, a nurse or a government letter. Pick the source before the wording.

sparks.hook: Tastes are not fixed, and that breaks a core assumption.
sparks.insight: Economics usually treats preferences as given and stable, then argues about how people pursue them. But what people want is shaped by who they talk to, and modern platforms sort people into groups that mostly talk to themselves. Preferences over politics, spending and even facts drift with the group. Once that is true, a market can deliver exactly what people want and still leave them worse off, because the wanting was manufactured upstream.
sparks.why: Evidence on social media and polarisation is genuinely mixed, with some deactivation experiments finding modest effects and others finding little. The weaker claim, that preferences are socially shaped, is well supported.
sparks.apply: Change one input to your own preferences deliberately this month, whether a source, a room or a person who disagrees, and watch what your opinions do.

sparks.hook: High top tax rates did not stop the rich from working.
sparks.insight: The claim that raising top rates destroys effort and growth is weaker than its confidence suggests. Rich countries ran very high top marginal rates through decades of strong growth, and cross-country evidence tying rate cuts to faster growth is thin. What responds sharply is not effort but reported income: people shift the timing, the form and the country of their earnings. That is an argument about enforcement and design, not about whether taxing is possible.
sparks.why: The elasticity of taxable income is much larger than the elasticity of real work effort, a distinction that public argument almost always collapses. Avoidance is a design problem rather than proof of a growth cost.
sparks.apply: Whenever an effort effect is claimed, ask whether the measured response is people producing less or people reporting the same income differently.

sparks.hook: The unemployed are told to move. Capital never is.
sparks.insight: Policy asks workers in a declining region to be flexible: retrain, relocate, accept a lower wage. It asks very little of capital, which moves freely and is courted for doing so. The asymmetry is not only unfair, it may be inefficient, because the person is the input with the highest cost of moving. If adjustment has to happen somewhere, helping a place recover can be cheaper than dissolving a community and rebuilding those lives elsewhere.
sparks.why: Place-based policy has a poor historical reputation among economists, but the authors argue the balance of evidence shifted as the true cost of forcing people to move became clearer. This remains a live disagreement.
sparks.apply: In any restructuring you run, price the cost of moving people as seriously as the cost of keeping the site open, and put both in the paper.

sparks.hook: Respect is cheaper than money and harder to deliver.
sparks.insight: Much of the anger in rich democracies is not straightforwardly about income. It is about being treated as surplus: a region written off, a job described as obsolete, a person processed by a system that assumes they are lying. A programme that hands out money while humiliating the recipient buys resentment along with the transfer. Designing for dignity is not sentimentality, because it changes take-up, compliance and the political survival of the policy.
sparks.why: Take-up of benefits rises when stigma falls and application friction is removed, and that is measurable. The link from humiliation to political backlash is argued rather than proven, and is presented as interpretation.
sparks.apply: Read one letter your organisation sends to people in trouble, then rewrite it to assume they are honest and short of time.

actions: Take a position you hold strongly on trade or immigration and find the best natural experiment that tests it, including one that cuts against you.
Redesign one process you own for take-up: remove a document, extend the hours, change the messenger, and measure the difference it makes.
Write down what your plan delivers under a growth rate a full point below forecast, and circulate that version alongside the main case.
Identify the concentrated losers from a change you support and specify exactly what compensation they receive and when it arrives.
books.not_for_you_if: You want one ideology applied consistently. It is deliberately piecemeal, follows evidence into inconvenient places, and often ends in uncertainty.

verification.notes: First published 2019 by PublicAffairs. Banerjee and Duflo shared the 2019 Nobel Memorial Prize with Michael Kremer. The Mariel boatlift findings remain contested.

books.title: Manias, Panics, and Crashes
books.subtitle: A History of Financial Crises
books.author: Charles P. Kindleberger
books.why_it_matters: It rescued Hyman Minsky's theory of financial instability from obscurity and paired it with three centuries of actual crashes. Almost every serious account of bubbles written since borrows its sequence: a real story, cheap credit, euphoria, then a scramble for the exit.

crux.headline: Bubbles follow a script, not a surprise
crux.body: Crises are not random shocks landing on healthy markets. They grow inside them. Something genuinely new arrives, credit expands to chase it, prices rise, and the rising price is then read as proof the story was true. Late buyers are borrowing against the price rather than against anything the asset produces. When credit stops expanding the price stops rising, and the whole structure only ever worked while it rose.

sparks.hook: Every mania begins with a story that is actually true.
sparks.insight: Bubbles do not start with delusion. They start with a real change: a new trade route, a railway, a technology, a currency reform, a fall in interest rates. That change genuinely does make some assets worth more, and the first buyers are right. The trouble is that being right early attracts money with no view at all, only the observation that prices went up. By the time the crowd arrives, the original story is still true and completely irrelevant to the price.
sparks.why: This is why sneering at bubbles as mass stupidity misreads them. The entry ticket is usually a correct forecast. The damage comes from the extrapolation that follows it, not from the forecast itself.
sparks.apply: When you meet an investment story you believe, write down the price at which the true story stops being a good deal. Decide that number before you buy.

sparks.hook: No bubble has ever run on savings alone.
sparks.insight: Prices cannot keep rising unless new money keeps arriving, and past a certain point that money has to be borrowed. So the real question about any boom is not whether the asset is good but where the credit is coming from: a bank loosening its terms, a new lender with no history, a product that lets buyers put down less. Credit expansion turns a price rise into a mania, and its exhaustion is what ends one, usually before any bad news arrives.
sparks.why: Kindleberger builds on Hyman Minsky. Stability encourages borrowing, borrowing raises prices, higher prices appear to justify more borrowing. The instability is generated inside the system rather than imported from outside it.
sparks.apply: For a market you are exposed to, find out who is lending into it and on what terms. Track that for one month instead of tracking the price.

sparks.hook: A crash is the last act of a play that started years earlier.
sparks.insight: The sequence repeats with such regularity across three centuries that it works as a rough map. Something real happens, credit expands to chase it, prices detach from any cash the asset produces, insiders quietly leave, and then everyone tries to sell to each other at once. The details change completely: tulips, canals, Florida land, dot-coms, houses. The shape does not. Knowing where you are in the arc is usually more useful than knowing whether the asset looks cheap.
sparks.why: The pattern is descriptive rather than predictive. It has matched crises since the 1600s, but it will never tell you the year, and being honest about that limit is what keeps it useful.
sparks.apply: Name the stage you think your largest holding is in, write one sentence of evidence for that stage, and revisit the note every quarter.

carousel.title: Something real arrives
carousel.body: A war ends, a technology lands, rates fall. Profit opportunities genuinely shift and the first movers make real money for real reasons. Nothing at this stage is irrational.

carousel.title: Credit stretches to meet it
carousel.body: Banks lend, new lenders appear, terms loosen, and instruments show up that let buyers borrow more against the same asset. The money available to this market quietly expands.

carousel.title: Euphoria takes over
carousel.body: Buying is justified by the price rise itself. People who know nothing about the asset pile in because staying out now feels like losing. Volume and prices accelerate together.

carousel.title: Insiders step back
carousel.body: The quiet stretch. Prices stall rather than fall, the best-informed holders sell into strength, and lenders start asking for slightly more collateral than they did last quarter.

carousel.title: Everyone reaches the exit
carousel.body: A small failure triggers a scramble for cash. Selling becomes forced rather than chosen, prices gap through anything a valuation model would call fair, and credit disappears.

sparks.hook: The phrase that marks the top is a claim about arithmetic.
sparks.insight: Late in every boom, someone explains why the old measures no longer apply: a new economy, a permanently higher plateau, a shortage that cannot end. The argument is rarely stupid and it is always specific to that decade, which is exactly why it works. What it always does is remove the ceiling. If the usual limits are void, no price is too high. Watch for the moment valuation gets replaced by a story about why valuation is obsolete.
sparks.why: New-era reasoning is not a personality flaw. It is the device that lets a crowd hold a position ordinary arithmetic would reject, and it recurs in almost every mania on record.
sparks.apply: Ask a holder of any hot asset what would make it too expensive. If no number exists, treat that as information about the market rather than about the person.

sparks.hook: Fraud is committed in the boom and discovered in the bust.
sparks.insight: Swindles cluster at the end of manias, and not by coincidence. Rising prices hide bad accounting, because a bad asset can always be sold on at a profit. Easy credit funds anyone with a plausible story. Enormous unearned gains make small lies feel survivable. When credit tightens, the same behaviour becomes visible almost instantly, because you now need cash rather than a buyer. Booms do not merely precede fraud, they manufacture the conditions for it.
sparks.why: What changes in the bust is detection more than behaviour. The downturn removes the cover, refinancing and rising collateral values, that let the boom's misreporting go unchallenged.
sparks.apply: Before you trust a company's numbers, ask whether they still work if it cannot raise money for two years. If not, treat them as provisional.

sparks.hook: The rescue rule is nearly two centuries old and still argued about.
sparks.insight: In a panic everyone wants cash at once, and even solvent institutions fail because assets cannot be sold fast enough. The classic answer, inherited from Victorian banking, is that someone must lend without limit, at a punishing rate, against collateral that would be good in normal times. The severity is the point: it saves the system while making the rescue expensive for whoever needs it. The hard question is never whether to do it but who is willing.
sparks.why: Walter Bagehot set out the doctrine in 1873 and central banks broadly followed it in 2008. The unresolved part is international, because in a global panic there is no clear lender of last resort with the authority to act.
sparks.apply: Read one page on what your own central bank actually did in the last crisis. Knowing its reflex tells you how the next panic is likely to end.

sparks.hook: Every rescue makes the next crisis a little more likely.
sparks.insight: If lenders learn that catastrophe will be absorbed by the public, the rational response is to take more risk next time, so the following boom starts from a more fragile position. But refusing to rescue turns a financial fire into a depression that lands on people who never made a bet. There is no clean resolution. The practical answer has been deliberate vagueness: never promise a rescue, never rule one out, and keep any rescue humiliating enough to hurt.
sparks.why: This is a genuine dilemma rather than a policy failure, and both horns have historical bodies attached. The years from 1929 show the cost of restraint; the years after 2008 show the cost of the alternative.
sparks.apply: When you hear a confident answer about bailouts, ask what the speaker would have done in the opposite case. The test of a rule is the case it handles badly.

sparks.hook: Panic travels by balance sheet, not by border.
sparks.insight: Crises spread between countries that have little in common because the same lenders are exposed to both. A fund forced to sell in one market raises cash by selling whatever it can in another, so healthy assets fall alongside sick ones. Trade links, currency pegs and shared creditors all carry the shock. This is why an economy can be wrecked by trouble it had no part in, and why saying that the local fundamentals are sound is a weak defence in a panic.
sparks.why: Contagion through common lenders and forced selling is documented across the 1873, 1929, 1997 and 2008 episodes. It works even when two economies have no meaningful direct trade relationship.
sparks.apply: Check whether your holdings share a big lender, broker or index. Correlations that look low in calm markets often come from a single source of funding.

sparks.hook: There is a quiet stretch between the top and the crash.
sparks.insight: Prices usually do not fall off the peak. They wander sideways while something changes underneath: insiders sell into strength, lenders tighten terms without announcing it, the ratio of new buyers to old holders turns. This is the period when it is still easy to sell at a good price and nobody feels any reason to. By the time the news arrives that everyone later calls the cause, the market has been fragile for months and the exit has narrowed.
sparks.why: The lag explains why waiting to sell until the news turns bad fails as a plan. Once the news turns, the price has already moved and the liquidity you were relying on has gone.
