sparks.apply: Decide your exit conditions while a market is calm and boring, and write them down. A rule invented during distress is not a rule.

sparks.hook: This framework explains every crash and predicts none of them.
sparks.insight: The stages are convincing in hindsight and nearly useless as a timing device. Credit has expanded for years without a crash. Prices have looked insane and gone higher. Several people who identified bubbles correctly were ruined by being early. Critics of the Minsky framework make a fair point: it is a narrative rather than a testable model, and it can be fitted to almost any episode after the fact. Use it to size your exposure, never to pick a date.
sparks.why: Being honest about the limit makes the framework more useful, not less. Knowing a system is fragile is valuable even when nothing tells you which week the fragility pays out.
sparks.apply: Convert any bubble call into a position you could hold for three years without being forced out. If you cannot, do not take it at all.

actions: Map the credit behind one market you own: who lends into it, on what terms, and how those terms have changed over the past two years.
Write a one-page history of a crash you lived through, marking where each stage began and what you personally believed at the time.
Set position limits that assume you cannot sell at the price on your screen, then check whether your current holdings already break them.
Read a contemporary newspaper account written at the top of a past bubble and note how reasonable every argument in it sounded.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a trading system or a forecast. This is economic history, sceptical about timing, and it will not tell you when to sell.

verification.notes: First published 1978. Later editions were revised and, after Kindleberger's death in 2003, co-authored with Robert Aliber. All prose here is original.

books.title: Margin of Safety
books.subtitle: Risk-Averse Value Investing Strategies for the Thoughtful Investor
books.author: Seth A. Klarman
books.why_it_matters: It is the clearest modern statement of investing where avoiding permanent loss comes first and return comes second. Long out of print and traded at absurd prices, it shaped a generation of professional value investors who read photocopies of it.

crux.headline: Worry about losing money first, returns second
crux.body: Most investors start by asking how much they could make. Reverse it. Ask what would have to go wrong for this position to be permanently impaired, and how much you would lose if it did. Buy only when the price is low enough that ordinary bad outcomes still leave you whole. Returns follow from a long sequence of decisions where the downside was already covered before you began.

sparks.hook: Risk is the chance of permanent loss, not the wiggle in a price chart.
sparks.insight: Finance defines risk as volatility because volatility is easy to measure. But a share that halves and recovers cost you nothing if you did not have to sell, while a business that quietly loses its market cost you everything at low volatility. The question that matters is whether the capital comes back. Measuring risk by price movement means you will call a cheap asset dangerous precisely when it has become safe.
sparks.why: Volatility is a proxy chosen for convenience. It correlates with permanent loss sometimes, and inverts at exactly the moments of maximum opportunity, which is when the proxy is most expensive to trust.
sparks.apply: For each holding, write the scenario in which the money never comes back. If you cannot describe one, you have not analysed it.

sparks.hook: Holding cash is a position, and sometimes it is the best one available.
sparks.insight: If nothing meets your standard, buying something that nearly does is how discipline dies. Cash earns little and feels like failure while others are making money, but it is the only asset that keeps its option value: it lets you act decisively when prices finally fall and everyone else is forced to sell. The willingness to look wrong for a year or two is a large part of what produces the eventual return.
sparks.why: The constraint is career risk, not analysis. Professionals rarely hold cash because underperforming while fully invested is forgiven and underperforming while cautious is not.
sparks.apply: Set a minimum quality and discount standard in writing, and let cash accumulate whenever nothing clears it.

sparks.hook: Bargains appear when someone must sell for reasons unrelated to value.
sparks.insight: Prices detach from value when a holder is compelled to act: a fund removing a company because it left an index, a mandate that forbids holding debt below a rating, a manager selling to meet redemptions, or a spin-off that arrives in portfolios that never wanted it. None of these sellers is expressing a view about the business. They are obeying a rule. Those forced trades are among the most reliable sources of mispricing available.
sparks.why: The mechanism is structural rather than psychological, so it repeats. A seller acting under constraint is indifferent to price, which is exactly the counterparty you want.
sparks.apply: Watch index deletions, spin-offs and ratings downgrades. Screen for securities that changed hands for reasons no analyst chose.

carousel.title: Find the forced seller
carousel.body: Ask who has to sell this and why. Index rules, credit-rating limits, redemption pressure and fund mandates all create sellers who never looked at value.

carousel.title: Check the security is unwanted, not broken
carousel.body: Distinguish a business in trouble from a business nobody is permitted to own. Only the second is a gift; the first is usually priced correctly.

carousel.title: Value it from the bottom up
carousel.body: Estimate what a private buyer would pay, what the assets would fetch in liquidation, and what the cash flows are worth. Use the most conservative figure.

carousel.title: Buy in tranches
carousel.body: Assume it gets cheaper after you buy. Sizing your entry in stages means a further fall becomes an opportunity rather than an emergency.

sparks.hook: Chasing relative performance is how sensible investors end up owning nonsense.
sparks.insight: When your goal is to beat a benchmark or your peers, you start owning things because not owning them is uncomfortable, not because they are worth the price. The logic compounds during a mania: the more overvalued an asset becomes, the more it dominates the index, and the more painful staying out becomes. Absolute standards, where you simply refuse to buy above a price you can justify, are the only defence against this.
sparks.why: Relative benchmarks encode whatever the crowd already owns. Measuring yourself against them imports the crowd's mistakes into your portfolio automatically.
sparks.apply: Judge your results against your own required return, not against an index, and write that number down before the year starts.

sparks.hook: You are not paid for forecasting. You are paid for buying below value.
sparks.insight: A great deal of investment work consists of predicting interest rates, currencies or next year's economy, and the record for such predictions is poor even among specialists. Value investing sidesteps the problem. If you buy an asset far below a conservative estimate of what it is worth, you do not need to know when the gap closes or what the economy does meanwhile. The discount, not the forecast, does the work.
sparks.why: Forecast-dependent strategies compound two uncertainties: the prediction and the timing. A discount to value only requires that value be roughly right and that time eventually pass.
sparks.apply: Strip every macro assumption from your next investment case. If the case collapses without them, it was a forecast, not a valuation.

sparks.hook: Value three ways, then trust the lowest number.
sparks.insight: There is no single correct valuation. Estimate what the future cash flows are worth today, what the assets would realise if the business were wound up, and what a knowledgeable private buyer would pay for the whole company. Each method rests on different assumptions and each fails in different conditions. When the three converge, you have a range you can act on. When they diverge wildly, that divergence is telling you the analysis is not finished.
sparks.why: Using several independent methods surfaces the assumptions doing the heavy lifting. A valuation that only works under one method is a valuation resting on one fragile input.
sparks.apply: Value your next candidate three ways on one page, and size the position from the most pessimistic of the three.

carousel.title: Discount the cash flows
carousel.body: Project conservatively and discount at a rate that reflects real uncertainty. Small changes in growth assumptions swing this figure enormously, so test the extremes.

carousel.title: Price the assets
carousel.body: Ask what the property, inventory and receivables would raise in an orderly wind-down. This sets a floor that does not depend on future earnings.

carousel.title: Think like a buyer of the whole
carousel.body: Look at what similar businesses changed hands for privately. Public prices can stay detached for years; acquisition prices reflect what control is worth.

carousel.title: Take the lowest and discount again
carousel.body: Use the most conservative of the three, then demand a further gap below it. That second gap is what protects you when one input is simply wrong.

sparks.hook: A rising price is not evidence you were right.
sparks.insight: Outcomes in markets are noisy over any period short enough to notice. A careless purchase can rise for two years and a careful one can fall for three, so grading yourself by the scoreboard trains the wrong lessons. Judge the decision instead: was the research sufficient, was the valuation conservative, was the position sized so that being wrong was survivable? Good process eventually produces good outcomes. Good outcomes teach you nothing about process.
sparks.why: Skill and luck are entangled in short-run results. Only the reasoning is fully observable at the time you act, so only the reasoning can be reliably audited afterwards.
sparks.apply: Keep a decision journal: the thesis, the valuation, the risks and the position size. Review the reasoning, not the return.

sparks.hook: Leverage turns a temporary decline into a permanent loss.
sparks.insight: Borrowed money removes your ability to wait, which is the value investor's only genuine advantage. A position bought with debt can be correct and still destroy you, because the lender decides when you sell. Every borrowing arrangement contains a clause that gets exercised at the worst possible moment. Staying solvent through the ugly stretch is not caution for its own sake, it is the precondition for every return that comes afterwards.
sparks.why: Debt converts price volatility into forced selling. It is the common ingredient in the failures of otherwise sophisticated investors, because it removes the option to be early rather than wrong.
sparks.apply: Stress-test your portfolio against a fifty percent fall. If any part of the plan requires borrowing or selling, reduce the leverage now.

sparks.hook: Complexity in a security is often where the compensation is hiding.
sparks.insight: Instruments that are tedious to analyse, involve legal documents, or need several steps to understand attract fewer buyers, and fewer buyers means better prices. Bankruptcy claims, restructurings and unusual corporate structures all fall in this category. The compensation is real but so is the danger: complexity also hides risks that a simple screen would never reveal, and a mistake in the documents can wipe out the position entirely.
sparks.why: The edge is the effort barrier, not cleverness. That barrier only pays if you genuinely have the expertise to read what others skipped, which most private investors do not.
sparks.apply: Only enter a complicated situation if you have read the primary documents yourself and can explain the downside in plain sentences.

sparks.hook: The book preaching patience became the most impatiently priced book on the shelf.
sparks.insight: It went out of print, demand kept rising, and secondhand copies have sold for hundreds or thousands, which is a small joke at the expense of everyone who preaches valuation discipline. Take the point seriously though: scarcity and status can inflate the price of anything, including investment wisdom. The ideas are freely available in letters and interviews, and paying an extreme price for the physical object is precisely the behaviour the contents argue against.
sparks.why: Its scarcity value is a live demonstration that price and worth separate whenever supply is fixed and demand is emotional. That applies to collectibles, to housing and to shares.
sparks.apply: Before paying a premium for anything scarce, ask what you would pay if a hundred identical ones existed tomorrow.

actions: Write a one-page risk statement for each holding describing the scenario in which the capital does not come back, and how much you would lose.
Set an absolute return standard for the year and stop comparing your portfolio to any index or to other people.
Build a watchlist of quality assets with the price at which each becomes a buy, so that a market fall gives you a shopping list rather than a panic.
Remove or cap any leverage in your portfolio, including margin facilities you are not currently using.
books.not_for_you_if: You invest in index funds and have no interest in analysing individual securities, or you are unwilling to hunt down a copy of an out-of-print book.

verification.notes: Published 1991 by HarperBusiness and long out of print. Klarman runs the Baupost Group in Boston. Secondhand copies trade at very high prices; the underlying ideas appear in his public letters. All prose original.

books.title: One Up on Wall Street
books.subtitle: How to Use What You Already Know to Make Money in the Market
books.author: Peter Lynch
books.why_it_matters: It argued that ordinary people could analyse companies at least as well as professionals, and it explained how, in plain language. A generation of individual investors learned to read a business rather than a price chart from it.

crux.headline: You see companies before Wall Street prices them
crux.body: You encounter businesses every week as a customer, a supplier or an employee, and you often notice a product working long before it shows up in an analyst's model. That head start is real, but it is only a lead, not a decision. The observation gets you a candidate. What earns you the money is doing the research the professionals do afterwards: the balance sheet, the growth rate, the price you are being asked to pay, and the story you can defend in two minutes.

sparks.hook: Your job gives you a research advantage no fund manager can buy.
sparks.insight: If you work in construction you know which supplier's product actually holds up. If you manage a shop you see which brand sells out. If you are a nurse you see which device staff trust. Professionals get that information filtered through investor relations, months later. The edge is not that you shop somewhere. The edge is that you have specialist knowledge of an industry and can judge whether something is genuinely better before the numbers say so.
sparks.why: Fund analysts cover dozens of companies at a distance. A practitioner has narrow but deep knowledge in one industry, and narrow depth is exactly where mispricing survives longest.
sparks.apply: List three companies your job gives you real insight into. Research one of them properly this month, starting with its accounts.

sparks.hook: Buy what you know is the most misread advice in investing.
sparks.insight: The idea was never that liking a shop is a reason to buy its shares. A good product tells you nothing about the price, the debt, the competition or the growth already priced in. Lynch was explicit that the observation is step one of a longer process, and he spent most of the book on the rest of it. Read casually, the advice produces portfolios full of familiar consumer brands bought at any price, which is how a sensible idea became a marketing slogan for bad decisions.
sparks.why: Familiarity feels like knowledge and is not. Investors who buy familiar names tend to be under-diversified and home-biased, both well documented and both costly.
sparks.apply: For each stock you bought because you liked the product, write its current price-to-earnings ratio and growth rate. Decide again on those numbers.

sparks.hook: You can be wrong on most of your picks and still do very well.
sparks.insight: A stock can only fall to zero, but it can rise many times over. That asymmetry means a portfolio's outcome is usually decided by two or three enormous winners rather than by the average pick. Practically, this changes what you should worry about. It matters far less that some holdings fail than that you sell your best performer after it doubles. Small losses are survivable arithmetic. Cutting a ten-fold winner short is the mistake you cannot make up elsewhere.
sparks.why: Stock returns are heavily skewed: research on long-run market histories consistently finds most of the total return comes from a small minority of companies, with the majority underperforming cash.
sparks.apply: Look at your biggest past winner and note why you sold. If the reason was the size of the gain rather than the business, change the rule.

sparks.hook: Six kinds of company, six completely different ways to be right.
sparks.insight: Treating every share the same is why people hold a utility expecting it to triple and a fast grower expecting it to be safe. Sorting a company into its type tells you what to expect, what to check and when to sell. A cyclical is bought and sold on the industry cycle, not held forever. A stalwart is a modest, defensive holding. A fast grower deserves close attention to whether growth is slowing. The categories do more work than any single ratio.
sparks.why: Different business types have different return distributions and different failure modes. Using one mental model for all of them guarantees you will apply the wrong sell rule to something.
sparks.apply: Sort every holding you own into a category, write the expected return and exit trigger for each, and note where the two disagree.

carousel.title: Slow growers and stalwarts
carousel.body: Large, mature businesses growing with the economy. You buy them for stability and dividends, and you should never expect a multiple of your money from them.

carousel.title: Fast growers
carousel.body: Small, expanding companies with room to multiply. The highest returns and the highest risk. Watch for the quarter when store or unit growth stops accelerating.

carousel.title: Cyclicals
carousel.body: Airlines, chemicals, carmakers, steel. They look cheapest at the top of the cycle when earnings peak. Timing the industry cycle matters more than the valuation ratio.

carousel.title: Turnarounds
carousel.body: Damaged companies that may recover. Returns come fast when they work and the losses are total when they do not. Check whether the balance sheet can survive the wait.

carousel.title: Asset plays
carousel.body: Businesses worth more for what they own, such as property, spectrum or cash, than for what they earn. You need a reason the value will ever be realised.

sparks.hook: If you cannot explain the holding in two minutes, you do not own it yet.
sparks.insight: Before buying, say out loud why this company will be bigger in a few years, what has to go right, and what would prove you wrong. If the explanation needs charts, jargon or a story about interest rates, the thesis is not clear enough to hold under pressure. The point of the exercise is not the buy decision. It is that you now have a written statement you can check against reality every quarter, instead of quietly rewriting your reasons as the price moves.
sparks.why: Investors reliably reconstruct their reasoning after the fact. A dated written thesis makes that impossible and turns a vague feeling into something that can be tested and falsified.
sparks.apply: Write a two-minute thesis for your largest holding today, date it, and reread it after the next earnings report.

sparks.hook: A growth rate is only impressive next to the price you paid for it.
sparks.insight: A company growing at twenty percent a year is not automatically a better buy than one growing at ten. What matters is the multiple attached. Comparing the price-to-earnings ratio with the growth rate gives you a rough sense of whether you are paying for growth you have not yet received. A ratio far below the growth rate suggests the market has not caught up. A ratio far above it means the future has to arrive on schedule to leave you level.
sparks.why: The comparison is crude and breaks down for cyclicals, loss-makers and businesses with unstable growth. Used as a first screen rather than a valuation, it usefully separates cheap growth from expensive growth.
sparks.apply: Divide the price-to-earnings ratio by the expected growth rate for each holding, and flag anything above two for a closer look.

sparks.hook: The dullest company on the list is often the best one to own.
sparks.insight: Businesses with unglamorous names, tedious products or unpleasant work attract fewer analysts and fewer buyers, so their prices are more likely to lag their results. Add the signals that management believes in the company: insiders buying with their own money, shares being bought back, a business the institutions have not yet crowded into. None of these are reasons on their own. Together they describe the corner of the market where genuine mispricing is most likely to survive.
sparks.why: Neglect is the precondition for mispricing. Where twenty analysts publish, information is already in the price. Where none do, your own work can still be worth something.
sparks.apply: Screen for companies with low analyst coverage in an industry you understand, then check the last year of insider purchases.

sparks.hook: Nobody can tell you where the economy goes next. Stop paying them to try.
sparks.insight: Investors spend enormous energy on predictions of rates, recessions and elections, then use those predictions to postpone or panic. The forecasts have a poor record, and even a correct one is only useful if you also guess how much of it the market has already priced. Meanwhile the things that decide whether your company thrives, including its products, its costs and its competitors, are researchable and largely independent of the macro narrative you are worrying about.
sparks.why: Economic forecasts of turning points have a weak track record, and market reactions depend on the surprise relative to expectations rather than the outcome itself. Two forecasts are needed, not one.
sparks.apply: Spend the next hour you would have given to market commentary reading one company's annual report instead.

sparks.hook: Selling your winners to fund your losers is the standard way to lose slowly.
sparks.insight: Taking a profit feels like discipline and cutting a loss feels like defeat, so investors do the reverse of what the businesses justify. The winner is usually winning because the company is executing, and the loser is usually losing because it is not. Unless something has changed in the business, the honest question at any moment is which company you would buy today at today's price. Answer that and the emotional accounting about your own entry price stops mattering.
sparks.why: This is loss aversion combined with mental accounting: the purchase price is treated as a reference point even though it has no bearing on the company's future cash flows.
sparks.apply: Review each holding by asking whether you would buy it today at this price. Sell whatever fails, regardless of your entry price.

carousel.title: Forget what you paid
carousel.body: Your purchase price is a fact about your history, not about the company. The market has no memory of it and it should not appear anywhere in your decision.

carousel.title: Recheck the original story
carousel.body: Read the thesis you wrote when you bought. Ask whether the specific things you predicted are happening, on the timeline you expected.

carousel.title: Ask the buy question
carousel.body: Would you open this position today at this price, with what you now know? A no is a sell, and a maybe usually means the position is too large.

carousel.title: Act on the business, not the chart
carousel.body: Sell because the story broke, not because the price fell. Falling prices on an intact story are the reason to add, not the reason to leave.

sparks.hook: The author's own record is the strongest argument against copying him.
sparks.insight: Lynch ran an extraordinary fund for thirteen years, in a period and a market segment that suited the method: an enormous bull run, a rich supply of under-followed small companies, and a research team behind him. Very few readers matched it. That is not an argument to ignore the book, but it is a reason to treat the results as one exceptional sample rather than proof of the process. Survivorship makes every successful method look more repeatable than it is.
sparks.why: We hear from the managers who succeeded and not from the many who used similar approaches and did not. Any track record selected after the fact overstates the odds facing you.
sparks.apply: Before adopting any method from a famous investor, ask what conditions made it work and whether those conditions still hold today.

actions: Write down three industries you understand from work or life, and pick one company in each to research properly from its annual report.
Write a two-minute thesis for every holding, date each one, and diary a quarterly review to check what has actually happened.
Sort your portfolio into company types and write the expected return and sell trigger appropriate to each type.
Check the debt, cash and inventory trend for your three largest holdings before you buy anything else.
books.not_for_you_if: You have no intention of researching individual companies, or you want a modern treatment. The examples come from 1980s America and some of the companies are long gone.

verification.notes: First published 1989, co-written with John Rothchild. Lynch managed the Fidelity Magellan fund from 1977 to 1990. All prose original.

books.title: Poor Charlie's Almanack
books.subtitle: The Wit and Wisdom of Charles T. Munger
books.author: Charles T. Munger
books.why_it_matters: It is the clearest available statement of a way of thinking that treats investing as applied psychology, engineering and biology rather than as finance. The multidisciplinary checklist habit has spread far beyond the people who ever bought a share.

crux.headline: Borrow the big ideas from every field, then check yourself
crux.body: Anyone trained in a single discipline reaches for the same tool regardless of the problem, and gets the wrong answer with great confidence. The remedy is to learn the handful of genuinely load-bearing ideas from several fields, mathematics, psychology, biology, engineering and accounting among them, and to run a decision past all of them before committing. Most large errors come not from missing information but from a familiar reflex applied to an unfamiliar problem.

sparks.hook: To a person with one theory, every problem obligingly fits that theory.
sparks.insight: Specialist training gives you a small number of powerful tools and a strong habit of using them. That habit is efficient inside the discipline and dangerous outside it: the economist sees incentives everywhere, the engineer sees systems, the lawyer sees liability, and each is confidently wrong in the same predictable direction. The alternative is to collect the few big ideas that each field genuinely got right, and to keep enough of them in reach that no single one dominates.
sparks.why: Real problems are not sorted into academic departments. A wider set of models increases the chance that at least one of them matches the actual structure of the situation in front of you.
sparks.apply: Take a decision you are working on and force yourself to describe it three ways: as an incentive problem, as a system with feedback, and as a psychology problem.

sparks.hook: Ask how to guarantee failure, then refuse to do those things.
sparks.insight: Forward planning is hard because the paths to success are many and unknown. The reverse question is much easier and often more useful: what would reliably ruin this. For a career, a portfolio or a marriage you can usually list the guaranteed destroyers in five minutes, and they are concrete. Avoiding them does not guarantee a good outcome, but it removes most of the outcomes you cannot recover from, which is where the real damage lives.
sparks.why: Failure modes are fewer, more repetitive and better documented than success routes. Inversion turns a vague optimisation problem into a short checklist of things not to do.
sparks.apply: Write the five actions that would most reliably wreck your finances in three years. Then check which of them you are already doing a small version of.

sparks.hook: Never ask a person for a judgement their salary depends on.
sparks.insight: People do not usually lie about their interests, they simply come to believe the thing that suits them, and they believe it sincerely. A salesperson genuinely thinks the product fits. A consultant genuinely finds work worth doing. A fund manager genuinely believes activity adds value. Because the distortion is honest it is invisible from the inside, which makes structure the only defence: change who decides, or change what they are paid for, before you change anyone's mind.
sparks.why: Self-serving belief is well documented and does not require dishonesty, which is exactly why arguing with it fails. Only altering the incentive or the decision rights reliably changes the answer.
sparks.apply: For your next significant purchase or hire, get one assessment from someone with nothing to gain from the outcome, and weight it more heavily than the expert's.

sparks.hook: Most bad judgement comes from a short list of predictable pulls.
sparks.insight: Human misjudgement is not random. It repeats through a limited set of tendencies that are usually useful and occasionally catastrophic, and they compound when several fire at once. The dangerous cases are the combinations: an authority figure, a room that already agrees, a decision you have publicly committed to, and time pressure. Learning the list is not the point. Running it as a checklist before an irreversible decision is the point, because in the moment you will not notice.
sparks.why: These tendencies are drawn from experimental psychology, and while some individual findings in that literature have failed to replicate, the broad patterns of conformity, authority and commitment effects have held up well.
sparks.apply: Before your next irreversible commitment, run the five checks below in writing. If two or more are firing, wait a week before deciding.

carousel.title: Check the payer
carousel.body: Ask who benefits from the decision you are about to make, including yourself. Incentive-driven belief is the single most common source of confident error.

carousel.title: Check the room
carousel.body: If everyone around you agrees, that is weak evidence and strong pressure. Find out what someone outside the group thinks before you treat consensus as confirmation.

carousel.title: Check the debt
carousel.body: A favour, a gift or a good lunch creates a pull towards saying yes. Notice what you have received from the person asking, and discount accordingly.

carousel.title: Check your past words
carousel.body: Once you have said something publicly you will defend it beyond the evidence. Ask what you would conclude if you had never stated a position at all.

carousel.title: Check the clock
carousel.body: Artificial urgency exists to prevent exactly this checklist. If a decision cannot survive a week of delay, that is information about the decision, not about your speed.

sparks.hook: Good opportunities are rare, so most of the work is waiting.
sparks.insight: If genuinely mispriced opportunities appear a handful of times per decade, then the skill being tested is not analysis but the ability to do nothing for years without losing your nerve or your job. Most professional investors cannot wait, because clients pay for activity and an empty quarter looks like idleness. The individual investor has no such constraint and throws the advantage away anyway, because waiting feels like failure while trading feels like work.
sparks.why: Trading costs, taxes and mistimed entries all scale with activity, while the returns from a correct position accrue whether you watch it or not. Patience is structurally advantaged and psychologically expensive.
sparks.apply: Write down in advance what would make you buy, then take no action until those conditions appear. Count your no-action months as work completed, not time wasted.

sparks.hook: Knowing the edge of what you know is worth more than expanding it.
sparks.insight: Everyone has a domain where their judgement is genuinely better than average, and it is usually much smaller than they think. The valuable skill is not making that domain large, it is knowing exactly where the boundary sits and refusing to act outside it. A confident opinion about an industry you cannot explain to a fifteen-year-old is a liability. Outside the boundary the correct move is not a smaller bet, it is no bet at all.
sparks.why: Returns depend on being right where others are wrong, which requires real informational or analytical edge. Outside your competence you are the counterparty who is providing the edge, not using it.
sparks.apply: List three industries you could explain end to end without notes. Restrict any concentrated position to that list and index everything else.

sparks.hook: A wonderful business at a fair price beats a fair business at a bargain.
sparks.insight: The early value tradition hunted for statistically cheap companies and sold them when they rose, which works but leaves you constantly reinvesting into new mediocrity. The shift was towards paying a reasonable price for businesses with a durable advantage and then holding for decades, letting the company itself compound. That change is what turned a good investment record into an extraordinary one, and it required abandoning a method that had been working.
sparks.why: A cheap but weak business must be sold to realise a gain, while a strong one grows its value over time, which also defers tax. The catch is that identifying a durable advantage in advance is far harder than measuring cheapness.
sparks.apply: For each holding, write one sentence explaining why a well-funded competitor cannot copy it within five years. Sell anything where you cannot finish the sentence.

sparks.hook: Consistently avoiding stupidity beats occasionally being brilliant.
sparks.insight: Long-run results are dominated by the errors you did not make. Brilliance produces occasional outsized wins, but a single ruinous mistake, excessive borrowing, a fraud you did not check, a concentrated bet on something you did not understand, erases years of them. So the discipline is unglamorous: refuse the deals you cannot assess, keep leverage low enough to survive a bad decade, and accept that this will make you look unimaginative during booms.
sparks.why: Compounding is destroyed by drawdowns far more than it is helped by spikes, because recovering from a large loss requires a much larger gain. Avoiding ruin is mathematically prior to being clever.
sparks.apply: Set a hard rule for the maximum you can lose in any single position or venture, write it down, and treat it as a constraint rather than a guideline.

sparks.hook: Two men, one country, one extraordinary era. Weigh that before copying.
sparks.insight: The record behind this advice was built over decades in the American stock market, by a partnership with access to permanent capital, cheap insurance float and deals unavailable to ordinary investors. Thousands of people followed similar principles and did not produce similar results, and you will not read their books. The reasoning is genuinely valuable. The implied promise that following it produces the same outcome is a survivorship illusion, and the honest version says so.
sparks.why: Success stories are selected after the fact from a large pool of similar attempts, so the visible sample tells you little about the base rate. The structural advantages here were also unusual and largely unavailable to individuals.
sparks.apply: Take the thinking habits and ignore the return expectations. Benchmark yourself against a low-cost index fund and check honestly whether you are beating it.

sparks.hook: A latticework is built by reading, not by collecting clever phrases.
sparks.insight: Mental models are frequently reduced to a list of named concepts memorised for social use, which is worse than useless because it produces the confidence without the understanding. Building the real thing is slow: you learn a field well enough to know which of its ideas do actual work, then you apply them to problems outside that field and watch what happens. It is a decades-long reading habit disguised as a decision technique.
sparks.why: A model only helps if you know its assumptions and its failure conditions, which comes from studying the field rather than the summary. Names without mechanisms give you a vocabulary and no judgement.
sparks.apply: Pick one discipline outside your own and read a serious introductory textbook this quarter, rather than another summary of somebody's model list.

carousel.title: Pick a distant field
carousel.body: Choose something far from your training: thermodynamics if you are in finance, accounting if you are an engineer. Distance is what makes the borrowed idea useful.

carousel.title: Learn the load-bearing ideas
carousel.body: Every field has a handful of concepts that everything else rests on. Find those, understand where they break, and skip the specialist detail you will never use.

carousel.title: Apply them off-domain
carousel.body: Deliberately explain a problem from your own work using the new field's vocabulary. The places where the analogy fails are usually more informative than where it fits.

carousel.title: Write your checklist
carousel.body: Turn what survives into questions you ask before deciding. A model you cannot phrase as a question is a phrase you are collecting, not a tool you are using.

actions: Write an inversion list for your finances: the five actions most likely to ruin them within three years, then audit which ones you are already doing in miniature.
Build a one-page pre-decision checklist covering incentives, consensus, obligation, prior commitment and time pressure. Use it before anything irreversible.
Choose one discipline outside your training and work through a real introductory textbook this quarter instead of another book of summaries.
Benchmark your own investing results honestly against a low-cost global index fund over five years, and act on the answer rather than on your best trade.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a structured argument rather than a compiled collection of talks, or you dislike investment wisdom delivered with a great deal of certainty.

verification.notes: A compiled collection of Munger's talks and writings, edited by Peter Kaufman, first published 2005 with later expanded editions. Survivorship concerns are addressed directly in the sparks.

books.title: Poor Economics
books.subtitle: A Radical Rethinking of the Way to Fight Global Poverty
books.author: Abhijit V. Banerjee and Esther Duflo
books.why_it_matters: It replaced a decades-long shouting match about whether aid works with a method for finding out programme by programme. The randomised approach it popularised now shapes how governments and charities across the world decide what to fund.

crux.headline: Stop arguing about aid and test the programme
crux.body: The big question of whether foreign aid helps or hurts has no answer, because aid is thousands of different things done in different places by different people. The productive question is smaller and answerable: does this bed net, this fertiliser subsidy, this way of teaching reading do what it claims, here, compared with a similar group that did not get it? Poverty is not one problem. It is a stack of specific, testable ones.

sparks.hook: The poor are not poor because they are irrational.
sparks.insight: Watch closely and decisions that look baffling from outside usually make sense from inside. Skipping a cheap preventive treatment is rational when the clinic is shut half the time and the nurse may not be there. Borrowing at a terrible rate is rational when the alternative is no capital at all. Buying a television before improving your diet is rational when your life contains very little else. Poverty is an environment, not a character trait.
sparks.why: This comes from years of detailed household surveys of spending and time rather than anecdote. It is the difference between explaining behaviour by the person and explaining it by the situation.
sparks.apply: Before calling a customer or a user irrational, spend an hour doing what they do. Look for the constraint you have never had to notice.

sparks.hook: Extra income buys tastier food before it buys more calories.
sparks.insight: The simplest poverty trap story says the poor cannot afford enough food to work hard, so a little more food would break the cycle. When incomes rise, people generally do not buy many more calories. They buy better-tasting food, or a phone, or a festival. That is not a mistake. At the margin, one more bowl of grain buys less life than something that makes life bearable or keeps you connected to other people.
sparks.why: Their consumption data across several countries showed calories rising far less than income. The exception matters, because for the severely undernourished, and for children in the womb and early years, more food does have large effects.
sparks.apply: Ask what the person you are trying to help would actually spend the money on, then decide whether your programme respects that answer.

sparks.hook: A comparison group is the difference between opinion and evidence.
sparks.insight: Programmes almost always look like they work, because the people who sign up differ from the people who do not: more motivated, better connected, closer to the road. The only reliable way to separate the programme from the people is to decide by chance who gets it first, then compare the two groups. It is unglamorous and slow, and it has repeatedly reversed conclusions that entire industries were confident about.
sparks.why: Randomisation removes selection bias by construction. Its limits are real, since a result from one district may not transfer, and trials can only measure what is measurable within a few years.
sparks.apply: Before your next rollout, hold back a randomly chosen tenth of sites for six months. That tenth is the only honest thing to compare against.

carousel.title: Ask something answerable
carousel.body: Not whether education helps, but whether hiring a second teacher raises reading scores in these schools. A testable question names the change, the outcome and the place.

carousel.title: Split by chance
carousel.body: Choose who gets it first at random. Any other rule, such as keenest first or easiest first, smuggles back in the differences you were trying to measure around.

carousel.title: Measure what people do
carousel.body: Attendance, doses taken, crops planted, money repaid. Reported satisfaction moves for many reasons that have nothing to do with whether the programme worked.

carousel.title: Replicate before you scale
carousel.body: One trial in one district is a finding, not a policy. Repeat it somewhere different before spending at national scale, and expect the effect to shrink.

sparks.hook: A bag of lentils moved immunisation more than better clinics did.
sparks.insight: In one rural Indian programme, reliable monthly camps raised full immunisation somewhat. Adding a small food incentive for each visit raised it far more, and it cut the cost for each fully immunised child, because staff time was no longer wasted on empty sessions. The lesson is not that people are bribable. It is that when a benefit is distant and abstract while the effort is immediate, a small immediate reward is what closes the gap.
sparks.why: This was a specific randomised evaluation in Udaipur, Rajasthan, run with the organisation Seva Mandir. It is one place and one design, though the general principle of small immediate incentives has held up more widely.
sparks.apply: Attach a small, immediate, cheap reward to any behaviour whose real payoff arrives months later. Make the reward instant rather than large.

sparks.hook: Free is not the same as nearly free.
sparks.insight: Charging a token amount for a health product is often defended on the grounds that people value what they pay for and that free goods get wasted. Trials of bed nets and water treatment repeatedly found the opposite. Even tiny prices cut take-up sharply, and people who received items free used them at similar rates to those who paid. For preventive products whose benefits spill over to everyone, the price is the barrier rather than a filter for seriousness.
sparks.why: Multiple randomised studies across malaria nets, deworming and water chlorination found steep drops in demand at small positive prices. The sunk-cost argument for charging did not survive the tests.
sparks.apply: If you want maximum uptake of a preventive good, make it free and remove the transaction entirely. Save pricing for products whose use is self-evident.

sparks.hook: Cheap schooling is not the same thing as children learning.
sparks.insight: Enrolment across the developing world rose enormously, and learning did not follow. Millions of children sat in classrooms for years without being able to read a paragraph, because teaching was aimed at the top of the class and at the syllabus rather than at the child in front of the teacher. The intervention that worked repeatedly was mundane: group children by what they can currently do rather than by age, and teach exactly that.
sparks.why: Teaching at the right level was tested by the organisation Pratham in India across several randomised evaluations and replicated in other countries, making it one of the better-supported findings in education research.
sparks.apply: Test what your learners can already do before you teach them, and group by that result rather than by year, grade or job title.

sparks.hook: Microcredit works. It just does not do what it promised.
sparks.insight: Small loans reliably do something useful. They let a household buy stock, smooth a bad month, and avoid a moneylender charging brutal rates. What multiple randomised studies did not find was the transformation in the marketing: mass business creation, incomes lifting a whole village, women's status changed within a few years. Rigid weekly repayment suits a market stall, not a risky venture that might take a year to pay off. It is a useful product, not an escape route.
sparks.why: Several randomised evaluations across countries found modest effects on business investment and little average effect on income, health or education. What is being demoted is the hype rather than the product.
sparks.apply: Check the strongest claim your favourite intervention makes and find out whether it was ever tested. Fund the modest proven effect, not the story.

sparks.hook: The poor run their own hedge fund, and it is expensive.
sparks.insight: Without insurance, a family self-insures: keep a goat, spread plots across villages, plant a low-yield crop that never fails, send a son to work far away. Each is a rational hedge and each is costly, and together they lock in low returns forever. Formal insurance would be far cheaper, but the market rarely appears, because claims are hard to verify, trust is low, and people will not pay today for a promise about a bad year.
sparks.why: Weather-indexed insurance was designed to solve the verification problem, and take-up stayed stubbornly low even when subsidised, which suggests trust and comprehension matter as much as price.
sparks.apply: Look at where you personally hold expensive private insurance, such as extra cash, over-hiring or duplicate suppliers, and price a real contract against it.

sparks.hook: Most programmes fail for three reasons, and none is corruption.
sparks.insight: When something good on paper fails on the ground, the usual suspects are theft and greed. More often the cause is duller: a belief held so firmly that nobody checked it, a piece of information the designer or the user simply did not have, or a default that nobody had any reason to change. All three are fixable at low cost, and all three are far less satisfying to blame than a villain.
sparks.why: The pattern comes from repeated field evaluations where fixing information or changing a default produced improvements that neither more money nor more monitoring had achieved.
sparks.apply: For a failing initiative, write one line each on the belief, the missing information and the default. Attack whichever is cheapest to change first.

carousel.title: Name the ideology
carousel.body: The unexamined belief driving the design: the poor need discipline, markets solve this, teachers are lazy. Write it down and ask what evidence would show it is wrong.

carousel.title: Find the ignorance
carousel.body: Something the designer or the user does not know: what the treatment does, when the clinic opens, what the loan really costs. Information is usually the cheapest available fix.

carousel.title: Break the inertia
carousel.body: Nobody chose the current arrangement, it simply persisted. Change the default and measure, because effort spent persuading people often moves less than changing what happens by itself.

sparks.hook: The most cited result in development is still disputed.
sparks.insight: School deworming was reported to raise attendance and later earnings at very low cost, and it became a flagship case for evidence-based aid. A reanalysis a decade later found coding errors and argued the effects were weaker and less certain than claimed. The original authors disputed much of that, and some effects survived. The honest summary is that the programme is probably cheap and probably helpful, and that the confident version was oversold.
sparks.why: The dispute matters beyond worms. It showed that a randomised trial is not a final verdict, that independent reanalysis is necessary, and that the field's own showcase result was fragile under scrutiny.
sparks.apply: For any headline finding you rely on, check whether an independent reanalysis exists before you build a plan around its effect size.

actions: Pick one thing your organisation believes about the people it serves and design a small randomised test of it before the next budget cycle.
Remove every fee, form and journey standing between a person and a preventive service you offer, then measure take-up before and after.
Attach a small immediate reward to a behaviour whose benefit arrives much later, and run it against a randomly chosen control group.
Read one published reanalysis of a study you have quoted in the past year, then update or drop the claim accordingly.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a grand theory of why nations are poor, or you distrust randomised trials as a way of knowing. This is deliberately small-scale and empirical.

verification.notes: First published 2011 by PublicAffairs. The deworming evidence is genuinely contested; both the original findings and the later reanalysis are described here as disputed.

books.title: Principles
books.subtitle: Life and Work
books.author: Ray Dalio
books.why_it_matters: A hedge fund manager wrote down the rules he actually used and published them, including the unflattering ones. Whatever you make of the culture it describes, the habit of turning every expensive mistake into a written, reusable rule is the part anyone can steal.

crux.headline: Write the rule down, then test it against reality
crux.body: Most people meet a problem, react, and forget. The alternative is to treat each encounter as one case of a recurring type, decide in advance how you will handle that type, write the decision down, and then check it against what actually happens. Over years you accumulate a personal operating manual that beats your mood on any given morning. Pain plus reflection is the engine. Pain on its own just hurts.

sparks.hook: Pain plus reflection is progress. Pain on its own is just pain.
sparks.insight: The instinct after a bad outcome is to move on quickly and stop feeling it. That wastes the most expensive information you will ever buy. The discipline is to stop at the moment of discomfort and ask three things: what type of situation was this, what did you do, and what rule would have produced a better result. Then write the answer where you will read it again. A mistake you never examined comes back in a slightly different costume, and you pay for it twice.
sparks.why: Reflection converts a single event into a rule that covers a whole class of events. Without it you keep relearning the same lesson, because memory of an episode fades much faster than a written principle does.
sparks.apply: Open a note today and record your last real mistake in three lines: the situation type, what you did, and the rule you will use next time.

sparks.hook: Ego and blind spots will cost you more than the market ever does.
sparks.insight: Two things stop you seeing straight. The first is the part of you that treats being wrong as an attack, so it argues instead of listening. The second is structural: every mind is built to notice some things and miss others, and you cannot find your own gaps by looking harder at them. The fix is not more confidence or more effort. It is finding people whose blind spots differ from yours and giving them real permission to tell you what you are missing.
sparks.why: You can partly correct for a bias you know you have, but a blind spot is invisible by definition. Only an outside view detects it, which is why the remedy has to be social rather than personal.
sparks.apply: Name one decision you are close to making, then ask someone who disagrees to argue the other side for ten minutes while you take notes and say nothing.

sparks.hook: Politeness in meetings is usually just failure with a delay on it.
sparks.insight: Most organisations run on a quiet agreement that nobody says the harsh version out loud, so problems stay hidden until they are expensive. The alternative is deliberately uncomfortable. Criticism goes to a person's face rather than around them, disagreements get recorded instead of smoothed over, and the awkwardness is treated as the price of finding errors early. It is not cruelty, and it only works if it applies to the most senior person in the room first.
sparks.why: Hidden problems compound, and the cost of raising one grows the longer it stays unsaid. Openness survives only when leaders absorb the criticism publicly, otherwise everyone reads the invitation as a trap.
sparks.apply: In your next team meeting, say the thing everyone is thinking but nobody has said, and make the first example a criticism of your own work.

sparks.hook: Every ambition breaks at one of five points. Find out which is yours.
sparks.insight: Getting what you want runs through five stages, and a failure at any one of them looks identical from the outside. Most people are strong at some stages and reliably weak at others, which is fixable once you know which. Someone who sets vivid goals but cannot bear diagnosing a problem will keep starting over. Someone excellent at diagnosis who never ships will keep producing analysis. The aim is not to master all five yourself, it is to know your weak stage and staff it.
sparks.why: Splitting one vague ability into five separate skills turns a character judgement into a diagnosis. You stop asking whether you are capable and start asking which specific step keeps breaking.
sparks.apply: Walk your last failed project through the five stages, mark the one where it actually broke, and ask someone who worked on it whether they agree.

carousel.title: Set a clear goal
carousel.body: Pick what you actually want, not the acceptable version. Vague goals make every later stage impossible to judge, because nothing can be measured against a target that keeps moving.

carousel.title: Find the problems
carousel.body: Hunt for whatever stands between you and the goal, and do not flinch at what turns up. Problems you refuse to look at do not stop existing, they only stop being solvable.

carousel.title: Diagnose the cause
carousel.body: Go past the symptom to the reason it happened, which is usually a person, a process, or a missing skill. Skip this stage and you get busy fixes that repair nothing.

carousel.title: Design the fix
carousel.body: Build a specific plan with named tasks, owners and dates, as if sketching a machine. A plan with no person's name attached to it is a hope, not a design.

carousel.title: Push it through
carousel.body: Finish the work, including the dull parts. This stage kills more good diagnoses than any other, because it needs no cleverness and a great deal of persistence.

sparks.hook: One opinion is not one vote. Some people have earned more weight.
sparks.insight: In most rooms the loudest voice or the most senior one wins, which quietly assumes that confidence tracks accuracy. It does not. A better rule weights opinions by demonstrated record on the specific question being decided: who has been right about this kind of thing before, and can they explain the reasoning rather than just assert the conclusion. That is neither a democracy nor a dictatorship, and it forces you to keep score honestly and in advance.
sparks.why: Track record is a noisy signal but a real one, and far better than seniority or volume. It works only if the record is kept before the outcome, not reconstructed afterwards by whoever happened to win.
sparks.apply: For one recurring decision, write down who has been right about it before and why, then give their view more weight than the org chart currently does.

sparks.hook: A mistake that repeats is a broken process, not a character flaw.
sparks.insight: When the same error keeps happening, blaming yourself is a dead end, because guilt changes nothing about the machinery that produced it. Log the error instead. Write what happened, what it cost, and which step let it through. Once you have twenty entries the patterns are obvious, and most of them are structural: a missing check, a handoff nobody owns, a decision made at the end of a long day. Fix the structure and the error rate drops without anyone becoming a better person.
sparks.why: Errors cluster around the weak joints of a process. A log turns invisible repetition into a visible pattern, which is the only thing that makes a root cause addressable rather than merely regrettable.
sparks.apply: Start a running mistake log this week with three columns: what happened, what it cost, which step let it through. Read the whole thing every Friday.

sparks.hook: Hire for values first. Skills are the cheapest thing on the list.
sparks.insight: Interviews drift towards whoever performs best in a conversation, which mostly measures interview skill. A more useful order is to check what someone values, then what they are natively capable of, then what they happen to know already. Values almost never change, raw capability changes slowly, and skills can be taught in months. Hiring in the wrong order means trying to correct the uncorrectable parts later, which is where most painful exits actually begin.
sparks.why: The three attributes differ enormously in how changeable they are. Ordering the filter by changeability puts the irreversible judgements first, where a mistake is hardest and most costly to undo.
sparks.apply: Before your next interview loop, write the three values the role genuinely requires and give one interviewer the sole job of testing for them.

carousel.title: Name the values you need
carousel.body: Be specific: high standards, appetite for criticism, follow-through. Generic words like integrity and passion cannot be tested in an interview, so they end up filtering nobody out.

carousel.title: Test thinking, not knowledge
carousel.body: Watch how someone reasons through an unfamiliar problem in front of you. Knowing your tools is a temporary advantage. Working through a mess without panicking is not.

carousel.title: Check skills last
carousel.body: Skills matter, but they are the part you can teach and the part that ages fastest. Treat a missing skill as a training plan rather than an automatic rejection.

carousel.title: Record your prediction
carousel.body: Write what you expect this person to be good and bad at before they start. Reading it back a year later is the only reliable way your hiring judgement improves.

sparks.hook: The closest thing to a free lunch is owning things that move apart.
sparks.insight: Chasing the single best asset is a losing game, because you cannot know in advance which one it will be. Holding several bets driven by genuinely different forces is a different proposition: the swings partly cancel while the returns still add up, so you can keep roughly the same expected gain with far less violence on the way there. The hard part is that holdings which look unrelated in calm markets have a habit of moving together on the worst day.
sparks.why: Combining imperfectly correlated bets lowers portfolio volatility, which is arithmetic rather than opinion. The honest caveat is that correlations tend to rise sharply in a crisis, exactly when you were counting on them not to.
sparks.apply: List what you own and write beside each holding what would damage it. If the same event appears next to most of them, you own one bet in several costumes.

sparks.hook: Most of what people call money is credit, and credit moves in cycles.
sparks.insight: Spending drives an economy, and a great deal of spending is made with borrowed money rather than earned money. That means today's demand can be pulled forward from tomorrow, which feels exactly like growth while it lasts. Debt builds in a short cycle that central banks can smooth by moving interest rates, and in a much longer one they eventually cannot smooth, because rates reach a floor while borrowers still owe more than their income can service.
sparks.why: This framework is descriptive rather than predictive, and other economists model debt cycles differently. It earns its place mainly by explaining why recoveries after credit busts look nothing like recoveries after ordinary recessions.
sparks.apply: Run the same test on yourself: work out how much of last year's spending was borrowed, and what happens to those payments if your income drops for six months.

sparks.hook: The culture behind the record is the part you probably cannot copy.
sparks.insight: Written rules look transferable, and some of them are. The management system around them is a different matter. It ran inside one firm with unusual selection, unusual pay and a founder who could impose it, and later reporting by journalists who interviewed former staff describes daily life in harsher terms than the book does. Take the practice of writing your rules down and checking them against outcomes. Be much slower to import somebody else's regime.
sparks.why: One firm's success is a single data point, and the people who left rarely write books. Judge any management system by whether it still works somewhere the founder is not standing in the room.
sparks.apply: Adopt the habit rather than the regime: write your own decision rules, review them each quarter, and import no rituals from another company for now.

actions: Start a personal principles document. Each time something goes badly, add one rule that would have changed the outcome, and reread the whole list once a month.
Run your last significant failure through the five stages, name the exact one that broke, then ask a colleague whether they agree with your diagnosis.
Ask the person who disagrees with you most often to write down what you are systematically wrong about. Sit with it for a day before you reply.
Map your income sources and investments by what would damage each one, then add a single source driven by something genuinely different from the rest.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a tight argument rather than a long list of rules, or you distrust management systems described by the person who built and benefited from them.

verification.notes: Published 2017 as Principles: Life and Work. Later journalism about the firm's internal culture is flagged inside the sparks rather than hidden. All prose original.

books.title: Reminiscences of a Stock Operator
books.author: Edwin Lefevre
books.why_it_matters: A century on it remains the most accurate description of what speculation does to a person's judgement. Traders keep rediscovering it because the technology changed completely and the psychology did not change at all.

crux.headline: Being right is not the same as making money
crux.body: Markets do not reward correct opinions, they reward correct positions held at the right size for long enough. A speculator can identify the move perfectly and still be destroyed by entering early, borrowing too heavily, or losing patience the week before it happens. The recurring lesson of the book is that the analysis is the easy half. Everything difficult is about timing, position size and the ability to sit still while nothing happens.

sparks.hook: Early and wrong feel identical while your money is running out.
sparks.insight: You can diagnose a bubble accurately and still be ruined by it, because the market can stay irrational for longer than your borrowed money lasts. Being early is not a badge of insight, it is a position you have to finance. The distinction matters most for anyone using leverage, where a temporary move against you closes the position permanently and you are not there for the vindication. The graveyard of speculation is full of people who were eventually right.
sparks.why: Leverage converts a temporary price move into a permanent loss by forcing the exit. Without borrowed money you can be early and merely bored, which is a survivable condition.
sparks.apply: Before any contrarian position, work out how far it can move against you before you are forced to sell. If that number is small, cut the size until it is not.

sparks.hook: The market does not know your opinion and would not care.
sparks.insight: A price is the current result of everyone else's buying and selling, not a verdict on the quality of your reasoning. When the market moves against a well-argued position, the useful response is to treat the movement as information about what other people are doing, rather than as an insult to be answered by adding more. Arguing with a price is the most expensive form of being right, because the price collects payment continuously while the argument is unresolved.
sparks.why: Prices aggregate the actions of everyone with money at stake, including people who know things you do not. That makes them a noisy signal worth listening to even when you disagree with the conclusion.
sparks.apply: Write your thesis and the specific price move that would prove it wrong before you buy. When that move happens, act on it rather than restating your reasoning.

sparks.hook: The money was never made in the trading. It was made in the holding.
sparks.insight: Finding a good position is the part that feels like skill, and it is not where the returns came from. The large gains arrived from staying in a correct position through months of noise, resisting the urge to take a small profit every time the screen flickered. That urge is strong precisely because acting feels like control. The discomfort of sitting on an unrealised gain while nothing happens is the actual job, and almost nobody finds it comfortable.
sparks.why: Returns in trending markets are concentrated in a few long moves, so cutting winners early removes most of the profit while leaving all of the losses. The skill is behavioural rather than analytical.
sparks.apply: For your next investment, set an exit condition based on the thesis breaking rather than on a profit target, then leave the position alone until one occurs.

sparks.hook: The house you play in matters more than the hand you are dealt.
sparks.insight: The story opens in bucket shops, venues that took the other side of small leveraged bets and profited when customers were wiped out by tiny price moves. The structure guaranteed that a customer who was right often enough would be barred, and everyone else would lose slowly. Modern equivalents exist wherever a platform earns from your activity rather than your results. The first question about any venue is not what you can win but how it makes its money.
sparks.why: When the counterparty profits from your losses, the game is adversarial by design regardless of how fair each individual trade looks. Fee and spread structures tell you more than any marketing does.
sparks.apply: For every platform you trade on, find out exactly how it earns from your order. If the answer is volume or spread, reduce your frequency rather than your bet size.

sparks.hook: A tip is somebody else's position looking for a buyer.
sparks.insight: Speculators collect opinions from people who already own the thing they are recommending, which means the recommendation and the sales pitch are the same message. Even honest tips are useless, because you receive the entry point and never the exit. When the person who told you sells, nobody calls. The deeper problem is that acting on a tip leaves you holding a position whose reasoning you cannot reconstruct, so you have no basis for deciding anything afterwards.
sparks.why: You cannot manage a position you did not reason your way into, because you have no criteria for when the thesis breaks. Tips also arrive most abundantly near the top of a move, when holders want company.
sparks.apply: Refuse to buy anything you cannot explain in four sentences without naming the person who suggested it. Write the four sentences before you place the order.

sparks.hook: Take the small loss while it is still small enough to be boring.
sparks.insight: Losses are easiest to accept in the first hour and hardest after a month of hoping. What starts as a manageable mistake becomes an identity problem: selling means admitting you were wrong, so the position is held, averaged into, and eventually becomes the reason for everything that follows. The only reliable defence is a rule set before the position exists, at a moment when you have no money at stake and therefore no need to protect your self-image.
sparks.why: Loss aversion and commitment bias both push towards holding losers, and both grow stronger as the loss grows. A pre-set rule moves the decision to a time when neither pressure is acting on you.
sparks.apply: Set the exit level for your next position before you enter, in writing, and place the order at the same time as the buy so it is not a live decision later.

carousel.title: Decide the size first
carousel.body: Work out the total amount you can lose on this idea before you look at the price. Position size is the only variable you fully control, so it is where risk is actually managed.

carousel.title: Name the invalidation
carousel.body: Write the specific event or price that would mean your reasoning was wrong. Something vague like it keeps going down is not a rule and will not be obeyed.

carousel.title: Place the exit early
carousel.body: Enter the exit instruction at the same moment as the entry, while you are still calm and the position costs you nothing emotionally to abandon.

carousel.title: Never average into a loser
carousel.body: Adding to a position that is going against you converts a bounded mistake into an unbounded one. If the thesis truly improved, that is a new trade with a new size limit.

sparks.hook: The urge to do something is the most expensive habit you own.
sparks.insight: There is no rule requiring you to have a position. Most days offer nothing worth acting on, and the trader who must be involved will manufacture reasons, take marginal setups and pay costs for the privilege of feeling busy. Boredom, not fear or greed, is what empties most accounts. Recognising that doing nothing is a legitimate and frequently optimal action is the difference between a strategy and a habit that happens to involve money.
sparks.why: Every trade carries costs and a chance of error, so marginal trades have negative expected value even before anything goes wrong. Activity feels productive because effort and results are usually correlated, and in markets they are not.
sparks.apply: Track your trades for a month and mark each as planned or impulsive. Total the results of the impulsive column and read the number out loud.

sparks.hook: Your biggest enemy has your name and sits in your chair.
sparks.insight: The recurring mistakes in a speculator's record are not varied. The same weakness appears in the same market conditions for a whole career: getting bored in quiet stretches, oversizing after a run of wins, refusing to sell a position that has become personal. Knowing the general principles is worthless because everyone knows them. What separates people is whether they have identified their own specific failure and built a rule that removes the decision from their hands.
sparks.why: Trading errors are individual and highly repetitive, so a personal record reveals patterns that general advice cannot. The rule has to be structural, because in the moment you will believe this time is different.
sparks.apply: Read back six months of your own decisions and name the single mistake that appears most often. Write one mechanical rule that makes repeating it difficult.

sparks.hook: The man who taught these lessons died broke. Read it with that in mind.
sparks.insight: The narrator is a lightly fictionalised version of a real speculator who made and lost several enormous fortunes, went bankrupt more than once, and died by suicide in nineteen forty. His tactical insight was genuine and his rules were sound. He could not follow them consistently, and no amount of trading skill compensates for the absence of a rule that preserves capital permanently. The book is a warning that happens to be written in the voice of a winner.
sparks.why: Repeated ruin despite exceptional skill is evidence that skill is not the binding constraint. It also shows how narrative selects for the exciting phase of a career and quietly omits the ending.
sparks.apply: Ring-fence a portion of your capital that no strategy may ever touch, in a separate account, and treat that boundary as permanent rather than as a target.

sparks.hook: Rules written before the money is on the table are the only ones you keep.
sparks.insight: Everything useful here reduces to the same structure: make the decision in advance, while calm, and then remove your later self's ability to overrule it. Judgement in the moment is compromised by the position you are holding, which is exactly when you feel most certain. Writing the rules down is not a bureaucratic exercise, it is the only way to get a fair fight between the version of you who reasons and the version who panics.
sparks.why: Decisions made under financial stress are systematically worse and systematically feel better. Precommitment works because it shifts the choice to a moment when nothing is at stake.
sparks.apply: Draft a one-page trading or investing policy this week covering size, exit and review, and refuse to act outside it for the next three months.

carousel.title: Write the entry condition
carousel.body: State what must be true before you buy anything, in terms specific enough that another person could check whether the condition has been met.

carousel.title: Fix the maximum size
carousel.body: Decide the largest share of your capital any single idea may take, and make it small enough that being wrong is a bad week rather than a bad decade.

carousel.title: Define the exit both ways
carousel.body: Write what makes you sell at a loss and what makes you sell at a gain. Only one of those will feel necessary now, and you will need both.

carousel.title: Review on a schedule
carousel.body: Read your own decisions once a quarter against the policy, and change the policy deliberately between reviews rather than in the middle of a losing position.

actions: Write a one-page personal investing policy covering entry conditions, maximum position size, exit rules in both directions, and a fixed quarterly review date.
Review six months of your own decisions and identify the single mistake that repeats most. Build one mechanical rule that makes committing it harder.
Find out exactly how every platform you use earns money from your orders, then reduce your trading frequency accordingly.
Move a fixed portion of your capital into an account no strategy may touch, and treat that boundary as permanent rather than as a floor to be tested.
books.not_for_you_if: You want an analytical method or a modern market. It is a period narrative about short-term speculation, and it will teach you nothing about valuing a business.

verification.notes: Published 1923 after serialisation in a magazine. A lightly fictionalised account widely understood to be based on the speculator Jesse Livermore, whose bankruptcies and 1940 death are noted in the sparks.

books.title: Security Analysis
books.author: Benjamin Graham and David Dodd
books.why_it_matters: It created security analysis as a discipline with rules rather than a trade based on tips, and it was written by two men who had just watched the 1929 crash destroy a generation of investors. Every professional valuation method descends from it.

crux.headline: Value is a range, and cheapness is the only edge
crux.body: You will never know what a business is precisely worth, and you do not need to. You need a defensible range, built from what the company has actually earned across good years and bad, and a price so far below that range that the imprecision cannot hurt you. Analysis is not forecasting. It is establishing what is known, marking clearly what is not, and buying only when the gap between price and demonstrable value is wide enough to make the unknown unimportant.

sparks.hook: Trying to value a company to the nearest pound is the beginner's mistake.
sparks.insight: A valuation is not a single number, it is a band, and the honest analyst says so. You might conclude a business is worth somewhere between eighty and a hundred and twenty. That looks like failure until you notice it is enough: if the share trades at forty, you do not need to resolve the range to know it is cheap. The precision people chase in spreadsheets is usually false anyway, because it comes from extending assumptions further than the evidence supports.
sparks.why: Ranges are honest about model uncertainty. A point estimate hides it, and hidden uncertainty encourages positions sized as though the number were reliable.
sparks.apply: Value a company twice, once with pessimistic assumptions and once with optimistic ones. Only act if the price sits below the pessimistic figure.
