sparks.apply: Sort your recurring failures into predictable and unpredictable. Write a list for the first group and a communication point for the second.

carousel.title: Name the failure type
carousel.body: Ask whether the thing that goes wrong is a known step being missed or an unforeseen situation being mishandled. The answer decides everything that follows.

carousel.title: Script the predictable
carousel.body: Where the right sequence is known and stable, write it down and run it at a fixed pause point. This is the cheapest reliability you will ever buy.

carousel.title: Force talk on the unpredictable
carousel.body: Where conditions vary, do not script the actions. Script the conversation: who must speak, at what moment, and who holds the decision when they disagree.

carousel.title: Push authority downward
carousel.body: The people closest to a novel problem usually see it first. Give them the power to act inside defined limits rather than routing every judgement upward.

sparks.hook: Aviation did not adopt checklists after a debate. It adopted them after a crash.
sparks.insight: The practice took hold in flying because an advanced aircraft was lost in a demonstration flight when an experienced crew missed a step, and the machine had simply become too complex to fly from memory alone. The response was not a simpler aeroplane or a better pilot. It was a short card of the items that must not be skipped. That history is useful because it dates the moment a profession accepted that competence alone had stopped being sufficient, and every field eventually reaches it.
sparks.why: The aviation case is well documented and is the origin point for the practice. It matters because it shows the shift being forced by complexity rather than chosen by preference.
sparks.apply: Ask whether any part of your work has quietly outgrown what one person can hold in memory. Write the card for that part first.

sparks.hook: The checklist is only finished when it has been rewritten by reality.
sparks.insight: A first draft written at a desk is always wrong in ways you cannot predict: an item is ambiguous, another arrives at the wrong moment, a third turns out to be someone else's job. The only way to find these is to run it on real work and watch what happens. Expect three or four revisions before it settles, and expect to cut more than you add. A list that has never been revised is usually a list that has never actually been used.
sparks.why: Field testing surfaces failures of wording, timing and ownership that are invisible on paper. This iteration is the difference between a document that exists and one that catches things.
sparks.apply: Run your draft checklist on five real jobs, note every hesitation or argument it causes, and rewrite it before asking anyone to adopt it.

actions: Pick your highest consequence recurring process and write a checklist of five or six killer items that runs in under sixty seconds.
Decide the exact pause point where the list is run and whether it is read before acting or used to confirm afterwards.
Have the people who do the work write the list themselves, then run it aloud with a senior person visibly participating.
Test it on five real jobs, record every point of confusion, and rewrite it before rolling it out any wider.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a practical manual rather than a narrative argument, or your work is genuinely one-off with no repeated process to systematise.

verification.notes: Published 2009 by Metropolitan Books. The later Ontario province-wide rollout that found no significant improvement is noted honestly; no figures are quoted for either study.

books.title: Becoming a Supple Leopard
books.subtitle: The Ultimate Guide to Resolving Pain, Preventing Injury, and Optimizing Athletic Performance
books.author: Kelly Starrett
books.why_it_matters: It moved mobility work from a warm-up afterthought to a daily practice with a vocabulary, and gave a generation of lifters a way to talk about position and range instead of only load. Its influence on gym culture is far larger than its evidence base.

crux.headline: Position first, then load, then speed
crux.body: Strength built on a bad shape is strength you will eventually pay for. Treat every movement as a technical skill with a standard you can check, get into a stable position before adding weight, and add speed last. When a position is unavailable, that is a specific restriction to work on rather than a personal limit. The daily ten minutes spent restoring range is what keeps the training going for decades instead of years.

sparks.hook: You can be strong and still move like the hinge is rusted shut.
sparks.insight: Strength and range of motion are separate qualities, and training one hard does not maintain the other. Plenty of people can lift heavy through a shape their joints hate, because muscle will happily compensate for a joint that has quietly stopped moving. It works until it does not. Treating range as a trainable quality with its own daily practice, rather than something you either have or lack, is the entire premise here.
sparks.why: Range of motion responds to regular loading at end range, and it declines with disuse. The claim that restoring it prevents injury is plausible and popular but not well supported by trials.
sparks.apply: Test one position you avoid, like a full-depth squat or arms overhead against a wall, and note exactly where it stops rather than how it feels.

sparks.hook: Movement is a skill with standards, not a talent you were issued at birth.
sparks.insight: Nobody would say you either can play the piano or you cannot. Movement gets treated that way constantly. The alternative is to define what a good squat, hinge, press and carry actually look like, then practise them the way you would practise a technical skill: slowly, with feedback, at a load light enough that the shape survives. You are not born with a squat. You are either practising one or losing one.
sparks.why: Motor learning research supports deliberate practice of movement patterns with feedback. What remains contested is whether any single prescribed shape is correct for every body, given real anatomical variation in hips and shoulders.
sparks.apply: Film one set of your main lift from the side this week and watch it once without judging it, just describing what your joints actually did.

sparks.hook: Set the trunk before you move, not while you are moving.
sparks.insight: Most people organise their spine and pelvis somewhere in the middle of a lift, which means the first part of every rep happens in a shape nobody chose. The alternative is a fixed sequence you run before load: stand tall, set the pelvis, bring the ribcage down, create tension, then breathe into that shape and keep it. It takes about two seconds and it turns the setup from an accident into a decision.
sparks.why: Bracing measurably increases trunk stiffness and is standard in strength coaching. The stronger claim, that spinal flexion under load is inherently dangerous, is disputed by pain researchers and should be held loosely.
sparks.apply: Run a fixed setup sequence before every working set this week, and refuse to start the rep until the shape is set and you have taken one breath.

carousel.title: Stand and stack
carousel.body: Feet under hips, weight through the middle of the foot. Get tall before anything else, so the spine starts from a neutral position rather than finding one mid-lift.

carousel.title: Set the pelvis
carousel.body: Squeeze the glutes lightly to stop the pelvis tipping forward. You are looking for a small correction, not a clench that locks up the hips.

carousel.title: Bring ribs down
carousel.body: Drop the front of the ribcage so it sits over the pelvis rather than flaring up. This is what actually connects the trunk into one unit.

carousel.title: Breathe and brace
carousel.body: Take air into the belly and sides, then tighten as if expecting a light punch. Pressure, not breath holding for its own sake.

carousel.title: Keep it, then move
carousel.body: The shape has to survive the whole rep. If it collapses at a particular point, that is your working depth for now, not a failure of effort.

sparks.hook: The sore knee is often reporting on the ankle nobody has checked.
sparks.insight: Joints work in a chain, and a joint that will not move hands its job to the neighbours. A stiff ankle forces the knee inward or the heel up in a squat. A locked mid-back makes the shoulder do the reaching. So the place that hurts is frequently the place absorbing someone else's missing range, which is why treating the painful spot alone so often produces temporary relief and a returning problem.
sparks.why: Kinetic chain compensation is well established in biomechanics. Confidently predicting which restriction caused which pain is much shakier, and pain has drivers beyond mechanics, including sleep, load history and stress.
sparks.apply: When something aches, test the range of the joints directly above and below it before you do anything to the sore area itself.

sparks.hook: Test, work, retest. If nothing moved, you just spent ten minutes on nothing.
sparks.insight: Most mobility work is performed on faith. The fix is to treat every session as a small experiment: measure a specific position, do one intervention for a few minutes, measure the same position again. If it changed, keep the method. If it did not, drop it without sentiment. This single loop separates people who slowly gain range from people who have been rolling the same muscle for three years with nothing to show.
sparks.why: Immediate range changes are measurable and repeatable within a session. Whether short-term gains accumulate into lasting change is less certain, which is exactly why the retest habit matters.
sparks.apply: Before your next mobility session, pick one measurable test position. Do one thing for five minutes. Retest immediately and write down the result.

carousel.title: Pick one test
carousel.body: Something specific and repeatable: how deep the squat goes before the heels lift, or how far the arms reach overhead with the back flat against a wall.

carousel.title: Choose one intervention
carousel.body: One area, one method, five minutes. Changing several things at once means you learn nothing about which of them was worth the time.

carousel.title: Retest immediately
carousel.body: Same test, same setup, same day. Compare against what you recorded, not against how the position feels, because feeling is a terrible instrument.

carousel.title: Keep or bin it
carousel.body: Real change means keep it and repeat tomorrow. No change means bin it and try something else. Loyalty to a technique is the enemy here.

sparks.hook: Ten minutes every day beats an hour every fortnight, and it is not close.
sparks.insight: Tissue and nervous system adapt to what happens regularly, not to occasional heroic sessions. Ten focused minutes a day, aimed at whatever is currently most restricted, accumulates into range you keep. A long session once in a while mostly produces soreness and the feeling of having done something. The daily version also fits into life, which is the only reason it survives past the second week.
sparks.why: Frequency generally beats duration for flexibility and motor adaptation, in line with how other skills develop. The specific ten-minute figure is a practical recommendation, not a tested dose.
sparks.apply: Put ten minutes of mobility work directly after an existing daily anchor, such as after your evening shower, and do it in the same spot each time.

sparks.hook: Pain during a lift is information about position, not a toughness test.
sparks.insight: Training through sharp pain is treated as discipline in a lot of gyms, and it is mostly just a way of turning a small problem into a long one. Sharp or joint-specific pain is a signal to change something now: reduce the load, shorten the range, alter the setup. Discomfort from effort is different, and learning to tell them apart is one of the more valuable skills in training. Stop, adjust, retest, continue.
sparks.why: Pain is a protective output influenced by tissue state, sleep, stress and expectation rather than a direct damage readout. That makes it worth listening to and a poor instrument for diagnosing exactly what is wrong.
sparks.apply: Agree a rule with yourself now: sharp or joint pain means you change load or range within that same set, not at the end of the session.

sparks.hook: A chair is a position you hold for eight hours without any practice.
sparks.insight: Nobody would train a single position for forty hours a week and expect it to have no effect. Sitting is exactly that, and the issue is less the posture itself than the total absence of variation. The fix is not a perfect ergonomic setup but frequent change: stand sometimes, move every half hour, take a few minutes of the opposite shape. Variety is the active ingredient, and no chair provides it.
sparks.why: The link between specific postures and pain is weaker than commonly claimed, and studies have struggled to show that sitting position predicts back pain. Lack of movement variation has better support than posture correction.
sparks.apply: Set an alarm for every thirty minutes of desk work and change position for sixty seconds. Stand, walk, or take your hips through a full range.

sparks.hook: You cannot own a position you only visit under a barbell.
sparks.insight: If the bottom of a squat is a place you reach twice a week for a fraction of a second under load, you do not really have it. Owning a position means being able to sit in it, breathe there, look around, and get out under control. Spend unloaded time in the end ranges you need, and the loaded version stops being a place you fall into and becomes somewhere you can actually work.
sparks.why: Loading and spending time at end range does build usable range, and it holds better than passive stretching alone. The precise mechanism involves both tissue and nervous system tolerance, and is still argued over.
sparks.apply: Spend two minutes a day resting in the bottom of an unloaded squat, breaking it into shorter holds if that is all you can currently manage.

sparks.hook: This is a coach's system, and it is confident well past its evidence.
sparks.insight: The framework is detailed, internally consistent and mostly untested. Claims about fascia, specific tissue techniques, and mobility work preventing injury are far more certain in the writing than in the research, and some explanations for why a technique works have not held up. The practical parts still earn their place: move daily, respect position, test what you do. Take the practice, discount the mechanisms, and ignore anything promising to bulletproof a joint.
sparks.why: Systematic reviews have found little evidence that stretching or mobility work prevents injury, though strength training does show a protective effect. Naming that gap makes the useful parts more trustworthy, not less.
sparks.apply: Keep the daily practice and the test-retest habit from this book, and treat every anatomical explanation in it as a hypothesis rather than a fact.

actions: Film your three main lifts from the side, watch each once, and write down the single position that breaks down first under load.
Choose one test position, measure it today, and run a daily ten-minute session for a month with a weekly retest recorded in the same place.
Set a thirty-minute movement alarm for every working day and change position for a minute each time it goes off.
Add or keep a strength training programme, since that has better evidence for reducing injury than any mobility work you will do.
books.not_for_you_if: You want evidence-graded rehabilitation guidance, or you find long lists of prescribed techniques and confident anatomical explanations more discouraging than useful.

verification.notes: First published 2013 by Victory Belt; a revised second edition followed in 2015. Injury-prevention and fascia claims in the book are not well supported by current evidence and the content says so directly. All prose original.

books.title: Breath
books.subtitle: The New Science of a Lost Art
books.author: James Nestor
books.why_it_matters: It took a subject that sat between yoga studios and respiratory clinics and made it a mainstream health topic. The physiology it gets right is genuinely useful; the parts it oversells are a good lesson in reading health writing.

crux.headline: How you breathe changes how you feel
crux.body: Breathing is the one automatic system that also accepts instructions, and because it is wired into the same circuitry as heart rate and blood pressure, changing it changes your state. Two things carry most of the benefit: breathe through your nose rather than your mouth, and breathe more slowly than feels natural, with the exhale longer than the inhale. Almost everything else in this field is a variation on those two, or is still speculation.

sparks.hook: Your nose does about thirty jobs. Your mouth does one of them, badly.
sparks.insight: Air taken in through the nose is filtered, warmed, humidified and slowed, and it picks up nitric oxide produced in the sinuses, which helps open blood vessels in the lungs. Mouth breathing skips all of that. Do it habitually, especially at night, and you get a dry throat, more disturbed sleep and a mouth that stays open because it has learned to. The nose is the default the whole system was designed around.
sparks.why: Nasal nitric oxide production and the conditioning of incoming air are well-established physiology. Claims about long-term structural consequences are weaker and rest mostly on observational and orthodontic work.
sparks.apply: Spend one week breathing through your nose during easy exercise, slowing your pace as much as it takes to keep your mouth closed throughout.

carousel.title: Start at rest
carousel.body: Spend a few days noticing whether your mouth hangs open while you read, drive or work. Closing it is most of the change and costs nothing.

carousel.title: Clear the passage first
carousel.body: If your nose is genuinely blocked, fix that before anything else. Chronic congestion, allergy and structural problems need treating rather than pushing through.

carousel.title: Take it to easy exercise
carousel.body: Walk or jog slowly enough that your mouth stays shut. Your pace will drop noticeably at first and recover over a few weeks of practice.

carousel.title: Leave the night until last
carousel.body: Night breathing is the hardest to control and the easiest to get wrong. Get an airway assessment before trying to force anything while you sleep.

sparks.hook: The book's central experiment had two participants, and both wrote it.
sparks.insight: The most memorable evidence here is a self-experiment: two people blocked their noses for ten days, measured themselves throughout, and reported that blood pressure, sleep quality and snoring all worsened, then reversed when they went back to nasal breathing. It is vivid and it is consistent with known physiology. It is also a sample of two, unblinded, run by the people making the argument. That makes it a good illustration and poor proof.
sparks.why: Self-experiments cannot separate an effect from expectation, and two people cannot tell you how a result varies across a population. Treat it as a hypothesis worth testing on yourself, not a finding.
sparks.apply: Run your own version honestly. Pick one thing you can measure, change one variable for two weeks, and write your prediction down before you start.

sparks.hook: Around six breaths a minute is where your heart and lungs synchronise.
sparks.insight: Breathe slowly and evenly at roughly five to six breaths per minute and heart rate variability rises, blood pressure tends to drop slightly, and most people feel calmer within a few minutes. The rate is not mystical. It sits close to the frequency at which the reflex controlling your blood pressure naturally oscillates, so breathing at that pace amplifies it. This is the best-evidenced idea in the entire subject.
sparks.why: Slow-paced breathing has been tested in controlled trials for blood pressure, anxiety and heart rate variability, and the short-term effects are consistent even where the long-term ones look modest.
sparks.apply: Set a timer for five minutes and breathe in for about five seconds and out for about five, through your nose, once a day at a fixed time.

carousel.title: Sit up and close your mouth
carousel.body: Sit upright with your mouth closed and your tongue resting on the roof of your mouth. Everything that follows happens through the nose only.

carousel.title: Slow the count
carousel.body: Breathe in for roughly five seconds and out for roughly five. Adjust until it feels unforced. Straining for a longer count defeats the whole purpose.

carousel.title: Let the movement be low
carousel.body: The movement should be quiet and low, with the ribs widening sideways. A heaving chest and audible air mean you are pulling harder than you need to.

carousel.title: Stay for five minutes
carousel.body: The shift in heart rate variability takes a few minutes to appear. Five minutes daily does far more than one long session once a week.

sparks.hook: A long exhale is the closest thing you have to a manual brake.
sparks.insight: Your heart rate rises slightly on the in-breath and falls on the out-breath. Lengthening the exhale relative to the inhale leans on that asymmetry and shifts you toward the calming branch of the nervous system. It is a small effect per breath and a noticeable one after a minute or two. Unlike most calming advice it works during the situation rather than afterwards, and nobody in the room can tell you are doing it.
sparks.why: The rise and fall of heart rate with the breath is basic physiology, and extended-exhale breathing reliably raises vagal indices in short laboratory studies. It changes your state, it does not cure anxiety.
sparks.apply: Take six breaths with a four-second inhale and an eight-second exhale immediately before anything that makes you nervous.

sparks.hook: The urge to breathe is not your body asking for oxygen.
sparks.insight: What triggers the desperate need to inhale is rising carbon dioxide, not falling oxygen. Your blood stays well saturated far longer than the panic suggests. This is why people who train breath-holding are mostly training tolerance to discomfort rather than storage capacity, and why anxious over-breathing makes things worse: blowing off carbon dioxide changes your blood chemistry and produces the tingling and light-headedness that feel like proof something is badly wrong.
sparks.why: Carbon dioxide sensing driving air hunger is standard respiratory physiology, and the symptoms of hyperventilation can be reproduced deliberately in a clinic and resolved by slowing the breath.
sparks.apply: Slow down instead of gulping air the next time stress leaves you breathless, and make the out-breath longer than the in-breath for a full minute.

sparks.hook: Most people breathe more air than they actually need, all day long.
sparks.insight: Light chronic over-breathing is common and invisible: slightly fast, slightly deep, through the mouth, especially under stress. Because it feels like getting more oxygen it never registers as a problem. Correcting it is uncomfortable at first, since breathing less means tolerating a little more carbon dioxide, and that feels like air hunger even while your oxygen saturation is completely fine. The discomfort usually fades within a couple of weeks of practice.
sparks.why: Reduced-breathing methods have a plausible mechanism and small trials in asthma showing fewer symptoms and less reliever medication, though measured lung function itself changes little.
sparks.apply: Practise five minutes where the goal is to make each nasal breath so small and quiet that a mirror held under your nose would barely fog.

sparks.hook: Mouth taping went viral on far less evidence than you would guess.
sparks.insight: The idea is simple: hold your mouth closed at night so you breathe through your nose. Plenty of people report less snoring and a less parched throat. The published evidence is thin, limited to small studies, and it does not show that taping treats sleep apnoea. If your nose is blocked, or if you have undiagnosed apnoea, taping your mouth shut is an actively bad idea rather than a neutral one. Get the airway looked at first.
sparks.why: Small trials suggest a modest snoring reduction in mild cases. Sleep physicians warn against using taping as a substitute for diagnosis, because obstructive apnoea needs proper assessment and treatment.
sparks.apply: Get a sleep assessment before experimenting with your airway at night, especially if you snore heavily or wake up unrefreshed most mornings.

sparks.hook: Softer food may have given modern humans smaller jaws and worse airways.
sparks.insight: The argument runs that industrial food requires far less chewing than anything humans ate before it, that jaws develop partly in response to mechanical load, and that crowded teeth and narrow airways are the downstream result. It is genuinely interesting, and it fits the pattern of straighter, less crowded teeth in older skulls. It also runs well ahead of the evidence, and the proposed fixes range from mainstream orthodontics to devices with no support at all.
sparks.why: Bone does respond to mechanical loading, and skeletal comparisons are suggestive. But diet is confounded with everything else about industrial life, and no trial shows that chewing more prevents airway problems.
sparks.apply: Treat this as a hypothesis rather than a treatment plan. If you suspect an airway or jaw problem, see a specialist instead of buying a chewing device.

sparks.hook: Breathing is the only automatic system you can also drive by hand.
sparks.insight: Heart rate, digestion and blood pressure run without you and largely refuse instructions. Breathing runs without you but accepts them, and because it is wired into the same autonomic circuitry, changing the breath changes the rest. That is why breath practices appear independently across so many unrelated traditions. It is a real lever, and its limits are just as real: it changes your state for minutes at a time and it is not a treatment for disease.
sparks.why: Voluntary control of respiration influences heart rate and blood pressure through established reflex pathways. The effects are reliable in the moment and modest when measured over months.
sparks.apply: Attach two minutes of slow nasal breathing to one recurring stressful moment in your day, at the same point every time, for three weeks.

sparks.hook: Breathing through your nose while training feels worse and may pay off later.
sparks.insight: Switching to nasal-only breathing at easy intensity forces you to slow down, because the nose restricts airflow. Over a few weeks most people find that the same pace becomes possible with the mouth closed. Whether that improves performance is unsettled, since the studies are small and mixed. What it reliably does is give you an honest brake on easy days, and easy days are exactly what most amateur athletes ruin by running them too hard.
sparks.why: Direct performance benefits are weakly supported at best. The indirect benefit, keeping easy sessions genuinely easy, is well supported by endurance training research in general.
sparks.apply: Do your next three easy runs or rides with your mouth closed the whole way, and accept whatever slower pace that requires.

actions: Spend a week simply noticing when your mouth is open, and close it during every activity where you are not out of breath.
Practise five minutes of slow nasal breathing daily at a fixed time, in for about five seconds and out for about five.
Learn the extended-exhale pattern well enough to use it silently in a meeting, then actually use it the next time you are anxious.
Get a professional airway or sleep assessment before adopting any night-time breathing intervention you read about online.
books.not_for_you_if: You want careful science writing with proportionate claims. The reporting is enthusiastic, the sourcing is uneven, and the historical sections outrun the evidence.

verification.notes: First published 2020. Several central claims, including the craniofacial thesis and mouth taping, are speculative or thinly evidenced and are flagged as such above.

books.title: Burn
books.subtitle: New Research Blows the Lid Off How We Really Burn Calories, Lose Weight, and Stay Healthy
books.author: Herman Pontzer
books.why_it_matters: It took the most confident assumption in fitness — that moving more simply adds to what you burn — and showed the measured data does not behave that way. It changed how researchers argue about exercise and body weight.

crux.headline: Exercise moves your calories around, not up
crux.body: Measure daily energy expenditure properly and it turns out to be remarkably stable across wildly different activity levels. Bodies appear to work within a constrained budget, quietly trimming spending elsewhere when activity rises. The consequence is uncomfortable: exercise is a poor tool for losing weight and an excellent tool for almost everything else. What you eat determines the size of your body. What you do determines how well it works.

sparks.hook: Hunter-gatherers walking all day burn about what an office worker burns.
sparks.insight: Measurements of daily energy expenditure among the Hadza of Tanzania, who forage on foot for hours a day, came out close to those of sedentary adults in wealthy countries once body size was accounted for. That is not what anyone expected. Far more physical activity did not produce a far larger daily calorie total, which forces a rethink of the simple idea that expenditure is activity plus a fixed baseline.
sparks.why: The measurements used doubly labelled water, the accepted method for total expenditure in free-living people. The interpretation is contested; some researchers read the same data as showing a smaller, not absent, effect of activity.
sparks.apply: Stop using your workout as a calorie budget for later eating. Log a week of food without any exercise credit and see what the real total is.

sparks.hook: Your body has a budget, and it balances it behind your back.
sparks.insight: The constrained model says the body defends a fairly narrow total energy spend. Add a lot of activity and it economises elsewhere: reproductive hormones, immune activity, inflammation, background repair, fidgeting, stress responses. Nothing announces itself. You simply spend the same total on a different distribution. That reframes exercise as a way of reallocating your metabolism rather than as a way of enlarging it.
sparks.why: Evidence for the trade-offs is indirect, drawn from hormone and inflammation changes in training studies. The constrained model is a serious hypothesis with real support, not a settled consensus.
sparks.apply: Judge a training block by what improves alongside it — sleep, mood, blood markers, resting heart rate — rather than by weight on a scale.

sparks.hook: The reason exercise helps inflammation may be that it crowds inflammation out.
sparks.insight: If the daily energy total is roughly fixed, then energy given to muscles has to come from somewhere. One reading is that activity leaves less budget for chronic low-grade inflammation, elevated stress hormones and overactive reproductive signalling — all of which are implicated in cancers and cardiovascular disease. The health benefits of exercise would then come partly from what it stops the body doing, not only from what it makes it do.
sparks.why: This is a mechanistic proposal that fits the observed data rather than a proven pathway. Exercise reducing inflammatory markers is well established; the budget explanation for why is not.
sparks.apply: Treat regular moderate activity as maintenance for the system rather than as a weight tool, and keep it on days when the scale is not moving.

sparks.hook: Weight is lost in the kitchen. That cliché survived the measurement.
sparks.insight: If total expenditure barely moves when activity rises, the intake side carries nearly all the weight of the equation. This is not an argument against training; it is an argument against expecting training to do a job it is structurally poor at. People who lose weight and keep it off overwhelmingly changed what and how much they eat. Exercise then does the separate and vital job of keeping the result healthy.
sparks.why: Exercise-only interventions produce small average weight loss in trials, far less than the arithmetic of calories burned predicts. That gap has been visible for decades and this model explains it.
sparks.apply: Choose one intake change you can sustain for a year — not a diet, a single rule — and keep training entirely separate from it.

sparks.hook: Humans are the strange apes that share food and burn energy fast.
sparks.insight: Compared with other great apes, humans burn noticeably more energy per day for our size, and we grow bigger brains, have more children and live longer on the back of it. The evolutionary bargain that paid for it was cooperation: sharing food, hunting and gathering together, feeding people who are not currently productive. Our metabolism is not an individual trait. It is a social one, subsidised by other people.
sparks.why: Comparative measurements across apes and humans support the higher human expenditure. The cooperative explanation is a well-argued interpretation rather than a directly tested claim.
sparks.apply: Look at who feeds whom in your household and make one meal a week a shared, cooked, sit-down event rather than individual refuelling.

sparks.hook: Metabolism does not crash at forty. That story is folklore.
sparks.insight: Adjust for body size and composition and metabolic rate is remarkably stable from roughly the twenties into the sixties. It is high in early childhood, settles in the twenties, holds flat for decades, then declines late. Weight gained in middle age is therefore not the result of a suddenly slowing engine. It is the result of gradual changes in intake, muscle mass and movement that are far easier to blame on age than to examine.
sparks.why: This follows large pooled analyses of doubly labelled water data across the lifespan. It is one of the better-supported claims here and it contradicts a very widespread belief.
sparks.apply: Instead of blaming a slowing metabolism, compare your current weekly food and step count with what they were five years ago.

carousel.title: Infancy runs hottest
carousel.body: Energy use for body size peaks in the first years of life, when growth and brain development are consuming an extraordinary share of everything taken in.

carousel.title: Childhood settles down
carousel.body: The rate declines gradually through childhood and adolescence toward adult levels, which is why teenage appetite is about size and growth rather than a magic engine.

carousel.title: Adulthood holds flat
carousel.body: From roughly the twenties to the sixties, size-adjusted expenditure is remarkably stable. The middle-age slowdown people describe is not visible in the measurements.

carousel.title: Late life declines
carousel.body: A real decline appears later in life, alongside lost muscle. That is the stage where keeping strength training in the week pays the largest dividend.

sparks.hook: There is no ancestral diet. There are ancestral diets, and they disagree.
sparks.insight: Traditional societies eat wildly differently. Some take most of their energy from tubers and honey, some from fish, some from meat and milk. What they share is not a macronutrient ratio but the absence of industrially processed food and a lot of daily movement. That makes any diet sold as the way humans evolved to eat a marketing story. The variation is the actual finding.
sparks.why: Field studies of foraging and pastoral groups show enormous dietary range with generally good metabolic health, which undercuts single-macronutrient explanations of modern disease.
sparks.apply: Stop choosing between low-carb and low-fat. Cut one heavily processed item from your weekly shop and replace it with something you cook.

sparks.hook: Your brain runs on roughly a fifth of your energy while doing nothing visible.
sparks.insight: A resting adult spends a large share of daily energy on the brain, and that share is far larger in childhood. Thinking harder barely changes the bill; the organ is expensive whether you are doing calculus or staring out of a window. This is why mental work is not a route to burning calories, and why the human energy budget had to expand in the first place to afford the brain we have.
sparks.why: Brain energy use as a large fraction of resting metabolism is long-established from direct measurement. The small additional cost of effortful thinking is also well documented.
sparks.apply: Drop the idea that a demanding work day earns extra food, and set your intake by body size and activity rather than by mental effort.

sparks.hook: Calorie counts on labels and machines are estimates dressed as measurements.
sparks.insight: The number on a treadmill, a watch or a packet carries a precision it has not earned. Food labels are permitted meaningful error, absorption varies with cooking and processing, and wearable estimates of expenditure are built from population averages rather than from you. Using them as approximate signals is fine. Using them as a ledger where a session cancels a dessert is arithmetic with numbers that were never accurate enough for it.
sparks.why: Validation studies consistently find large individual errors in wearable energy expenditure estimates, and labelling regulations allow substantial tolerance on stated calorie content.
sparks.apply: Ignore the calorie readout on machines and wearables for a month. Track only sessions completed and how the food actually looked on your plate.

sparks.hook: Move for the machine, eat for the size. Two jobs, two tools.
sparks.insight: The whole argument reduces to separating what exercise is good at from what it is bad at. It is superb for cardiovascular health, strength, mood, blood sugar control and how long you stay independent. It is a weak lever on body mass. Confusing the two produces people who quit training because the scale did not move, which is the worst possible outcome of a good habit judged by the wrong measure.
sparks.why: Activity's effect on mortality and disease risk is robust across large cohort studies, while its direct effect on weight is small. Both facts can be true at once.
sparks.apply: Write two separate plans: one for how you will move each week, one for how you will eat. Do not let either one negotiate with the other.

carousel.title: Split the goals
carousel.body: Put fitness targets and body-composition targets on different pages. They need different actions and different timescales, and mixing them wrecks both.

carousel.title: Set intake by rules
carousel.body: Choose two or three food rules you can keep for a year — a protein floor, no drinking calories, one cooked meal a day — rather than a temporary deficit.

carousel.title: Set movement by minutes
carousel.body: Aim for a weekly total of activity you will actually hit, including strength work. Count minutes and sessions, never calories burned.

carousel.title: Review separately
carousel.body: Judge the eating plan by trend weight over months. Judge the movement plan by strength, stamina, resting heart rate and how you feel on stairs.

actions: Stop crediting yourself calories for exercise in any tracking app, and check what your intake looks like when the workout column is removed entirely.
Write down what you expect exercise to deliver, then cross out weight loss and replace it with the outcomes the evidence actually supports.
Build a weekly movement minimum you would keep even in a month where your weight did not change at all, and protect it first.
Replace one heavily processed staple in your weekly shopping with something you cook, and keep it for three months before adding another change.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a diet plan or a training programme. This is an argument about how metabolism works, with practical consequences left mostly to you.

verification.notes: Published 2021. Pontzer is an evolutionary anthropologist whose Hadza fieldwork underpins the book. The constrained total energy expenditure model is his own and remains actively debated; flagged as contested throughout. All prose original.

books.title: Eat, Move, Sleep
books.subtitle: How Small Choices Lead to Big Changes
books.author: Tom Rath
books.why_it_matters: It made the case that health is decided by hundreds of small daily choices rather than by occasional heroic ones, and it treats eating, moving and sleeping as one system instead of three separate projects.

crux.headline: Three levers, pulled daily, all pulling on each other
crux.body: Food, movement and sleep are usually tackled as separate campaigns, which is why fixing one so often collapses under the other two. They are the same system. A short night makes you hungrier and less likely to move; a day of sitting makes sleep worse; a heavy dinner does both. Improve any one of them a little and the others get easier, so the winning strategy is many small changes across all three rather than one dramatic change in a single lane.

sparks.hook: One bad night quietly rewrites tomorrow's eating and tomorrow's training.
sparks.insight: Sleep, food and movement are not three separate projects competing for your discipline. Short sleep raises appetite and lowers the odds you train. A day spent sitting makes the following night worse. A late heavy meal damages the sleep that then wrecks the next day. Because the loop runs in every direction, the cheapest place to start is whichever of the three you are currently worst at, not whichever feels most virtuous.
sparks.why: The links between short sleep, appetite regulation and reduced activity are well documented, though most of the evidence is observational and the direction of causation is not always clean.
sparks.apply: Rate your eating, movement and sleep out of ten for a week, then spend the next month improving only the lowest-scoring one.

sparks.hook: Sitting is not the new smoking, but sitting still all day is genuinely bad.
sparks.insight: Long uninterrupted sitting is associated with worse metabolic health, and the comparison to smoking gets repeated because it is punchy rather than because it is accurate. The more careful finding is that the harm shrinks considerably once total physical activity is accounted for, and that breaking sitting up matters more than the total. Standing desks are optional. Getting up regularly is the part that appears to do the work.
sparks.why: Large pooled analyses find the association between sitting time and mortality weakens substantially in people who are otherwise active. The smoking comparison is not supported by the size of the risk.
sparks.apply: Set an hourly reminder to stand and walk for two minutes during your working day, and keep it for a fortnight.

sparks.hook: The choice happens in the shop, not at the table.
sparks.insight: Willpower at dinner is a rematch you keep losing. The decision that actually determines what you eat happened days earlier, in a supermarket aisle, when you were not hungry and not tired. Whatever comes home gets eaten eventually. That makes shopping the highest-leverage twenty minutes of your food week, and it is far easier to make one good decision under fluorescent light than fifty good ones at nine in the evening.
sparks.why: Food choice is strongly shaped by availability and proximity. Removing a food from the house removes dozens of future decisions rather than one.
sparks.apply: Write a shopping list after eating, buy only from it, and decide what enters the house rather than what you resist inside it.

carousel.title: Shop fed, never hungry
carousel.body: Hunger reliably changes what goes in the trolley toward quick energy. Eat something first, even if it delays the trip by fifteen minutes.

carousel.title: Bring a written list
carousel.body: Decide at home what the week needs. A list turns fifty in-store decisions into one, made while you are calm and not being marketed to.

carousel.title: Fill the basket first
carousel.body: Put the vegetables, fruit and protein in before anything else. What goes in early takes up the room later choices would have used.

carousel.title: Guard the front door
carousel.body: Anything that comes home gets eaten by someone eventually. The decision that matters happened in the aisle, not at nine in the evening.

sparks.hook: Judge a food by what it does to you in an hour, not by its label.
sparks.insight: Marketing terms on packaging — low fat, natural, high in fibre, immune-supporting — are chosen for sales rather than for accuracy, and a product can carry several while being mostly sugar. A more useful test is how you feel and function afterwards: energy at 3pm, hunger two hours later, how the next meal goes. That is data about you specifically, and it is available for free every day.
sparks.why: Front-of-pack claims are regulated loosely enough to be near-useless as a health signal. Individual metabolic responses to the same foods also vary more than population averages suggest.
sparks.apply: For one week, note your energy and hunger two hours after lunch, and change the one lunch that consistently scores worst.

sparks.hook: Trading an hour of sleep for an hour of work is a losing exchange.
sparks.insight: The hour you take from sleep to finish something is repaid the next day with slower thinking, worse decisions and poorer mood, usually costing more than the hour bought. People are also poor judges of their own impairment when short of sleep, which is what makes the trade feel reasonable at midnight. Treating sleep as the fixed thing in a schedule, and letting work absorb the variability, is almost always the better arrangement.
sparks.why: Sleep restriction degrades attention and decision quality measurably, and self-rated impairment lags behind measured impairment, so people underestimate the cost of the hour they took.
sparks.apply: Set a fixed lights-out time and let unfinished work stay unfinished for two weeks. Judge output over the whole fortnight, not day by day.

sparks.hook: Health is not a mood problem or a Monday problem. It is a defaults problem.
sparks.insight: Motivation arrives unpredictably and leaves without notice, so anything that depends on it will run intermittently. Defaults run every day without asking. What is on the kitchen counter, what your usual lunch is, where your shoes live, when your alarm goes off: these produce almost all of your behaviour. Changing a default once is worth more than deciding well a hundred times, and it keeps working on the days you do not care.
sparks.why: Default options exert a large and repeatable influence on behaviour across domains from food to organ donation, because they operate without requiring a decision at all.
sparks.apply: Change one default this week: what is on the counter, what your standard lunch is, or where your phone charges at night.

sparks.hook: Twenty minutes of walking beats an hour of intending to go to the gym.
sparks.insight: The largest health returns come from moving people from doing nothing to doing something, not from moving fit people to doing more. A short daily walk is unglamorous and it clears the biggest hurdle in the data. It also requires no kit, no travel and no scheduling, which is why it survives busy weeks when a gym membership does not. Ambitious plans that never start lose to small plans that run.
sparks.why: Dose-response curves for activity and mortality are steepest at the low end, so the first small amount of regular movement delivers a disproportionate share of the benefit.
sparks.apply: Attach a fifteen-minute walk to an existing daily event — after lunch, after the school run — and do it whatever the weather.

sparks.hook: Who you eat with predicts what you eat better than what you know does.
sparks.insight: Portion sizes, food choices and drinking all move toward the people around the table, usually without anyone noticing. This is not weakness; it is how humans have always eaten. It means nutritional knowledge is a weak lever compared with company, and it means the practical move is social rather than educational: change one regular shared meal, or bring one person along on the walk, rather than reading another article.
sparks.why: Social influence on eating behaviour is a well-replicated finding across laboratory and field studies. People consistently deny being influenced while being influenced.
sparks.apply: Pick one recurring meal or activity you share with someone and change that one together, rather than trying to change alone.

sparks.hook: Small choices compound, which is also how people end up unwell without noticing.
sparks.insight: No single meal, missed walk or short night matters. The trouble is that none of them arrive alone. The same maths that makes a daily walk valuable over a decade makes a daily habit of sitting and snacking expensive over the same decade, and neither is visible at the scale of a week. This is why health problems feel sudden when they surface: the accumulation was silent the whole way.
sparks.why: Chronic disease risk accumulates over years of small exposures, which is precisely why it is so poorly served by short-term motivation and dramatic interventions.
sparks.apply: Pick one small choice you make daily and calculate what it looks like over a year, then decide whether that is the total you want.

sparks.hook: Score the day out of three and let a bad day stay a bad day.
sparks.insight: A simple scoreboard beats an elaborate plan. Did you eat reasonably, move at all, and sleep enough? Three answers, one number, ten seconds. The point is not accuracy — it is having a measure that is quick enough to survive and honest enough to notice a drift before it becomes a month. Aiming for good scores most days rather than perfect scores every day is the version that survives contact with real life.
sparks.why: Simple self-monitoring reliably improves adherence across behaviour change programmes, and its benefit comes from frequency and ease rather than from precision.
sparks.apply: Score today out of three tonight, then keep the count on paper for thirty days without changing anything else.

carousel.title: Define your three
carousel.body: Write one sentence each for what counts as a good eat, move and sleep day for you. Keep the bar low enough to hit on a bad week.

carousel.title: Score at night
carousel.body: One number out of three before bed, on paper or a note. Ten seconds. No app, no analysis, no explaining a low score to yourself.

carousel.title: Look weekly
carousel.body: Read the week, not the day. Three good days out of seven at the start is progress; chasing sevens produces two weeks and a quit.

carousel.title: Fix the weakest
carousel.body: Whichever of the three scores lowest across a month is your next project. Change one default in that lane and leave the other two alone.

actions: Score eating, movement and sleep out of three each night for a month, then pick your weakest lane and change exactly one default in it.
Do your food shopping from a written list after a meal, so what enters the house is decided while you are neither hungry nor tired.
Attach a fifteen-minute daily walk to something you already do every day, and protect it on the days you feel least like it.
Set a fixed lights-out time and let unfinished work wait, then judge your output across a fortnight rather than day by day.
books.not_for_you_if: You want depth, mechanism or a training programme. This is a book of short, plain nudges for people who are not going to read a physiology text.

verification.notes: Published 2013. Rath writes from a personal stake, living with a genetic cancer-predisposition condition diagnosed in his teens. The sitting-and-smoking comparison the book helped popularise is flagged here as overstated. All prose original.

books.title: Endure
books.subtitle: Mind, Body, and the Curiously Elastic Limits of Human Performance
books.author: Alex Hutchinson
books.why_it_matters: It is the fairest account of a fight that has run through exercise science for a century: whether your limit sits in the muscle or in the mind. It takes the brain seriously without turning effort into a self-help slogan.

crux.headline: Your limit is a decision your brain makes early
crux.body: You almost never stop because a muscle has physically failed. You stop because effort crosses a threshold your brain has been protecting all along, using signals from fuel, heat, oxygen and past experience to decide when enough is enough. That threshold moves. Train the body and it moves. Change what you believe, expect or feel and it moves too. Neither the pure physiology story nor the pure willpower story survives the evidence.

sparks.hook: Almost nobody collapses at the finish. They slow down first, and choose to.
sparks.insight: Watch the end of a hard race and you see people fading, not failing. Muscles that supposedly ran out of everything still have enough left for a sprint finish when a rival appears. That gap between what the body can do and what it will do is the whole subject. Something is holding a reserve back, and it responds to the situation: the distance you think is left, the person beside you, how much it hurts right now.
sparks.why: Muscle biopsies after exhausting exercise routinely show fuel still in the tank and metabolic conditions short of true failure. The stopping decision arrives before the physical ceiling does.
sparks.apply: Next hard session, note the exact moment you decide to ease off and what you were thinking. Write it down within a minute of finishing.

sparks.hook: Effort is not a measurement of your body. It is a feeling your brain issues.
sparks.insight: The single number that predicts when you stop is how hard it feels, not how hard it is. Two riders at identical power outputs can be in completely different places, because perceived effort is assembled from muscle signals, breathing, heat, fuel, mood and expectation. This is why anything that changes the feeling changes the performance, even when nothing measurable about the muscle has changed at all.
sparks.why: The psychobiological model, developed by Samuele Marcora, holds that you quit when effort feels maximal or the required effort exceeds what you are willing to give. It predicts a lot of odd results the pure physiology model cannot.
sparks.apply: Rate perceived effort out of ten at three fixed points in your next workout, then compare those ratings across weeks at the same pace.

sparks.hook: The two-hour marathon was treated as a physiological wall. It was a scheduling problem.
sparks.insight: For decades the sub-two-hour marathon looked like a hard biological limit. Then a coordinated attempt at Monza in 2017 put Eliud Kipchoge across the line in 2:00:25, with pacers, drafting and a flat closed circuit. Not a legal record, and not a normal race. But it moved the argument from whether a human could do it to what conditions were required, which is a completely different kind of question.
sparks.why: Extrapolating a limit from a record list assumes conditions stay fixed. Change shoes, pacing, course and fuelling and the extrapolation breaks, which is what happened.
sparks.apply: Take one number you treat as your personal ceiling and list the conditions it was set under. Change two of those conditions and test it again.

sparks.hook: Elite endurance athletes do not feel less pain. They argue with it differently.
sparks.insight: Tested in the lab, trained endurance athletes usually have ordinary pain thresholds — the point where a sensation first registers as painful is much the same as anyone else's. What differs is tolerance: how long they will stay with it once it hurts. That is a learned relationship, built by repeatedly going somewhere uncomfortable and coming back intact, rather than a gift of thicker nerves.
sparks.why: Studies comparing athletes and non-athletes tend to find similar thresholds but higher tolerance. Sample sizes are small and the direction of cause is unclear: training may build tolerance, or tolerant people may stay in the sport.
sparks.apply: Add one short interval each week that is deliberately uncomfortable but safe, and practise staying relaxed in the face and shoulders while it hurts.

sparks.hook: Rinse a sports drink around your mouth, spit it out, and still ride harder.
sparks.insight: Swill a carbohydrate solution for a few seconds without swallowing and short-duration performance improves anyway. There is no time for the sugar to be digested and delivered, so the effect cannot be fuel. Receptors in the mouth appear to signal incoming energy to the brain, which loosens the reins slightly. It is one of the cleanest demonstrations that the brain is regulating output on predicted supply, not just current supply.
sparks.why: The mouth-rinse effect replicates reasonably well for efforts of roughly an hour, especially when fasted, though the size of the gain is modest and it fades when you are already well fuelled.
sparks.apply: On a short fasted session, rinse a carbohydrate drink for five to ten seconds before a hard effort and compare it against your usual pacing.

sparks.hook: Thinking hard for 90 minutes makes your legs give up sooner.
sparks.insight: Give people a demanding computer task, then send them to exhaustion on a bike, and they quit earlier than a rested control group. Their hearts, muscles and oxygen use look the same. What changed is that everything felt harder from the first pedal stroke. Mental fatigue does not drain the body; it raises the price the brain charges for the same work, and the ceiling is reached at a lower output.
sparks.why: Marcora's mental-fatigue experiments have been repeated by several groups with broadly consistent results, though effect sizes vary and the mechanism is still argued over.
sparks.apply: Move your hardest training session before your most cognitively draining block of work, not after it, for the next two weeks.

carousel.title: Audit the day before
carousel.body: Note what your brain did in the four hours before a bad session. Long meetings, dense reading and decision-heavy work all count as load, even sitting down.

carousel.title: Move the hard sessions
carousel.body: Put the workouts that need real effort where your attention is freshest. For most people that is early, before the day has spent them.

carousel.title: Cut the pre-session scroll
carousel.body: Twenty minutes of rapid app switching before training is not rest. Sit still, walk, or do nothing at all instead.

carousel.title: Judge sessions in pairs
carousel.body: Compare like with like: fresh-brain sessions against other fresh-brain sessions. Otherwise you will read mental fatigue as lost fitness.

sparks.hook: You slow down in the heat before your temperature is anywhere near dangerous.
sparks.insight: In hot conditions people drop their pace early, well before core temperature reaches a genuinely risky level. The body is forecasting: at this heat, this pace, this distance, we will overheat before the finish, so we throttle now. Skin temperature and the feeling of heat drive the decision more than deep body temperature does. Cooling the skin or the mouth can lift performance without changing core temperature much at all.
sparks.why: Anticipatory pacing in the heat is well documented in both lab and field studies. The finding fits regulation by feedforward prediction rather than by a single trip switch at a fixed temperature.
sparks.apply: Before a hot session, cool your face, neck and hands with cold water for a couple of minutes, and start slower than feels necessary.

sparks.hook: Drinking to a schedule instead of to thirst is a marketing idea, not a physiological one.
sparks.insight: The advice to drink ahead of thirst, and the notion that a small percentage of body weight lost means performance falls off a cliff, both look shakier than they once did. Much of the underlying work came from studies that did not resemble real racing, and some of it was funded by companies selling drinks. Meanwhile drinking too much is genuinely dangerous, and has killed endurance athletes through diluted blood sodium.
sparks.why: Thirst-guided drinking performs about as well as fixed schedules in most field studies. Overdrinking causing low blood sodium is a documented and occasionally fatal risk, which reverses the usual advice.
sparks.apply: In your next long session, drink when you are thirsty rather than to a plan, and weigh yourself before and after to see what you actually lost.

sparks.hook: Tell someone their rival is up ahead and they find a gear that was not there.
sparks.insight: Riders racing against a video avatar of their own previous best will hold on even when the avatar has secretly been sped up slightly. Told the truth afterwards, they are surprised: they had believed they were at their limit the first time. Belief about what is possible and about how far is left both feed directly into the effort calculation. Deception works, which is exactly why the limit cannot be purely mechanical.
sparks.why: Several small deception studies show gains when athletes are misled about pace or distance, though the improvements are modest, vanish when the deception is too large, and rest on tiny samples.
sparks.apply: Run one session against a recorded version of your own previous effort rather than against a target number you set in advance.

sparks.hook: The mind matters and the body still sets the terms. Both halves are true.
sparks.insight: It is tempting to read all this as proof that limits are imaginary and grit is everything. That is not what the evidence says. Physiology sets the range within which the brain negotiates, and no amount of belief moves an untrained heart into elite territory. The practical version is unglamorous: build the machine with years of training, then work on the negotiation with pacing, fuelling, cooling, self-talk and experience.
sparks.why: The old central governor debate largely dissolved into this middle position. Treating either pole as the whole answer predicts results that do not occur in the lab or on the road.
sparks.apply: Split your next training block explicitly: one column for physical work, one for the mental and situational skills you will rehearse in it.

carousel.title: Build the base first
carousel.body: No mental technique substitutes for years of aerobic work. The negotiation only happens inside the range your training has already created.

carousel.title: Rehearse the discomfort
carousel.body: Practise the specific feeling of race pace in training so the sensation arrives as familiar information rather than as an alarm.

carousel.title: Script your self-talk
carousel.body: Decide in advance what you will say to yourself at the worst point. Motivational self-talk shows small but repeatable gains in endurance trials.

carousel.title: Control the inputs
carousel.body: Fuel, heat, hydration and mental freshness all feed the effort signal. Manage them and you shift the whole negotiation before it starts.

actions: Keep a two-column training log for a month: objective work done on one side, perceived effort and mental state on the other, then look for the sessions where they disagree.
Test one belief you hold about your own ceiling by changing the conditions around it rather than by trying harder inside the same conditions.
Practise drinking to thirst and fuelling by feel on long sessions, and stop treating fixed schedules from a bottle label as physiology.
Write a short script of what you will tell yourself at the hardest point of your next event, and rehearse it in training until it is automatic.
books.not_for_you_if: You want a training plan. This explains why limits behave the way they do and leaves the weekly schedule to somebody else.

verification.notes: Published 2018, with a foreword by Malcolm Gladwell. The Monza attempt described took place in May 2017 and was not a ratified record. Hydration and central governor material is deliberately presented as contested. All prose original.

books.title: Fast Asleep
books.subtitle: Improve Brain Function, Lose Weight, Boost Your Mood, Reduce Stress, and Become a Better Sleeper
books.author: Michael Mosley
books.why_it_matters: It put the one genuinely effective non-drug treatment for chronic insomnia — cognitive behavioural therapy — into a form an ordinary reader will actually attempt, instead of another list of bedroom tips.

crux.headline: Chasing sleep is what keeps you awake
crux.body: Chronic insomnia is usually maintained by the effort to fix it. You go to bed earlier, lie there longer, worry about the consequences, and teach your brain that the bed is a place for anxious wakefulness. The treatment that works runs the other way: spend less time in bed, not more, until sleep becomes solid, then expand. It feels wrong, it is uncomfortable for a week or two, and it has the best evidence of anything on offer.

sparks.hook: The cure for lying awake is to spend less time in bed, not more.
sparks.insight: When sleep goes badly, the instinct is to give it more room: earlier nights, later mornings, naps. That dilutes your sleep pressure across more hours and produces long stretches of frustrated wakefulness. Sleep restriction does the opposite. You compress time in bed to roughly the hours you are genuinely sleeping, build up a real drive to sleep, and only widen the window once you are sleeping through most of it.
sparks.why: Sleep restriction is a core component of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, which outperforms sleeping pills over the long term in trials and is recommended as first-line treatment.
sparks.apply: Track your actual sleep for a week, then set a fixed wake time and a bedtime that gives you only that much time in bed, with a floor of five hours.

sparks.hook: Waking in the night is normal. Believing it is a disaster is the problem.
sparks.insight: Everybody surfaces several times a night at the end of sleep cycles, and mostly does not remember it. Poor sleepers notice, check the clock, calculate how little is left and start dreading tomorrow. That reaction supplies exactly the alertness that keeps them awake. Treating a night waking as unremarkable, and refusing to look at the time, removes the fuel from the fire more reliably than any bedtime routine.
sparks.why: The cognitive half of insomnia treatment targets these catastrophic thoughts directly, and does so because arousal from worry is a documented maintainer of the disorder.
sparks.apply: Turn the clock to face the wall and remove your phone from the bedroom, so a night waking cannot be converted into a calculation.

sparks.hook: If you are awake for twenty minutes, get out of the bed.
sparks.insight: The bed should mean sleep and almost nothing else. When you lie awake in it night after night, it stops being a sleep cue and starts being a place where you worry. Stimulus control fixes this by making a simple rule: if you are clearly not sleeping, leave, go somewhere dim and dull, and return only when sleepy. It is annoying for a fortnight and then the association starts to rebuild.
sparks.why: Stimulus control is one of the best-supported behavioural components of insomnia treatment, with decades of trial evidence behind it. It works by conditioning, not willpower.
sparks.apply: Set up a chair, a dim lamp and a boring book in another room tonight, so leaving the bed at 3am requires no decisions.

carousel.title: Prepare the exit
carousel.body: Have a chair, a low lamp and something undemanding to read already waiting. Nothing bright, nothing with a screen, nothing you might want to finish.

carousel.title: Leave without checking
carousel.body: If you have clearly been awake a while, get up. Do not look at the time and do not calculate how much sleep is left.

carousel.title: Be dull on purpose
carousel.body: Read something slow in low light until your eyes get heavy. The aim is boredom, not relaxation techniques you have to perform correctly.

carousel.title: Return only when sleepy
carousel.body: Go back when you feel genuinely drowsy rather than when you feel it has been long enough. Repeat as many times as the night requires.

carousel.title: Keep the wake time
carousel.body: Get up at the same time regardless of how the night went. A fixed wake time is what rebuilds the rhythm; a lie-in undoes the whole week.

sparks.hook: Your wake time anchors the whole rhythm. Your bedtime barely does.
sparks.insight: Getting up at the same time every day, weekends included, does more for sleep than any bedtime ritual. The morning light and the fixed rise time set the clock that determines when you get sleepy roughly sixteen hours later. Sleeping in on Saturday shifts that clock later, which is why Sunday night feels like jet lag. Bedtime should be allowed to follow sleepiness; wake time should not be allowed to move.
sparks.why: Morning light and a consistent rise time are the strongest everyday inputs to circadian timing. Weekend shifts produce a documented pattern often called social jetlag.
sparks.apply: Set one alarm for the same time seven days a week for a month, and get bright light on your face within thirty minutes of it.

sparks.hook: Bad sleep and poor blood sugar control feed each other in both directions.
sparks.insight: A few nights of short sleep measurably worsens how healthy people handle glucose, and people with poor metabolic health tend to sleep worse. That makes sleep a metabolic variable, not just a comfort issue, and it is one reason improving sleep often helps appetite and cravings within days. The loop runs both ways, which is good news: intervene at either end and the other tends to follow.
sparks.why: Short-term sleep restriction reliably reduces insulin sensitivity in controlled laboratory studies. Whether improving sleep meaningfully reverses established metabolic disease is far less clear.
sparks.apply: Before changing your diet again, run two weeks of protected sleep and see what happens to your evening appetite without any other change.

sparks.hook: The bugs in your gut appear to have opinions about your sleep.
sparks.insight: Gut bacteria produce and respond to chemicals involved in mood and sleep, and populations of them follow a daily rhythm of their own. The suggestion is that feeding them better — more fibre, more plant variety, fermented foods — may improve sleep quality alongside everything else. It is a reasonable bet with a low downside, provided you hold the expectation loosely rather than treating it as established treatment.
sparks.why: The gut-sleep link in humans is early-stage, largely correlational, and nowhere near the evidence standard of the behavioural techniques. Eat more fibre for other good reasons and take any sleep benefit as a bonus.
sparks.apply: Add one more plant type to your daily food for a month — a different vegetable, pulse or seed — rather than buying a probiotic supplement.

sparks.hook: Sleeping pills buy you a night and cost you the next six months.
sparks.insight: Prescription sedatives do produce sleep in the short term. What they do not do is treat insomnia, and tolerance, dependence and rebound sleeplessness on withdrawal are common. They also change sleep architecture rather than restoring it. The behavioural treatment is slower, more irritating and takes several weeks, and it is the one that still works a year later when you are no longer doing anything.
sparks.why: Head-to-head comparisons find pills competitive in the first weeks and inferior at follow-up. Guidelines in several countries now recommend behavioural treatment first for chronic insomnia.
sparks.apply: If you are using sleep medication regularly, ask your doctor specifically about a course of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia rather than a different pill.

sparks.hook: The phone before bed is a problem because of what is on it.
sparks.insight: Screen light does suppress melatonin somewhat, but the blue-light story has been oversold and the filters and glasses sold to fix it do less than advertised. What reliably keeps you awake is the content: messages, arguments, news, work, an infinite feed engineered to hold you. The device is a stimulation delivery system first and a light source second, and the fix is the same either way — put it in another room.
sparks.why: Trials of blue-light blocking interventions show small and inconsistent effects on sleep. The arousal from engaging content is the better-supported explanation for why late phone use hurts.
sparks.apply: Charge your phone outside the bedroom and buy a cheap alarm clock, rather than installing another night-mode filter.

sparks.hook: Eight hours is an average, not a target you are failing to hit.
sparks.insight: Sleep need varies between people and shifts across a lifetime, and plenty of healthy adults do well on somewhat less than eight hours. Treating a round number as a requirement turns normal variation into a nightly test you can fail, which generates exactly the anxiety that damages sleep. The better measure is how you function: alertness in the afternoon, mood, and whether you fall asleep quickly without effort.
sparks.why: Population sleep duration is a distribution, and the observed link between duration and health outcomes is U-shaped and confounded. Chasing a fixed number is not supported by the data.
sparks.apply: Stop scoring your night with a tracker for two weeks and rate your daytime alertness out of ten at 3pm instead.

sparks.hook: Fix sleep in the order the evidence supports, not the order the shops suggest.
sparks.insight: There is a hierarchy here and most people run it backwards, starting with supplements, gadgets and mattresses and never reaching the behavioural work. The sequence that actually helps begins with a fixed wake time and morning light, then sleep restriction and stimulus control, then the worry and catastrophising, and only then the ambient details of the room. The boring steps at the top do nearly all the work.
sparks.why: This ordering follows the components of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia by strength of trial evidence. Environmental tweaks help at the margin and cannot substitute for the behavioural core.
sparks.apply: Work down the list in order and give each step three weeks before adding the next, starting with a fixed wake time this Monday.

carousel.title: Anchor the morning
carousel.body: Same wake time every day, bright light on your face soon after. This is the single highest-value change and it costs nothing.

carousel.title: Compress the window
carousel.body: Limit time in bed to roughly the hours you actually sleep, then extend by fifteen minutes a week once you are sleeping through most of it.

carousel.title: Protect the association
carousel.body: Bed is for sleep and sex only. If you are clearly awake, leave the room and come back sleepy rather than waiting it out.

carousel.title: Defuse the worry
carousel.body: Write tomorrow's concerns down before bed, and practise treating a bad night as an inconvenience rather than as evidence of a broken system.

carousel.title: Tidy the environment last
carousel.body: Cool, dark, quiet, phone elsewhere. Worth doing, but it will not rescue a sleep window and a rhythm that are still wrong.

actions: Keep a simple paper sleep diary for two weeks recording time in bed and estimated sleep, and use it to set a compressed sleep window rather than guessing.
Fix your wake time seven days a week for a month and get outdoor light within half an hour of getting up, even in winter.
Move all charging devices out of the bedroom and buy a basic alarm clock, so night wakings cannot become screen time or clock-watching.
If insomnia has lasted more than three months, ask a doctor about a structured course of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia by name.
books.not_for_you_if: You want the neuroscience of sleep rather than a treatment protocol, or you sleep well already and are looking for optimisation rather than repair.

verification.notes: Published 2020. Mosley was a medical journalist and presenter, not a sleep researcher; the strong behavioural material reflects established CBT-I evidence, while the gut microbiome and diet sections are flagged here as early-stage. All prose original.

books.title: How Not to Die
books.subtitle: Discover the Foods Scientifically Proven to Prevent and Reverse Disease
books.author: Michael Greger with Gene Stone
books.why_it_matters: It put the case for a whole-plant diet in front of a general audience with the citations attached, and tied particular foods to the particular diseases that kill most people. Disagree with the conclusions if you like; it still raised the bar for what popular nutrition writing has to show its reader.

crux.headline: Most of what kills you tracks with what you eat
crux.body: The dull, consistent finding in nutrition is that people who eat mostly whole plants get less heart disease, less type 2 diabetes and fewer of the cancers linked to diet. No food is a cure and no meal is decisive. The useful claim is narrower: a large share of the illness that ends lives early in wealthy countries sits downstream of a variable you handle three times a day. That is one of the few big risk factors you control yourself.

sparks.hook: Most of what kills people in wealthy countries is shaped by what they eat.
sparks.insight: Heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and several cancers do not fall randomly. They cluster in populations eating a particular way: heavy on refined grain, processed meat, sugar and oil, light on whole plants. That does not make food the only cause, and no single dinner decides anything. It means the largest block of early death in rich countries sits downstream of something you decide about three times a day, which is a strange thing to treat as fixed and unchangeable.
sparks.why: The link comes mostly from large observational cohorts, so it shows association rather than proof, and diet travels with income, smoking and exercise. The direction repeats across very different populations; the size of the effect for any one food does not.
sparks.apply: Pick the meal you eat most often on autopilot and rebuild it around one whole plant food - beans, lentils, oats or greens - every day for the next two weeks.

sparks.hook: Supplements keep failing the tests that the foods they came from keep passing.
sparks.insight: Find a compound that looks protective inside a food, isolate it, put it in a capsule, run a trial, and the benefit usually evaporates. Occasionally it inverts. Whole foods deliver hundreds of compounds at once, in amounts and combinations your body has met for a very long time. Pulling one out and giving it at a pharmacological dose is a completely different intervention, and it is the one that keeps coming back empty.
sparks.why: Two large trials in smokers, ATBC in Finland and CARET in the United States, found more lung cancer in the beta-carotene arms rather than less, and CARET was halted early. Outside genuine deficiency, single-nutrient pills have a poor record.
sparks.apply: Audit your supplement shelf tonight. Keep what treats a diagnosed deficiency or was prescribed, bin the speculative rest, and move that money to frozen vegetables.

sparks.hook: The cheapest thing in the shop is also one of the best-evidenced foods you can eat.
